item.title: Memorials
item.content:encoded:
Martin Persson, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

The Accounting Horizons Memorials Committee seeks nominations for memorials to be published in the journal, honoring deceased individuals who made significant contributions to accounting thought or practice. Nominees must have passed away at least 365 days before nomination.

Nominations should include a letter describing the nominee's contributions, three to five supporting letters, relevant primary source materials, and the nominee's vita or resume. All materials must be combined into a single PDF and submitted to memorials@aaahq.org.

Appel publié par Accounting Horizons. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Individuals whose work significantly advanced accounting thought
  • Individuals who revolutionized accounting practice and professional development

Timeline

  • November 30, 2026: Nomination submission deadline
  • March 1, 2027: Decisions will be announced

item.title: Advancing Entrepreneurship Science with Meta-Analysis
item.content:encoded:
This special issue seeks to advance entrepreneurship science through rigorous meta-analytic and systematic review methodologies. The call invites researchers to synthesize existing empirical findings in entrepreneurship, identifying patterns, contradictions, and knowledge gaps across the field. Meta-analyses can help consolidate fragmented research literatures and provide more robust conclusions about entrepreneurial phenomena.

The special issue is particularly interested in quantitative syntheses that examine both the drivers and outcomes of entrepreneurship, comparative assessments of different entrepreneurial approaches, and methodological innovations in applying meta-analytic techniques to entrepreneurship research. Contributions should leverage meta-analysis to advance theoretical understanding and practical knowledge in the entrepreneurship domain.

Appel publié par Journal of Business Venturing Insights. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Meta-analytic approaches to entrepreneurship research
  • Systematic reviews of entrepreneurship literature
  • Quantitative synthesis of entrepreneurship findings
  • Methodological advances in meta-analysis applied to entrepreneurship
  • Integration and reconciliation of conflicting entrepreneurship research findings
  • Meta-analyses examining antecedents and consequences of entrepreneurial behavior
  • Comparative effectiveness of entrepreneurial interventions and strategies
  • Temporal trends and evolution of entrepreneurship research

item.title: Is Progress Possible Without People? Navigating Quality of Life Between Homo Sapiens and Homo Digitalis
item.content:encoded:
This special issue examines the fundamental tension between technological progress and human welfare. It investigates whether societal advancement driven by digitalization and automation can meaningfully improve quality of life, or whether such progress may come at the expense of fundamental human values and well-being. The collection seeks scholarly work exploring the balance between homo sapiens and homo digitalis.

The issue targets researchers and practitioners interested in understanding how digitalization reshapes quality of life across social, economic, and personal dimensions. It welcomes diverse perspectives on measuring progress, evaluating technological impact on human flourishing, and envisioning sustainable development that prioritizes both innovation and human dignity.

Appel publié par Socio-Economic Planning Sciences. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • The relationship between human welfare and digital transformation

  • Socio-economic impacts of digitalization
  • Definitions and measurement of quality of life in the digital age

item.title: Advancing Project Management through Data Science: Methods, Applications, and Impacts
item.content:encoded:
This special issue examines how data science reshapes project, programme, and portfolio management practices. Rather than focusing on technical algorithmic details, it seeks to understand how managers can translate data and algorithmic insights into better decisions, governance, and value creation across the project lifecycle. The collection emphasizes managerial transformation rather than technology as an add-on.

Contributions should address how data-driven practices improve decision quality and accountability, how governance mechanisms adapt to data-intensive work, and how manager and team competencies evolve. The special issue particularly welcomes research on adoption conditions, implementation challenges, and safeguards for ethical use, bias mitigation, and transparency in decision-making.

Submissions should prioritize actionable insights for practitioners through conceptual frameworks, empirical case studies, and practical artifacts such as decision frameworks, governance templates, and maturity models. Cross-sector studies demonstrating tangible managerial outcomes and connections to organizational strategy and broader societal value are especially encouraged.

Appel publié par International Journal of Managing Projects in Business. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Data-driven decision-making in project environments: Exploring how data science enhances or transforms decision processes across the project lifecycle, including planning, monitoring, and risk management emphasizing chances, challenges and risk.
  • Integration of data science methodologies into project management practices: Studies applying or adapting methods such as machine learning, data mining, or predictive analytics to project-specific contexts.
  • Data science and project governance, ethics, and accountability: Examining the implications of algorithmic decision-making, data privacy, and ethical use of data in managing projects.
  • The evolving role of the project manager in data-rich contexts: Investigating new competencies, skills, and leadership styles required for managing data-intensive or AI-augmented projects. Discussing the relationship between project managers and data science experts in project management.
  • Real-time data, dashboards and analytics for project monitoring and control: Contributions on the design and limits, use and evaluation of real-time performance tracking and visualisation tools in project management.
  • Data ecosystems and infrastructure in large-scale or complex projects: Studies addressing the architecture, integration, and governance of data sources across distributed project networks.
  • Cross-disciplinary applications of data science in projects: Interdisciplinary work linking project management with fields such as operations research, information systems, computational social science, or engineering.
  • AI, big data and automation in project scheduling, forecasting, and resource allocation: Empirical or conceptual work on how intelligent systems are used to optimize project efficiency and adaptability.
  • Data-enabled project evaluation, benefits realisation, and impact assessment: Using data science to better measure and predict the value, outcomes, and sustainability of projects, including alignment with SDGs.
  • Theoretical and conceptual contributions linking data science and project studies: Frameworks and models that critically examine the intersection of data science and project management as evolving disciplines.
  • AI-empowered stakeholder engagement in large-scale or complex projects: Leveraging AI to enhance stakeholder analysis, communication, and collaboration in complex projects, optimizing engagement strategies and improving project outcomes through predictive insights and automated interaction tools.

item.title: Benchmarking Adaptive Supply Chains: Performance Metrics, Maturity Models, and Socio-Technical Configurations
item.content:encoded:
Aamir Rashid, City University of New York

Rizwana Rasheed, City University of New York

Organizations face ongoing disruptions and must adapt their supply chains while managing sustainability and digital transformation. However, there is limited frameworks for measuring and comparing adaptive supply chain performance across different organizations and contexts. This special issue seeks to advance research that uses benchmarking logic to systematically evaluate how well supply chains adapt.

The special issue emphasizes understanding adaptive performance through the interaction of people, technology, governance, and sustainability practices. Rather than treating adaptation as a general concept, research should operationalize adaptability with measurable constructs and benchmarking frameworks that highlight performance differences between configurations.

Contributions should employ rigorous comparative designs using quantitative, qualitative, or mixed methods to benchmark adaptive supply chains across industries and countries. By identifying which configurations perform better and under what conditions, the research will provide actionable insights for practitioners and policymakers.

Appel publié par Benchmarking: An International Journal. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Benchmarking adaptive supply chain performance across industries and regions

  • Performance frontiers and efficiency analysis of adaptive supply chains
  • Cross-country and institutional benchmarking of supply chain adaptability
  • Governance, collaboration, and coordination as benchmarked performance drivers

item.title: Beyond AI Adoption: People Management, Work Design and Sustainable Performance in AI-Enabled Organisations
item.content:encoded:
AI systems are increasingly used in HR functions such as recruitment, employee analytics, training, performance management and workforce planning. While organizations often expect these systems to improve efficiency and fairness, they raise concerns about transparency, employee wellbeing, job quality and whether such systems genuinely enhance organizational performance. This special issue shifts focus from simply whether organizations adopt AI to how AI-enabled HR systems should be designed, governed and experienced to benefit employees and organizational effectiveness.

The special issue examines the relationship between AI-enabled HR practices and sustainable organizational performance, considering both potential benefits and risks. It invites research exploring when and how AI strengthens or undermines work quality, fairness, employee voice, inclusion and capability development. The collection addresses emerging regulatory interest from bodies like the OECD and EU AI Act, which recognize that AI in employment decisions requires responsible governance.

Appel publié par Journal of Organizational Effectiveness: People and Performance. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • AI-enabled recruitment, selection and fair access to work: How AI screening, automated assessments, candidate ranking, video interviews and people analytics affect fairness, validity, transparency, accessibility and selection outcomes.
  • AI-supported training, development and capability building: How AI-enabled learning systems, skills analytics, career platforms and talent systems affect reskilling, development access, career visibility and employee capability.
  • AI-enabled performance management, monitoring and evaluation: How algorithmic monitoring, datafication and AI-supported appraisal affect fairness, trust, employee agency, wellbeing, reasonable adjustment and performance outcomes.
  • Work design, job quality and employee voice in AI-enabled workplaces: How AI changes autonomy, workload, coordination, meaningful work, participation, consultation and human oversight in people-management decisions.
  • Inclusion, disability, governance and sustainable organisational effectiveness: How organisations design AI-enabled HRM systems that reduce bias, support EDI, protect disabled workers and applicants, strengthen trust and contribute to sustainable organisational performance.

item.title: Beyond Black and White – Shades of Grey Leadership
item.content:encoded:
Anders Örtenblad, University of Agder

Louise Boulter, Lincoln Bishop University

Nilupulee Liyanagamage, University of Wollongong

Horia Moașa, Transilvania University of Brasov

This special issue examines grey leadership, a phenomenon occupying the spectrum between constructive and destructive leadership practices. Grey leadership encompasses ambiguous and contested behaviors that are neither clearly beneficial nor overtly harmful—such as subtle rule-bending, enabling harmful dynamics through inaction, or normalizing problematic conduct. These behaviors often escape clear moral judgment or legal consequences yet significantly impact organizational relationships and culture.

The concept integrates ethical, emotional, and contextual dimensions of leadership by recognizing mixed moral intent, inconsistent values signaling, and situationally contingent consequences. Grey leadership serves as a conceptual bridge across fragmented leadership literatures, revealing how contradictions in intent, signals, and outcomes interact dynamically within specific contexts and are negotiated through relational processes.

Appel publié par Leadership & Organization Development Journal. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: China and Fragile Countries: Investment, Initiatives, and Impact
item.content:encoded:
This special issue examines China's multifaceted engagement in fragile countries characterized by weak institutions, limited state capacity, and insecurity. The focus encompasses Chinese foreign direct investment, corporate initiatives, and government-level activities aimed at development and peacebuilding, from the "Going Out" period through the Belt and Road Initiative era to present-day involvement in conflict mediation and UN peacekeeping operations.

The collection seeks to advance understanding of how Chinese actors—including state-owned and privately-owned enterprises as well as government agencies—approach development and peace in fragile settings. Particular attention is given to the environmental and social impacts of these initiatives, how they differ from Western approaches, and how they interact with existing international frameworks and local contexts.

Appel publié par Society and Business Review. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Contexts: What are the types of contexts where Chinese organizations are active in social investments and initiatives for development and peace?
  • Strategies and modes: How do Chinese enterprises, including State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs) and Privately-Owned Enterprises (POEs), function as agents of development, peace and stability? How do the strategies and activities of Chinese POEs differ compared to SOEs as far as these activities are concerned?
  • Collaborations and alliances: How do Chinese enterprises collaborate with non-Chinese organizations in fragile settings?
  • Links to IGOs: How does China interact with Inter-Governmental Organizations (IGOs), such as the UN Peacebuilding Commission (PBC), Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs (DPPA), and Department of Peace Operations (DPO)? What role do IGOs play in facilitating social investment and initiatives by Chinese enterprises?
  • Contrasts to Western models: To what extent do the actions and impact of Chinese organizations in fragile settings necessitate a redefinition of development initiative, and how does its meaning differ compared to Western notions, such as that of 'liberal peace'?
  • Local and hybrid models: Beyond the "liberal vs. developmental" paradigms comparison, how do Chinese practices in fragile settings interact with existing international and local frameworks? Are we witnessing the emergence of hybrid models in countries where both Chinese and Western countries are active?

item.title: Crafting Shape in a Fluid World – The Intersection of Marketing and External Forces
item.content:encoded:
Marketing practice is being transformed by technological advances, geopolitical shifts, economic pressures, and growing demands for sustainability and social responsibility. Retail environments serve as key sites where these transformations unfold, with both physical and digital channels becoming laboratories for new consumer engagement and adaptive strategies. Consumers now demand greater brand ethics, transparency, and societal contributions, while external disruptions like supply chain fragility, inflation, and geopolitical tensions reshape pricing and sourcing. Simultaneously, artificial intelligence and platform ecosystems are fundamentally changing how consumers access information and make purchase decisions.

Appel publié par Journal of Consumer Marketing. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • How to enhance responsible consumption (e.g., reducing food waste and increasing adoptions of green energy and public transportation)
  • How to serve marginalized and disadvantaged consumers and enhance equality among gender, race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status through marketing and equitable practices

item.title: Developing Management Capability in Sustainability Leadership
item.content:encoded:
Scott Lichtenstein, Birmingham City University Business School

The focus spans macro outcomes related to compassionate flourishing and planetary health, meso-level organizational and community goals, and micro-level personal values and behavioral inputs of managers. Through contributions from diverse scholars, the special issue will examine how sustainability leadership capability can serve as a positive force in addressing global challenges, how it can be applied systematically within organizations and communities, and how managers' personal values and morals translate into sustainable behaviors and decisions. item.title: Doing Entrepreneurship at the Margins: Qualitative Insights
item.content:encoded:
While quantitative, positivist approaches have traditionally dominated entrepreneurship research, they often fail to capture the lived experiences of marginalized entrepreneurs who remain underrepresented in scholarship despite their significant contributions to local economies. Qualitative research is better suited to exploring the meanings, practices, and organizing processes that hypothesis-driven designs typically obscure.

This special issue invites qualitative research that examines entrepreneurship at the margins as a site for theory-building. The focus encompasses marginalized entrepreneurs across gender, race, migration, disability, age, and Indigenous contexts, particularly in Global South settings where research access challenges are compounded by institutional barriers and epistemic dominance of Global North perspectives.

Contributions should treat marginality as an analytical lens rather than merely a research setting, bringing together reflexive scholarship that advances cumulative qualitative understanding of entrepreneurship as organizing while exploring core themes of power, inequality, agency, legitimacy, and meaning-making.

Appel publié par Qualitative Research in Organizations and Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Financial inclusion strategies, technology, and risk management: emerging trends and global perspectives
item.content:encoded:
Juan Piñeiro Chousa, Santiago de Compostela University

Financial systems face evolving risks from climate change, digitalisation, and new financial ecosystems that challenge existing supervision and policy frameworks. Advanced technologies like artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and satellite systems enhance risk identification and monitoring, yet introduce new technological and cybersecurity threats. Sustainable finance and financial inclusion have emerged as instruments for managing long-term risks and strengthening financial system resilience, though questions persist regarding data quality and greenwashing.

This special issue seeks theoretical and empirical research examining the challenges and opportunities arising from the convergence of technology, sustainability, and financial inclusion. Contributions should adopt financial and risk management perspectives, with particular interest in studies addressing implications for financial stability, prudential supervision, and public policy design.

item.title: From theory to impact – how do organizations benefit from systems research?
item.content:encoded:
This special issue seeks research demonstrating how organizations apply systems theory and cybernetics to create tangible impact. Rather than focusing solely on theoretical development, the issue invites contributions showing practical benefits across management, education, engineering, and other domains where formal systems approaches are relevant. Diverse article types are welcomed, including case studies, practitioner papers, viewpoints, and technical reports, allowing authors to present their work in varied formats while maintaining clear arguments supported by suitable evidence.

The special issue addresses academia's responsibility to engage with grand societal challenges and sustainable development goals. Systems theory and cybernetics offer tools for understanding complex dynamics beyond simplistic solutions, enabling more comprehensive approaches to contemporary problems. Submissions examining applications in the Global South and Eastern Hemisphere, particularly those providing firsthand evidence of systems research's effectiveness in these contexts, are especially encouraged.

item.title: Green HRM in the Global South: Establishing Sustainability, Responsible Transformations, and Resilient Organizational Development
item.content:encoded:
Green HRM (GHRM) integrates environmental responsibility into HR practices and procedures, enabling organizations to achieve sustainability goals while transforming employees into sustainability advocates. However, most GHRM research originates from the Global North, leaving implementation in the Global South—Latin America, Africa, Asia, and the Middle East—insufficiently studied and scattered across specific contexts.

This gap in scholarship risks producing GHRM frameworks disconnected from the socioeconomic and institutional realities of Global South countries. The special issue seeks to address this by inviting conceptual papers, empirical research, and scholarly discussions that examine how GHRM can advance sustainability, social justice, and economic stability in resource-constrained environments while exploring the unique obstacles and opportunities for GHRM adoption in Global South organizations.

Appel publié par International Journal of Organizational Analysis. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Contextualizing GHRM in the Global South (i.e. the adoption of GHRM, implementation barriers, contribution to sustainability)
  • GHRM and work outcomes in the Global South (i.e. the effect of GHRM on green and non-green individual and organizational outcomes)
  • How GHRM can enhance staff well-being in informal staffing settings (i.e. the relationship between GHRM and workplace happiness, job security, and inclusive practices of staffing, etc.)
  • GHRM in sector-specific context in the Global South (i.e. manufacturing, IT, higher education, hospitality, etc.)
  • National perspectives of GHRM in the Global South (i.e. how GHRM can facilitate effective economic transitions given the frequent scarcity of the resources and climate vulnerability)
  • Leadership, organizational culture, management commitment to sustainable practices (how the aforementioned factors can shape GHRM practices in contexts where pro-environmental values may be nascent)
  • GHRM and Organizational Resilience in the Global South (i.e. why and how GHRM can serve as a tool that contributes to organizational resilience in the light of environmental and operational disruptions)
  • The role of AI and digital transformation in enabling GHRM in the Global South
  • Success stories and case studies of organizations that pioneered the implementation of GHRM in the Global South

Timeline

  • November 30, 2026: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: Immersive Technologies and Sensory Service Experiences: Redefining the Customer Journey and Value Creation in the Age of AI
item.content:encoded:
This special issue examines how immersive technologies like virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality are transforming service experiences by enabling multisensory digital environments. The focus is on understanding how visual, auditory, haptic, olfactory, and gustatory cues interact within these environments to shape customer perception and behavior across different stages of the customer journey.

Research on sensory marketing demonstrates that consumers process sensory information through cross-modal interactions rather than in isolation. While immersive technologies hold significant potential for creating rich multisensory experiences, existing research has primarily focused on audio-visual features, leaving a gap in understanding how diverse sensory stimuli collectively influence customer perceptions and value creation throughout their journey.

Appel publié par Journal of Service Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Sensory-enabled immersive service experiences across the customer journey
  • Multisensory cue interaction and cross-modal congruence in immersive services
  • Role of immersive technologies, including VR, AR, and MR, as strategic service touchpoints
  • AI-enabled adaptation, personalization, and orchestration of multisensory stimuli
  • Generative AI and learning systems in immersive service design and delivery
  • Customer perceptions, emotions, intentions, and real behaviors in immersive services
  • Value creation and value co-creation through multisensory immersive services

  • December 15, 2026: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: Industry 5.0-driven Product Lifecycle Management: toward human-centric, sustainable, and resilient manufacturing
item.content:encoded:
Romeo Bandinelli, University of Florence

Monica Rossi, Politecnico di Milano

Claudio Sassanelli, Politecnico di Bari

Virginia Fani, Universitas Mercatorum

This special issue addresses how Product Lifecycle Management systems must evolve to support Industry 5.0's three foundational principles: human-centricity, sustainability, and resilience. Traditional PLM systems, designed primarily for data integration and process efficiency, lack mechanisms to support operator well-being, embed circular economy strategies, ensure regulatory compliance, or enable rapid adaptation during disruptions.

The special issue introduces PLM 5.0 as a strategic governance platform that integrates lifecycle data, human interaction, sustainability metrics, and adaptive decision-making across industrial ecosystems. It seeks conceptual, empirical, methodological, and case-based contributions that explore how PLM systems should be redesigned, how organizations can integrate circular economy principles, what governance frameworks are needed, and how manufacturing can build resilience through lifecycle management.

Appel publié par Journal of Manufacturing Technology Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Sustainable Lifecycle Assessment and Net-Zero Strategies
  • Resilient Manufacturing and Adaptive Lifecycle Management
  • Governance, Interoperability, and Data Management Frameworks
  • Decision-Support and Managerial Transformation
  • Sector-Specific Applications with Cross-Industry Implications

item.title: Knowledge-enhanced Large Language Models for Web Information Systems in Health and Education
item.content:encoded:
Weimin Li, Shanghai University

Healthcare and education systems increasingly rely on complex, knowledge-intensive web platforms generating large-scale heterogeneous data. While Large Language Models excel at natural language understanding and human-computer interaction, directly applying general-purpose LLMs to these domains faces significant challenges including factual accuracy, lack of domain knowledge representation, and insufficient interpretability needed for sensitive applications.

Knowledge-enhanced LLMs address these limitations by incorporating structured knowledge, Web semantics, and multimodal representations into language models. This approach improves reliability, explainability, and controllability while enabling better integration with existing system components such as data retrieval and information management modules. The special issue seeks high-quality research on theoretical models, methods, frameworks, and applications of knowledge-enhanced LLMs specifically designed for healthcare and education web services.

Appel publié par International Journal of Web Information Systems. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Knowledge-enhanced LLM architectures for Web information systems
  • Knowledge graphs, ontologies, and Web semantics for LLM reasoning and generation

  • Web knowledge mining, information extraction, and knowledge integration for LLM-based systems
  • Multimodal knowledge representation and fusion for health and learning applications on the Web
  • Trustworthy, explainable, and privacy-preserving LLMs for sensitive Web environments
  • LLM-enhanced medical information retrieval, health question answering, and decision support
  • LLM-enhanced personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, automated assessment, and learning feedback
  • Agentic LLMs and AI agents for Web-based health and education service management
  • Benchmarks, datasets, evaluation metrics, and real-world applications of knowledge-enhanced LLMs in Web information systems

item.title: Leadership and Governance in Complex Learning Systems: Risk, Knowledge and Entrepreneurship
item.content:encoded:
Enis Elezi, University of Westminster

Knowledge-intensive organisations face mounting complexity from resource constraints, digitalisation, accountability demands, and geopolitical pressures. Existing research on these challenges remains fragmented across disciplinary silos and often lacks systemic understanding of how these institutions observe, interpret and respond to complexity.

This special issue integrates typically isolated scholarly conversations about leadership, governance, risk, knowledge and entrepreneurship within a cybernetic framework. It explores the interconnected processes of observation, communication, decision and learning that enable organisations to adapt and remain viable across sectors including universities, health systems, research institutes and public agencies.

Appel publié par Kybernetes. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Leadership and governance as systemic architectures of observation, decision and learning
  • Enterprise-wide risk management, knowledge management and entrepreneurship as interconnected cybernetic processes
  • Cross-sector analyses of universities, health systems, research institutes, public agencies and professional service firms as complex learning systems
  • Reflexive and second-order perspectives on how organisations construct and revise their own governance arrangements
  • Theory-as-method applications using cybernetics, systems thinking or complexity frameworks

item.title: Lifestyle Entrepreneurship: Challenges, Innovations, and Community Impact
item.content:encoded:
Lifestyle entrepreneurship represents a growing but fragmented research area that extends beyond traditional profit-maximization approaches to encompass quality of life, personal fulfillment, and work-life balance. These entrepreneurs prioritize autonomy and alignment with personal values while establishing ventures often in tourism, hospitality, crafts, and creative sectors, frequently in rural or low-density areas where they contribute to local economic development and cultural preservation.

Despite increasing recognition of its significance, existing research lacks an integrated perspective examining both entrepreneur characteristics and their operational ecosystems. Lifestyle entrepreneurs face persistent challenges including financial instability, seasonal market dependence, and insufficient institutional support, while contextual factors such as social networks, public policies, and cultural influences significantly shape their business structures and community interactions.

Appel publié par Journal of Enterprising Communities: People and Places in the Global Economy. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Profile of lifestyle entrepreneurs: sociodemographic characteristics, values and experiences
  • Motivations for lifestyle entrepreneurship: sense of belonging (roots) to the territory, maintaining the culture and traditions of the territory, quality of life, self-fulfillment, balance between personal and professional life
  • Contextual factors: impact of social networks, public policies, local entrepreneurial ecosystems and socioeconomic environment
  • Challenges faced: financial instability, lack of institutional support, technological and market barriers, lack of qualified human resources
  • Impact of lifestyle entrepreneurship on local development: job creation, stimulation of the circular economy and contribution to sustainability
  • Resilience and adaptation strategies: innovative and sustainable solutions adopted by entrepreneurs in territories
  • Comparative case studies between different regions and sectors

item.title: Management in Emerging, Developing, and Transition Economies: Context, Mechanisms, and Outcomes
item.content:encoded:
Most management research has been developed in Western contexts, leaving significant gaps in understanding leadership and organizational practices in emerging, developing, and transition economies—regions that now generate nearly half of global economic output. These economies operate under distinct institutional conditions where formal institutions are incomplete or unevenly enforced, requiring firms to rely on alternative coordination mechanisms and making context a primary determinant of business strategy and performance.

This special issue addresses this literature gap by centering emerging, developing, and transition economies as objects of theoretical inquiry rather than control variables. It invites studies across governance, entrepreneurship, sustainability, and leadership that examine how management practices evolve, adapt, or are translated when formal rules and infrastructures cannot be taken for granted. The call welcomes quantitative surveys, experiments, qualitative ethnographies, mixed-methods research, and conceptual work, particularly comparative studies spanning regions or contrasting different institutional settings.

Appel publié par Baltic Journal of Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How and with what consequences do firms substitute private or community governance for missing or unreliable formal institutions, and which mechanisms make these substitutes durable or fragile?
  • Which configurations of resources, networks, and legitimacy enable opportunity discovery and scaling in thin or nascent markets, and how do founders and top managers navigate uncertainty and institutional gaps across growth stages?
  • Under resource constraints and uneven enforcement, what capability bundles allow firms to align environmental initiatives with competitive outcomes, and how do local cultural or state priorities shape these trajectories?
  • How do reporting, budgeting, and control systems adapt when enforcement is uneven, and what are the implications for investment, innovation, market signals, and stakeholder trust in emerging markets?
  • How do contextual communication and power structures condition the effectiveness of leadership, employee voice, engagement, and performance systems in transition settings, and what are the boundary conditions for transferability?
  • How do commitments to learning and open innovation translate into performance when institutions are in flux, and which organisational routines, such as bricolage, mediate these effects?
  • How do political ties, state ownership, or party networks shape strategic decision-making, board dynamics, and accountability in firms and hybrid organisations operating under volatile or contested regulatory regimes?
  • How do gender, ethnicity, and other social cleavages intersect with institutional voids to shape leadership careers, informal influence, and patterns of inclusion and exclusion inside organisations?
  • In conflict-affected, fragile, or post-disaster settings, which leadership practices and governance arrangements enable organisational resilience, continuity of services, and recovery, and what trade-offs do they imply?
  • How do regional, cross-border, or diaspora networks among managers, professionals, and researchers mediate the transfer, translation, and contestation of management ideas and leadership models across institutional contexts?

Timeline

  • January 4, 2027: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: Meaning, Meaningfulness, and Purpose at Work: Towards Conceptual Clarity and Integration
item.content:encoded:
Mirit K. Grabarski, Lakehead University

Galina Boiarintseva, Niagara University

Maria Hameed Khan, Queensland University of Technology

This special issue addresses the interconnected but conceptually distinct notions of meaning, meaningfulness, and purpose in work contexts. While meaning relates to personal interpretations and values alignment, meaningfulness encompasses the emotional and experiential aspects of work fulfillment, and purpose refers to long-term direction and self-transcendent goals. The special issue seeks to clarify these constructs and their relationships to advance theoretical understanding of human fulfillment at work.

The collection welcomes empirical and theoretical research examining how workers assign meaning to their roles, experience fulfillment through work, and pursue purposeful careers. The focus extends across diverse occupational contexts and considers how meaning and purpose sustain over time and interact with broader life considerations, technological change, and the concept of decent work.

item.title: Nordic Consumer Culture
item.content:encoded:
The Nordic region exhibits a distinctive consumer culture marked by paradoxes: societies balance egalitarian values with status-consciousness, individualism with collective welfare systems, and modesty with aspiration. The Nordic welfare state uniquely aligns state and individual interests, creating a distinctive marketplace. Despite growing research examining Nordic consumption patterns—from branding and cultural phenomena to alternative food markets and immigrant experiences—significant gaps remain in understanding how these contradictions manifest across consumption practices and market formations.

This special issue seeks to advance comprehensive scholarship on Nordic consumer culture by publishing novel and critically grounded research that explores the interplay between state, market, and consumer practices. The editors welcome contributions analyzing market dynamics, investigating paradoxes inherent in Nordic consumption, and examining how macro-level contexts including welfare policies, cultural myths, and political ideologies shape consumer behavior, with particular interest in innovative methodologies and interdisciplinary approaches.

Appel publié par Qualitative Market Research. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Observing Intimacies: System-Theoretical Analyses of Love Relationships Today
item.content:encoded:
Intimate relationships have undergone significant transformations globally, with relationship ideals and forms becoming increasingly diverse across commitment types, duration, and organization. This special issue aims to advance knowledge production by promoting observational rather than normative approaches to intimacies, encouraging data-driven scholarship that moves beyond polarized public debates about relationships.

The issue revitalizes Luhmann's systems theory approach to intimate relationships and love as communication media in modern societies. It invites scholars to apply systems-theoretical concepts to examine contemporary transformations of intimate life across different sociocultural contexts, bridging gaps between geographically or culturally isolated scholarly conversations.

Contributions may adopt two perspectives: analyzing intimate systems through systems theory concepts and examining how other social systems (law, politics, media, education) observe and shape intimacies. The special issue welcomes diverse empirical work grounded in theoretical frameworks, particularly from varied sociocultural environments.

item.title: Observing the Future: Systems Theory Meets Science Fiction
item.content:encoded:
This special issue bridges systems theory and science fiction criticism to analyze speculative narratives as models of complex social systems. The editors argue that while science fiction commonly receives sociological interpretation, systematic application of Niklas Luhmann's theory and second-order cybernetics to the genre remains underexplored. The collection seeks to demonstrate how science fiction uniquely simulates social dynamics, including autopoiesis, operational closure, and functional differentiation, addressing contemporary concerns around artificial intelligence, fragmented discourse, and interconnected systems.

Appel publié par Kybernetes. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Investigations into the 'hypertrophy' of social subsystems (e.g., totalitarization of politics, economization of life) and dedifferentiation in utopian and dystopian literature
  • The emergence of non-human communicative systems, including Artificial Intelligence and alien consciousness, and their structural coupling with human society
  • Science fiction as a specific function of the art system, allowing society to observe its own evolution, paradoxes, and latent possibilities
  • Systems-theoretic readings of ecological crisis, the environment, and global interdependencies in speculative fiction
  • Examining the fragmentation of public discourse, 'echo chambers,' and the breakdown of communication through the lens of SF narratives

item.title: People at the Heart of Projectification: Rethinking Agency, Identity, and Value Creation
item.content:encoded:
Projectification—the embedding of project logic across organizations, public sectors, and society—has fundamentally transformed how work is organized. While this shift has been widely documented, scholarly attention has predominantly focused on systemic and organizational dimensions, often overlooking the human experience. This special issue seeks to redress this imbalance by centering individuals and their experiences within projectification processes.

The issue invites interdisciplinary contributions exploring how people exercise agency, construct identity, and create value within projectified contexts. It addresses researchers and practitioners interested in understanding the lived experiences of those who shape, participate in, or are affected by projectification across educational, occupational, cultural, and geographical contexts.

Appel publié par International Journal of Managing Projects in Business. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do individuals implement and negotiate their agency in the context of increasing projectification by navigating between structure, temporality, and autonomy?
  • How do individuals build and maintain their identities amid the fluidity and temporality of projectified work in a complex social environment?
  • How do people co-create and redefine value through their participation in - and contribution to - the ongoing projectification in our society?
  • What role do projects play in the development of people, from childhood to old age? Is there any difference between personal and occupational development?
  • How do different levels of education and educational opportunities affect people's participation in projects and projectification?
  • What expectations, aspirations, and objectives do individuals pursue through their involvement in projects, project management, and projectification?
  • What impact (positive and/or negative) does engagement in projects - as temporary endeavors - have on the people involved?
  • Which prerequisites have to be created by organizations, government, or society so that people engage in projects and turn them into success stories?
  • How much projectification can people tolerate, or is there a point at which over-projectification is reached and de-projectification starts?
  • How do cultural factors affect people's involvement in projects and projectification?
  • What are the main differences in projectification across the globe, and how does it influence individuals involved or eager to enter the project world?
  • To what extent is the use of professional project management beneficial or detrimental to the implementation of projects in the different areas of society?

item.title: Reducing Administrative Burdens: Strategies, Stakeholders, and Impact
item.content:encoded:
Matthias Döring, University of Southern Denmark

Ayesha Masood, Lahore University of Management Sciences

Johan Sandén, Södertörn University

Administrative burdens—the learning, compliance, and psychological costs citizens face when interacting with government—have become a significant research area. These burdens disproportionately affect vulnerable groups and threaten administrative equity, particularly in welfare systems. Scholars are increasingly investigating strategies to reduce or mitigate these burdens, including fostering citizen resources through intermediaries and improving organizational design and communication practices.

This special issue seeks contributions examining burden-reduction initiatives undertaken by various actors across different contexts and levels of governance. It welcomes research investigating how public organizations, managers, and street-level bureaucrats can reduce administrative burdens, which interventions are effective, whether they benefit all groups equally, and how burden-reduction efforts are perceived within public administration. The issue aims to generate societal impact by addressing challenges relevant to practitioners and policymakers working to reduce administrative burdens.

Appel publié par International Journal of Public Sector Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Digital initiatives to reduce burdens, including algorithms, automation, and AI
  • How burden-reduction initiatives are initiated and defined - and by whom

  • How do street-level bureaucrats perceive, avoid, or create burden reduction strategies?
  • How do different types of intermediaries (private companies vs. NGOs vs. public intermediaries) support citizens in their attempt to overcome burdens?
  • The relationship between burden-reduction interventions and social inequalities
  • What is the relationship between leadership and the responsiveness to burden reduction strategies?
  • The interplay between bureaucratization and administrative processes in producing burdens
  • How do administrative reforms affect administrative burden?
  • Which role do burden reduction strategies play in the political debate? Is there a connection to political action?
  • The materiality of burden reduction, administrative burdens, and responses.

item.title: Reimaging Entrepreneurship Education in the Era of Disruptive Emerging Technologies
item.content:encoded:
Entrepreneurship education must adapt to rapid technological change, as emerging innovations like AI, blockchain, and immersive platforms are fundamentally transforming how entrepreneurs identify opportunities, develop prototypes, and scale businesses. While these technologies offer unprecedented pedagogical potential through simulations and gamified learning, many educational programs continue using traditional, Western-centric approaches that prioritize information delivery over experiential learning.

This special issue addresses the urgent need to critically examine how entrepreneurship education can effectively integrate emerging technologies while remaining responsive to the entrepreneurial realities students will face. The issue is particularly relevant for emerging economies, where digital tools can overcome infrastructure limitations and resource constraints to democratize access to quality entrepreneurship education, though success requires institutional capacity building, thoughtful curriculum design, and supporting policies.

Appel publié par Journal of Entrepreneurship in Emerging Economies. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Emerging Technologies in Entrepreneurship Education - Application of AI, VR/AR, blockchain, and IoT in entrepreneurship teaching; effectiveness of technology integration in resource-limited settings; impact of digital tools on student engagement and learning outcomes; role of gamification and simulation in developing entrepreneurial competencies
  • Institutional Integration and Capacity Building - Organizational capabilities enabling technology adoption; leadership and faculty preparedness; university-industry collaboration models; digital infrastructure development; government policies and regulatory frameworks; creating entrepreneurial ecosystems beyond traditional classrooms
  • Curriculum Design and Assessment Innovation - Assessment methods for technology-integrated learning environments; addressing generative AI in student evaluation; metrics for measuring impact on learning outcomes and business creation; longitudinal studies on career development; cost-effectiveness evaluation; educator training and professional development models

item.title: Research with Impact: Qualitative approaches to social and behaviour change
item.content:encoded:
This special issue seeks to demonstrate how qualitative and interpretive research can drive meaningful social and behavioural change, particularly for underrepresented and marginalised groups. Rather than relying solely on quantitative metrics, the collection aims to show how deep qualitative inquiry uncovers the psychological and cultural factors that shape human behaviour and can inform ethical, inclusive interventions that address complex social problems.

The call reflects growing recognition that qualitative research must evolve to engage participatory and inclusive frameworks, especially when working with neurodivergent, trauma-affected, and marginalised populations. The special issue responds to an urgent need for research methodologies that empower rather than merely study neglected communities, drawing on approaches such as netnography and community-led participatory methods to create transformative social impact.

Appel publié par Qualitative Market Research. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Rethinking Entrepreneurial Finance: Multidisciplinary Perspectives in a Transforming Financial Landscape
item.content:encoded:
Enrico Battisti, University of Turin

Francesco Schiavone, University Parthenope

Digital transformation, artificial intelligence, and sustainability pressures are reshaping how entrepreneurs access capital and how value is created and financed. These changes have created new financing mechanisms while raising questions about equity and access to funding for small businesses and startups, particularly regarding collateral, legitimacy, and institutional visibility.

The special issue addresses emerging financing channels such as crowdfunding, peer-to-peer lending, and tokenized assets, while emphasizing that financial decisions are influenced by behavioral, social, institutional, and sustainability factors beyond technical considerations. Artificial intelligence is a key focus, as it transforms credit evaluation, investment screening, and venture creation, affecting SMEs' access to finance and requiring interdisciplinary approaches.

item.title: Rethinking Local Government Financial Management and Accountability through Comparative Perspectives
item.content:encoded:
Emanuele Padovani, University of Bologna

Christine Martell, University of Colorado Denver

Sungho Park, University of Alabama

Eric Scorsone, University of Virginia

Local governments play a crucial role in public service delivery and resource management, yet their financial management and accountability have traditionally been studied within national frameworks. Recent cross-national initiatives have made internationally comparable data more accessible, though existing analyses primarily focus on macroeconomic perspectives rather than managerial and operational dimensions at the individual local government level. This special issue seeks to advance understanding of how local governments manage finances and ensure accountability across different national and institutional contexts.

item.title: Revisiting theoretical pillars of HRM in the age of uncertainty: Contributions for performance
item.content:encoded:
Organizations face unprecedented challenges from uncertainty, technological change, and shifting work arrangements. This special issue calls for researchers to revisit fundamental HRM theories and examine whether established assumptions adequately explain the relationship between people, organizations, and performance in today's turbulent context. The issue seeks to move beyond incremental complexity by returning to core concepts and critically assessing whether traditional perspectives on HRM-strategy alignment, employee development, and performance outcomes remain sufficient.

The special issue welcomes theoretically grounded and methodologically rigorous contributions that challenge conventional HRM wisdom and propose new understandings relevant to uncertain environments. Research may address tensions and unintended consequences of HRM practices, sustainability concerns, digitalization, employee well-being, and emerging employment models. Empirical studies, conceptual papers, and literature reviews are all welcome, provided they offer clear advances to HRM theory and research.

item.title: Sustainable Paths in Digital Supply Chains: Navigating Environmental Challenges and Technological Frontiers
item.content:encoded:
Harshad Sonar, Indian Institute of Management Sambalpur

Bishal Dey Sarkar, Indian Institute of Management Bodhgaya

Sandeep Jagtap, Lund University

Hana Trollman, University of Leicester

This special issue examines how digital technologies can be integrated with sustainability objectives in modern supply chains. Organizations are increasingly pressured to reduce environmental impacts and ensure ethical operations while managing technological disruption. The issue explores how emerging tools like artificial intelligence, blockchain, and data analytics can enhance supply chain transparency, efficiency, emissions monitoring, and resilience while addressing climate risks and regulatory demands.

The collection seeks empirical, conceptual, and methodological contributions that bridge theory and practice in digital sustainability transitions. It recognizes that technological adoption alone is insufficient; successful transformation requires supportive leadership, training, and organizational culture change. The special issue draws on multiple theoretical perspectives to provide comprehensive understanding of how human and organizational factors influence sustainability-driven digitalization across different organizational contexts.

item.title: Sustainable Strategic Knowledge Management in the Era of AI
item.content:encoded:
Organizations face increasing complexity from shifting geopolitical, economic, and technological conditions, requiring strategic approaches to knowledge management for sustainability. The integration of knowledge management with AI offers potential benefits for problem-solving and decision-making, yet presents challenges that require responsible and ethical implementation. This special issue examines how organizations can leverage strategic knowledge management to balance the opportunities and risks of AI while maintaining sustainability across their operations.

The call seeks contributions exploring how organizations can effectively manage both human knowledge and AI-generated intelligent knowledge, addressing issues such as knowledge overload, loss, and duplication. It emphasizes the importance of codification and personalization strategies that align with organizational values and objectives. The special issue invites researchers to examine how sustainable strategic knowledge management enables organizations to adapt to rapidly changing environments while achieving economic, social, and environmental goals.

Appel publié par Journal of Strategy and Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Human-AI synergy and responsible AI use in knowledge systems
  • Strategic knowledge management for organizational decision-making and problem-solving

  • Addressing knowledge overload from AI, cloud computing, and big data
  • Sustainable knowledge-based organizations and resource optimization
  • AI's impact on critical knowledge management processes
  • Ethical and mission-aligned strategic knowledge for financial, social, and ecological benefits
  • Knowledge management in complex organizational environments and geopolitical uncertainty

item.title: The Architecture of Meaning: Reconstructing Luhmann's Dimensional Framework
item.content:encoded:
Michal Kaczmarczyk, University of Gdańsk

Krešimir Žažar, University of Zagreb

Lars Clausen, University College London

This special issue examines Luhmann's concept of meaning as a central medium for both psychic and social systems, structured across three canonical dimensions: factual, temporal, and social. The call argues that while these three dimensions are foundational to systems theory, the underlying logic of why meaning should be organized into exactly these three dimensions remains unresolved. Recent scholarship suggests that meaning may be better understood as a potentially expandable framework responding to basic questions of observation, with additional dimensions such as spatial, modal, and motivational warranting exploration.

The special issue aims to revisit and extend meaning theory in response to contemporary societal complexities, particularly the technological mediation of meaning through artificial intelligence and algorithmic systems, as well as challenges like polarization and meaninglessness. It invites interdisciplinary contributions that employ reflexivity and second-order observation to explore how meaning is currently being observed, transformed, and contested across different media and inter-systemic relations.

Appel publié par Kybernetes. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Theoretical work revisiting or extending established three-dimensional models of meaning (factual, temporal, social), including introduction of novel distinctions such as spatial, modal, or motivational dimensions and expanded sub-programmes within systems theory
  • Studies focusing on second-order observation, reflexivity, and the inherent paradoxes of observation within social and psychic systems
  • Analyses of how artificial intelligence, artificial communication, and algorithmic decision premises impact meaning-processing systems, technological co-evolution, and structures of expectation
  • Explorations of forms of meaning that resist operational closure, reduction, or authoritarian simplification, including the role of imagination, counterfactuals, and non-necessary social orders
  • Systems-theoretical approaches to current societal challenges, encompassing values, political polarisation, populism, inter-systemic relations, strategies for complexity reduction, and pathologies of meaninglessness
  • Renewed theoretical and empirical engagement with sense-making, consciousness, psychology, and psychotherapy, with a focus on identity formation and the structural coupling between psychic and social systems

item.title: Exploring the Interplay of Entrepreneurial Emotion, Judgment, and Decision Making
item.content:encoded:
This special issue examines how emotions influence entrepreneurial judgment and decision-making, particularly in community-based and localized ecosystems. While existing research has focused on positive emotions like passion and resilience, the issue seeks to explore understudied emotional domains such as despair, awe, humility, guilt, empathy, and regret that shape entrepreneurs' strategic choices, resilience, and ethical judgments.

The special issue welcomes interdisciplinary research on how diverse emotional experiences affect entrepreneurial cognition and behavior within small businesses, family firms, and social enterprises. It invites both quantitative approaches examining causal relationships and qualitative studies exploring contextualized experiences, alongside theoretical contributions offering new frameworks for understanding emotions in entrepreneurship.

Insights from this research aim to inform policy-making, entrepreneurial education, and support structures by revealing how emotional dynamics drive sustainable business practices, ethical decision-making, and community engagement in localized entrepreneurial ecosystems.

Appel publié par Journal of Enterprising Communities: People and Places in the Global Economy. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: The role of social capital in knowledge management
item.content:encoded:
This special issue explores the interconnection between social capital and knowledge management in organizations. Social capital—networks of relationships, trust, and shared norms—facilitates knowledge exchange and integration, enhancing intellectual capital development and organizational competitiveness across sectors including technology, finance, healthcare, and creative industries.

The call addresses critical research gaps including the lack of general theory explaining how social capital translates to intellectual capital across different contexts, inconsistent measurement approaches, and limited longitudinal studies. It seeks contributions examining how social capital functions as a mediating mechanism in digital environments, how it evolves over time, and how cultural and technological factors influence these dynamics.

The special issue invites empirical and theoretical research from academics and practitioners investigating social capital's role in knowledge creation, innovation outcomes, and competitive advantage, with particular attention to measurement frameworks, trust mechanisms, and organizational structures that enable effective knowledge management.

Appel publié par VINE Journal of Information and Knowledge Management Systems. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • In what ways does social capital act as a mediator of knowledge management in digital and dynamic environments?
  • How can social capital in knowledge management be measured? To what extent do trust, networks, and norms function as distinct versus overlapping dimensions of social capital?
  • How does social capital evolve over time, and what are its long-term effects on knowledge creation and sharing?
  • How do individual employee networks aggregate to create firm-level intellectual capital?
  • How is social capital value disclosed?
  • How do national cultures influence the relationship between social capital and knowledge management?
  • In what ways do organizational structures influence the effectiveness of social capital in enabling knowledge management?
  • How do emerging technologies impact the development and role of social capital in knowledge management?
  • What role does trust play in knowledge sharing and knowledge application processes?
  • How can organizations foster trust to strengthen social capital in virtual and hybrid workplaces?
  • How does social capital-driven knowledge management contribute to organizational innovation?
  • What is the relationship between social capital, knowledge management, and competitive advantage in dynamic markets?

item.title: The Systemic Paradox of Democracy: Cybernetics, Threat and Resilience in Complex Governance
item.content:encoded:
Mehmet Recai Uygur, Kaunas University of Technology

Eglė Celiešienė, Kaunas University of Technology

Sami Çoksan, Western University

This special issue examines democracy through a systems-theoretical lens, addressing the structural tension between democratic openness and the need to manage threats to institutions and public order. The editors invite contributions that apply cybernetics and complexity theory to understand how democratic systems observe, communicate about and respond to various pressures including war, pandemics, disinformation, migration and technological disruption.

The issue seeks to integrate perspectives from multiple fields including democratic theory, governance, securitisation studies, media research and resilience thinking. It particularly welcomes work that moves beyond linear explanations to analyse feedback loops, recursive processes and unintended consequences of governance interventions, examining paradoxes such as liberty versus security and inclusion versus exclusion.

Appel publié par Kybernetes. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Multilevel governance, polycentric coordination and state-business-civil society relations

item.title: Beyond the Island: The Rise of Project Ecosystems
item.content:encoded:
Samuel MacAulay, University of Queensland

Llewellyn D. W. Thomas, University of Sydney

Andrew Davies, University of Sussex

Projects operate within complex ecosystems of interdependent actors, institutions, and relationships that shape value creation and capture far beyond traditional project boundaries. Rather than treating projects as isolated endeavors, this special issue examines how projects are shaped by and shape their broader contexts, addressing gaps in understanding contextual influences on project outcomes. Emerging challenges such as digital transformation, sustainability transitions, and global interconnectedness create new contextual complexities requiring both theoretical and practical attention.

The special issue seeks research that conceptualizes project ecosystems, explores governance and orchestration mechanisms, and investigates temporal and evolutionary dynamics. Contributions should examine how contextual embeddedness affects project ecosystem outcomes, how governance mechanisms evolve throughout project life cycles, how historical contexts shape current ecosystems, and what long-term impacts project contexts have on subsequent projects and relationships.

Appel publié par Project Management Journal. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Conceptualizing Project Ecosystems: Theoretical refinement and boundary clarification of project ecosystems and related constructs such as project ecologies and networks
  • Empirical investigations of project ecosystems in various industries examining value creation opportunities and complementarities between ecosystem participants

  • Measurement and assessment tools and frameworks for identifying and analyzing value creation and capture in project ecosystems
  • Multilevel governance: Coordination mechanisms across different types of project ecosystems and organizational levels
  • Network orchestration and activity integration: Leadership, participant cooperation, coordination, and balancing diversity and integration in project ecosystems
  • Formal and informal governance: Contractual arrangements, relational governance, and how governance configurations shape value creation or destruction
  • Dynamic governance: Evolution of ecosystem governance mechanisms throughout project ecosystem life cycles and the role of leaders and dynamic capabilities
  • Context evolution: How project ecosystems evolve over time, project phases, and drivers of evolutionary processes
  • Path dependencies: Historical contexts shaping current project ecosystems and antecedents and consequences of different contextual configurations
  • Life cycle dynamics: How contextual influences shape different stages of project ecosystem development and interaction with temporal factors
  • Legacy effects: Long-term impacts of project contexts on subsequent projects and relationships within ecosystems

item.title: Making Space: Creative and Inclusive Research Methods for Management Learning
item.content:encoded:
Frederike Scholz, HU University of Applied Sciences Utrecht

Paulina Segarra, Universidad Anáhuac México

Zuzanna Staniszewska, Kozminski University

Richard Longman, The Open University Business School

This special issue addresses debates about how management and organizational research is conducted and evaluated, particularly regarding inclusion and equity. It builds on participatory and emancipatory research traditions—including disability studies, feminist approaches, and arts-based methodologies—centered on the principle that research should not be conducted about marginalized groups without their participation. The issue argues that conventional methodologies can sideline or misrepresent lived experience, and seeks to open new possibilities for research that is attentive to power, voice, and epistemic justice.

  • Researcher Reflexivity and Positionality: Critical examination of the researcher's role, including biases, assumptions, and relational positioning
  • Ethical Considerations: Work addressing ethical tensions of inclusive research, including consent, access, representation, and power
  • Longitudinal and Mixed-methods Approaches: Research tracing lived experience over time and/or challenging rigid separations through integrative designs

item.title: Tensions and Paradoxes in Project Environments
item.content:encoded:
Anna Wiewiora, Queensland University of Technology (QUT)

Jörg Sydow, Freie Universität Berlin

Josh Keller, University of New South Wales (UNSW)

Medhanie Gaim, Oslo Metropolitan University

This special issue examines how tensions and paradoxes emerge, interact, and evolve across project environments at multiple levels—individual, team, organizational, and interorganizational. Rather than viewing tensions as problems to eliminate, the issue encourages research that explores how project actors and leaders can navigate, leverage, and productively work with persistent, interdependent contradictory demands that are inherent in complex project work.

The call invites theory-informed contributions that move beyond binary either/or framings to adopt both/and and more-than approaches for understanding tensions. Topics of particular interest include tensions in project learning, sustainability integration, stakeholder management, and the emerging role of algorithmic technologies in project decision-making. The special issue welcomes conceptual, qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-method research, with emphasis on longitudinal and comparative designs that capture how tensions evolve over time.

  • Tensions in complex and megaproject environments with multiple institutional contexts and knowledge domains
  • Project learning paradoxes and tensions between knowledge creation, transfer, and performance pressures
  • Sustainability tensions between environmental goals and traditional project delivery objectives
  • Stakeholder-related tensions including inclusion versus exclusion, cooperation versus competition, and competing narratives
  • Tensions involving artificial intelligence and human judgment in project decision-making and knowledge management

item.title: Sustainability by Projects: Rethinking Stakeholder Engagement, Legacy, and Impact
item.content:encoded:
Kirsi Aaltonen, University of Oulu

Siavash Alimadadi, King's College London

Marina Bos-de Vos, Delft University of Technology

Ermal Hetemi, KTH Royal Institute of Technology

Projects increasingly serve as platforms for translating sustainability goals into concrete actions, yet the relationship between stakeholder engagement and sustainability outcomes is complex and multifaceted. This special issue examines how projects and programs generate, mediate, and shape sustainability outcomes and legacies through stakeholder engagement across their entire lifecycle, extending beyond traditional project success metrics to encompass long-term societal and environmental impacts.

The special issue identifies five central tensions: the paradox of inclusion and exclusion in stakeholder participation; the mismatch between global sustainability ambitions and local contextual realities; conflicts between project temporal constraints and extended sustainability time horizons; tensions between managerial control approaches and emergent sustainability dynamics; and the reconfiguring influence of artificial intelligence on stakeholder engagement processes. These tensions reflect competing demands and values that cannot be fully resolved simultaneously but require careful conceptual and empirical examination.

Appel publié par Project Management Journal. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Inclusion, exclusion, and stakeholder voice in projects and how these dynamics shape legitimacy and sustainability outcomes
  • Global ambitions and local realities: how global sustainability goals are interpreted, translated, and contested in local project contexts
  • Project temporality and sustainability time horizons: tensions between short-term delivery pressures and long-term sustainability objectives
  • Managerial control and emergent sustainability dynamics: control-oriented approaches versus emergent and value-laden aspects of sustainability
  • Artificial intelligence and the reconfiguration of tensions: how AI shapes stakeholder engagement, participation, bias, accountability, and legitimacy in sustainability-oriented projects
  • Sustainable project legacy: long-term value and lasting impacts that projects leave for communities and the environment
  • Stakeholder engagement mechanisms through which sustainability outcomes are negotiated, contested, and realized
  • Power asymmetries and their role in shaping sustainability outcomes and project trajectories
  • Temporal work and how actors mobilize visions of futures to coordinate action across divergent timeframes
  • Portfolio governance, intermediary organizational structures, and their mediation between strategic sustainability ambitions and project delivery practices

item.title: Rethinking Technology Transfer: Ensuring Resilience, Economic Impact and Social Value
item.content:encoded:
James Cunningham, Newcastle University

Jungho Kim, Newcastle University

Chiara Marzocchi, University of Padua

Natalya Radko, Newcastle University

Technology transfer from universities and industry has been central to economic development, but rapidly advancing research and technology demand continuous evolution of university transfer structures and processes. While established frameworks have driven economic impact, emerging disruptions including AI advancement, geopolitical shifts, and intellectual property challenges are testing the resilience of current systems. This special issue examines how technology transfer systems can effectively balance economic impact with social value creation.

The issue invites exploration across multiple levels: macro-level policy frameworks and government R&D investments, meso-level institutional configurations and TTO designs, and micro-level academic entrepreneur behaviours and professional competencies. It particularly addresses how universities can simultaneously pursue economic commercialisation while meeting expectations to address societal grand challenges, and how these dual objectives create tensions requiring new business models and support structures.

  • Inclusivity and participation in technology transfer systems from multiple perspectives
  • Public policy mixes and instruments supporting technology transfer systems for economic and social value
  • Emerging university TTO configurations addressing societal challenges and geopolitical changes
  • Intellectual property leakage, open science models, and evolving legal frameworks affecting value creation
  • Future capabilities and competences required by technology transfer actors across sectors
  • Influence of stakeholder needs and AI-driven digitalisation on university TTO methodologies and processes
  • Non-market strategies driving university TTOs economic and social value creation

item.title: 2SLGBTQIA+ Entrepreneurship: Advancing Theory, Method, and Practice on Identity, Institutions, and Inclusion
item.content:encoded:
Shawna Chen, Brock University

Michael Lounsbury, University of Alberta

While entrepreneurship research has increasingly recognized identity as central to entrepreneurial processes, 2SLGBTQIA+ entrepreneurs remain significantly underexplored in the core literature, particularly regarding how sexuality and gender identity interact with entrepreneurial ecosystems and institutional structures. This special issue aims to advance conceptual, empirical, and methodological understanding of 2SLGBTQIA+ entrepreneurship by examining how these entrepreneurs navigate visibility, stigma, belonging, and legitimacy within broader institutional and spatial contexts.

The special issue welcomes diverse theoretical and methodological approaches, including identity theory, queer-feminist perspectives, intersectionality, institutional theory, and institutional logics. Submissions may employ qualitative, quantitative, or mixed methodologies and are encouraged to bridge theory and practice by including diverse scholarly teams with practitioners involved in entrepreneurship.
