item.title: Accounting, accountability, and animal flourishing
item.content:encoded:
Lisa Powell, Monash University

Eija Vinnari, Tampere University

Niina Ylönen, Tampere University

This special issue examines how accounting and accountability frameworks can address animal flourishing, extending beyond traditional focuses on organisational profitability and human welfare. Drawing on the Capabilities Approach, which emphasises innate freedoms and opportunities for creatures to exercise agency through movement, autonomy, sensory experience, and social relations, the issue explores how accounting might enable these conditions across different animal contexts: domesticated animals in human-controlled spaces, liminal animals occupying boundaries between wild and domestic, and wild animals in conservation settings.

Appel publié par Social and Environmental Accountability Journal. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How could accounting help shape conditions for animal flourishing?
  • How could we account for or enable the flourishing of individual animals, including those with preferences diverging from species-specific capabilities?
  • How would we account for animal flourishing and what forms would these accounts take?
  • Where could we find existing examples of accounts of flourishing beyond sanctuaries for rescued animals?
  • What opportunities exist for accounting and what does flourishing mean for animals across domestic, liminal, and wild spaces?
  • How could multispecies justice inform alternative forms of accounting that recognise agricultural animals beyond inputs and production units?
  • What accounting practices could address better justice for domesticated and liminal animals?
  • To what extent is flourishing possible for domesticated animals in asymmetrical dependency relationships or liminal animals considered pests?
  • How could accounting contribute to conservation efforts recognising individual wild animals alongside ecological collectives?
  • How could accounting navigate ethical tensions when working towards simultaneous flourishing of individual animals and ecological collectives?
  • What should organisations be accountable for in terms of animal flourishing?
  • To what extent are organisations accountable for animal flourishing and how could they demonstrate this accountability?
  • What collaborative opportunities exist between companies and other organisations regarding animal flourishing?
  • How could accountability approaches resist the human/nature binary and enhance understanding of reciprocal human-nonhuman relations?
  • What responsibilities do organisations have in supporting wild animal flourishing and what form could interventions take?

item.title: Action Learning in Asia
item.content:encoded:
George Boak, York St John University

Wooyong Eom, Keimyung University

This special issue invites contributions exploring action learning across Asia. While previous journal issues have featured individual papers on action learning in various Asian countries, this collection seeks to expand representation to underrepresented regions throughout the continent.

The editors are particularly interested in how cultural contexts shape action learning approaches. Submissions should examine whether distinctive characteristics emerge in action learning design and facilitation across different cultural settings, and how cultural factors influence both the aims and processes of action learning.

The issue welcomes empirical studies, conceptual papers, and practitioner accounts that contribute to understanding action learning theory and practice in Asian contexts. Authors are encouraged to consult with editors before submitting full papers.

  • Cultural influences on action learning design, aims and processes

item.title: Advancing Excellence in Professional Selling and Sales Management Education
item.content:encoded:
Leff Bonney, Florida State University

Jessica Ogilvie, Marquette University

Professional sales education faces mounting pressures from evolving student expectations, institutional demands for demonstrable value, and rapid industry transformation. This special issue addresses how sales educators can effectively bridge theory and practice by developing rigorous curricula while equipping students with career-ready skills across diverse learning contexts, from university degree programs to corporate training and entrepreneurial ventures.

The journal seeks empirical, conceptual, and methodological contributions examining foundational questions and contemporary challenges in sales education. Topics span pedagogical innovation and curriculum design, assessment of learning outcomes and career trajectories, sales management and leadership development, industry-academic partnerships, and ethical and global dimensions of sales instruction.

Appel publié par Marketing Education Review. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Effectiveness of different teaching modalities (in-person, online, hybrid, asynchronous) in sales courses

  • Development and validation of instruments and rubrics to assess sales skills and competencies
  • Longitudinal studies connecting sales education to career outcomes, employment rates, and performance metrics
  • Factors driving student engagement, motivation, and success in sales, including mentorship and role models
  • Pedagogical approaches for teaching sales management topics including compensation, territory alignment, and performance management

item.title: AI-driven marketing and Sustainability
item.content:encoded:
Pham Van Hau, Unitec Institute of Technology

Carolyn Strong, Cardiff University

Park Thaichon, University of Southern Queensland

This special issue focuses on the emerging intersection of artificial intelligence and sustainable marketing. AI technologies like machine learning and predictive analytics are rapidly transforming marketing practices, while sustainability challenges demand new approaches to shift consumption patterns and market systems. The special issue seeks research examining how AI-driven marketing influences sustainability outcomes at individual, organizational, and system-wide levels.

The integration of AI in marketing presents both opportunities and challenges for sustainability. AI tools can enable personalized sustainability nudges, improve resource efficiency, and support circular economy initiatives. However, concerns include algorithmic bias, privacy issues, transparency challenges, and the risk of reinforcing unsustainable consumption through hyper-personalized marketing. Understanding these dynamics is critical to ensure AI contributes positively to sustainable futures rather than exacerbating environmental and social challenges.

Appel publié par Journal of Strategic Marketing. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Transparency, fairness, and accountability in AI-driven marketing systems

item.title: AI in the Built Environment: Opportunities, Risks, and Future Directions
item.content:encoded:
Sara Wilkinson, University of Technology Sydney

Johnny Wong, University of Technology Sydney

Biyanka Ekanayake, University of Technology Sydney

This special issue examines how artificial intelligence is transforming the built environment across construction, real estate, facilities management, and urban planning. While AI technologies offer significant opportunities for innovation and efficiency through applications like energy optimization, smart building control, and predictive maintenance, the sector faces critical challenges regarding data integrity, algorithmic bias, privacy, and transparent decision-making.

The special issue seeks high-quality original research exploring AI's use, impact, risks, and future potential in the built environment. It welcomes contributions spanning construction automation, property valuation, smart buildings, urban planning, generative design, AI governance and ethics, sustainability applications, security systems, human-AI collaboration, and professional education in AI.

Appel publié par Building Research & Information. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • AI in property and real estate: valuation models, market intelligence, customer engagement, asset management, predictive analytics
  • Smart buildings and facilities management: IoT-enabled optimisation, energy management, predictive maintenance, AI-driven knowledge systems
  • AI in urban planning and infrastructure: spatial modelling, forecasting, environmental assessment, transport and mobility analytics
  • Design and engineering applications: generative design, simulation, optimisation, digital twins, parametric modelling
  • Explainable AI (XAI): AI governance, ethics, and regulation: transparency, bias, data integrity, privacy, and responsible GenAI in the built environment

item.title: Arts Organizations and Street-Level Bureaucracy
item.content:encoded:
Jonathan Paquette, University of Ottawa

Street-level bureaucracy, a concept developed to describe how front-line professionals implement public policies through discretionary decision-making, remains highly relevant to contemporary policy studies across multiple sectors. The special issue seeks to extend this framework to arts and heritage organizations, an area where street-level bureaucracy has received limited scholarly attention despite growing evidence that cultural professionals operate as street-level bureaucrats navigating policy implementation, resource constraints, and complex social mandates.

The call invites manuscripts examining how arts professionals engage with street-level bureaucracy, particularly focusing on care work dimensions as cultural organizations increasingly participate in social cohesion and vulnerability integration initiatives. Submissions should explore the creative strategies, routines, and coping mechanisms that cultural professionals develop, and analyze how the street-level bureaucracy concept illuminates arts management across varied global contexts.

Appel publié par The Journal of Arts Management, Law, and Society. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Street-level bureaucracy and care work in arts and heritage organizations
  • Work, routines and coping mechanisms in cultural organizations
  • Conceptual analysis of street-level bureaucracy in arts management
  • How street-level bureaucrats navigate policy implementation in cultural institutions
  • Discretionary power and professional strategies in arts organizations
  • Social missions and emotional labor in cultural work
  • Application of street-level bureaucracy concept across diverse global cultural policy contexts
  • Intersections between street-level bureaucracy and artistic/cultural intermediaries

  • September 5, 2026: Manuscript deadline

item.title: Business in Korea and China in the Age of Geopolitical Rivalry: Industrial Policy, Non-market Strategy, and Global Value Chain Realignment
item.content:encoded:
Seong-jin Choi, Hanyang University

Khan-Pyo Lee, Sogang University

Chris Rowley, University of Oxford

The global business environment is undergoing a major transition where geopolitical considerations and economic security now shape corporate strategy alongside market factors. South Korea and China represent critical contexts for studying how businesses respond to institutional uncertainty, particularly in strategic sectors like semiconductors and EV batteries. This special issue examines how firms in these countries manage their strategic responses amid shifting state policies, regulatory changes, and rising protectionism that demand significant organizational adaptation.

  • Resource reconfiguration and organizational responses to techno-nationalism and protectionism in strategic industries such as semiconductors, EV batteries, and AI

item.title: Children of the Platform Society: Generation Alpha, Beta, and Digital Advertising Cultures
item.content:encoded:
Liselot Hudders, Ghent University

Steven Holiday, The University of Alabama

Regina Ahn, University of Miami

This special issue addresses how Generation Alpha and Beta, the first generations growing up within datafied, algorithmically curated platform ecosystems, experience commercial digital environments and advertising cultures. Children in these generations navigate seamlessly blurred boundaries between online and offline worlds, where algorithmic recommendations, creator content, and virtual participation increasingly shape their identity formation, consumer practices, and social relationships in ways that fundamentally differ from previous generations.

The issue seeks to move research on child consumers from the periphery to center stage by examining how commercial platforms construct, represent, and govern childhood while recognizing children as active social agents. It welcomes interdisciplinary perspectives that explore the theoretical, empirical, and methodological dimensions of children's participation in platformized consumer culture, moving beyond traditional vulnerability-versus-empowerment binaries toward more nuanced understandings of children's lived experiences within commercial digital infrastructures.

Appel publié par Journal of Interactive Advertising. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How platformization reshapes childhood, including identity formation, play, learning, friendship, and consumer socialization within datafied and algorithmically curated environments
  • How children construct, negotiate, and express identity through commercial and digital practices, including engagement with brands, creators, digital commodities, and virtual worlds
  • How platform architectures, affordances, and commercial logics transform commercial persuasion directed toward children, including immersive, interactive, personalized, and AI-driven advertising practices
  • Theoretical perspectives on children's consumer socialization, including reverse socialization and children's roles as producers of marketplace knowledge
  • Consumption as a cultural and social practice through which children construct meaning, belonging, status, and self-expression
  • Commercialization of children's everyday lives and the blurring of boundaries between advertising, entertainment, education, play, and family life

  • Innovative methodological approaches for studying children's lived experiences within platformized consumer cultures, including participatory, ethnographic, computational, and mixed-method designs
  • Children's agency and participation within platformized consumer and advertising cultures as content creators and brand advocates

Yanmin He, Otemon Gakuin University

This special issue addresses how digital technologies, institutional environments, and governance mechanisms interact to shape firm behavior and market evolution. Contemporary firms face complex transformations driven by digitalization and artificial intelligence alongside institutional frictions such as regulatory uncertainty and financing constraints. The special issue seeks to integrate fragmented research streams on digital transformation, corporate governance, and institutional dynamics to develop a more comprehensive understanding of firm-level adaptation in emerging markets.

The call welcomes submissions exploring how digital governance frameworks, enterprise transformation, and corporate governance mechanisms jointly influence innovation and firm competitiveness. Research may examine topics including digital transformation strategies, artificial intelligence adoption, corporate governance structures, institutional frictions affecting finance and trade, geopolitical impacts, and new measurement approaches. Submissions should make significant theoretical or empirical contributions to understanding emerging market dynamics.

item.title: Decarbonisation: cross cutting enablers for a net-zero carbon built environment
item.content:encoded:
An Le, Massey University

Niluka Domingo, Massey University

Sepani Senaratne, Western Sydney University

Soojin Yoon, Oklahoma State University

This special issue addresses the fragmented nature of current decarbonisation efforts in the built environment, which typically focus on isolated phases rather than adopting a comprehensive lifecycle perspective. The editors seek research that demonstrates how building design can serve as a central mechanism for reducing emissions throughout all stages, from initial conception through construction, operation, and eventual deconstruction.

Contributions should explore holistic design approaches that integrate carbon assessment early in the design process, alongside strategies for managing buildings during operation and end-of-life phases. The issue particularly emphasizes the importance of cross-cutting enablers such as multidisciplinary collaboration, workforce development, and supportive policy and financial frameworks that facilitate the transition toward net-zero carbon buildings.

Appel publié par Building Research & Information. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Holistic design and planning: Integrating lifecycle carbon assessment in early-stage design; design management strategies for net-zero carbon pathways; forecasting and modelling; circular economy strategies; holistic approaches.

Post-occupancy evaluation and facilities management for sustained low-carbon outcomes. Designing for adaptability, disassembly, and material recovery at end-of-life.
  • Cross-cutting enablers: Multidisciplinary collaboration and stakeholder engagement across the building lifecycle; workforce skills and competences for low-carbon design and delivery; financial, business, and policy mechanisms to support lifecycle decarbonisation initiatives.

Femi Olan, University of Essex

Uchitha Jayawickrama, Loughborough University

This special issue seeks high-quality research on Decision Support Systems (DSS) that address sustainable and resilient transitions across organisations, societies, and supply chains. In environments characterised by technological disruption, environmental threats, and changing workforce demands, DSS models, frameworks, tools, and applications are essential for enabling evidence-based decision-making and strategic adaptation.

The call welcomes contributions exploring both theoretical foundations and practical applications of DSS across four main areas: green and sustainable transitions, digital transformation, workforce and skills transitions, and resilient supply chains. Submissions should demonstrate how DSS support organisations and societies in balancing efficiency with sustainability and resilience objectives while navigating rapid change.

Relevant submissions include conceptual models, quantitative frameworks with performance indicators, empirical case studies, interdisciplinary approaches, and critical analyses of adoption barriers and governance considerations for DSS implementation in transitions.

item.title: Digitalization-Greenization Synergy in Emerging Markets
item.content:encoded:
Haijie Wang, Zhengzhou University

Yanchao Feng, Zhengzhou University

Emerging markets are experiencing structural transformation through the integration of digital technologies with green energy systems, creating opportunities for economic growth and sustainability. This digitalization-greenization synergy aims to enhance efficiency and resilience, yet emerging markets face significant obstacles including regulatory gaps, financial limitations, and unequal access to digital and energy infrastructure.

The special issue seeks research on how this digital-green transition influences macroeconomic dynamics, financial systems, investment patterns, and trade in emerging economies. Theoretical and empirical studies examining inclusive growth, green finance, trade competitiveness, and policy design are particularly welcome, with focus on the economic and financial dimensions of this dual transformation.

This special issue examines how geopolitical tensions, particularly conflicts in West Asia, influence international trade dynamics and economic development across the Asia-Pacific region. item.content:encoded:
Susan Sharma, Deakin University

Zhenhua Zhang, Lanzhou University

Geopolitical tensions are causing significant disruptions in global energy markets, fundamentally affecting energy security and economic stability in emerging markets. These shocks create complex challenges including energy accessibility issues, imported inflation, trade imbalances, and capital flow disruptions that threaten macroeconomic stability and development trajectories.

This special issue seeks to understand how energy security and economic dynamics interact within emerging markets facing geopolitical pressures. The focus is on examining transmission channels between energy sector shocks and broader economic effects, as well as policy responses that emerging economies are implementing through energy diversification, financial hedging, supply chain resilience, and green energy transitions.

The special issue welcomes theoretical and empirical research exploring the interconnections between energy security and economic dynamics, with emphasis on implications for macroeconomic stability, financial resilience, industrial restructuring, sustainable growth, and socioeconomic development in emerging markets.

item.content:encoded:
Georgia Allen-Baker, Northumbria University

This special issue explores the purpose and meaning of leisure in the early years of child development, from birth to five years, and its role in family wellbeing and social-emotional development. The special issue recognizes leisure practices during this period as foundational yet understudied, shaped by economic resources, cultural norms, gender roles, policy environments, and access to spaces and services.

The call welcomes research examining diverse leisure practices including play, cultural activities, outdoor engagement, travel, and digital leisure across different global contexts. Submissions should critically examine the structural conditions that influence participation and access, considering intersectional inequalities and representation in leisure provision.

Contributions from various theoretical and methodological perspectives are encouraged, including qualitative and quantitative research, with particular interest in interdisciplinary work from sociology, education, public health, psychology, geography, and childhood studies.

item.title: Finding Afrotopia in Times of Technological Transformation – Toward Pluriversal African Future-Making
item.content:encoded:
Natasha Winkler-Titus, Stellenbosch University

Emamdeen Fohim, University of Bern

Rebecca Namatovu-Dawa, Copenhagen Business School

Thomas Anning-Dorson, University of the Witwatersrand

Renate E. Meyer, Vienna University of Economics and Business

Joel Gehman, George Washington University

This special issue seeks manuscripts exploring how technological transformation can support African futures aligned with the concept of Afrotopia—a vision for African modernization rooted in the continent's diverse histories, epistemologies, and cultures rather than Western models. The issue bridges research on future-making practices and pluriversal perspectives in management and organization studies with critical examination of Africa's rapid technological change, considering both opportunities and risks.

The special issue invites scholars to examine conditions under which digital and technological change can genuinely serve African communities and address threats such as data extraction, algorithmic colonialism, and Western-designed technological solutions unsuited to local contexts. Contributions may employ any methodology, with particular welcome for approaches grounded in African and indigenous epistemologies.

item.title: Global Trends, Homegrown Systems: Developing Global South-First Frameworks for Managing the Sport Ecosystem
item.content:encoded:
Sarthak Mondal, University of Portsmouth

Sahen Gupta, University of Portsmouth

Govindasamy Balasekaran, National Institute of Education, Singapore

Jo Clarke, Leeds Beckett University

The global sport industry has historically been shaped by theories and management approaches originating in the Global North, which often fail to account for the institutional, political, economic and cultural realities of sport in the Global South. This epistemic gap means that practitioners and policymakers in emerging economies lack conceptual tools tailored to their specific contexts, limiting the effectiveness of governance and development initiatives.

This special issue positions the Global South as a primary site of theoretical production and institutional innovation rather than merely a testing ground for Northern theories. Recent developments in cricket franchises, African football, Southeast Asian esports, and Gulf sport mega-events demonstrate distinctive governance and investment configurations that require bespoke analytical frameworks.

item.title: Intelligent Transformation of Tourism Development in Asia-Pacific
item.content:encoded:
Boyu Lin, Macao University of Tourism

Jinwei Wang, Beijing International Studies University

Hongwen Chen, Nanchang University

Xin-Jean Lim, Universiti Putra Malaysia

This special issue examines how artificial intelligence is reshaping tourism planning and development across the Asia-Pacific region. Rather than focusing narrowly on technological efficiency, the call addresses broader transformations in destination governance, spatial flows, and how communities benefit from intelligent tourism systems. The collection seeks critical, theoretically informed research that explores the social, environmental, cultural, and economic implications of AI adoption in tourism contexts.

The Asia-Pacific region offers a particularly valuable setting for this inquiry due to its diversity: advanced smart cities coexist with rural destinations and climate-vulnerable communities, creating uneven experiences of AI-driven transformation. The region simultaneously faces urgent development challenges including overtourism, environmental pressures, and inequality, while becoming a global laboratory for experimental intelligent tourism systems. This context makes the region essential for understanding both opportunities and risks of AI-mediated tourism change.

item.title: Leadership and Change in M&As
item.content:encoded:
David Kroon, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

Olimpia Meglio, University of Naples "Federico II"

Nicola Mirc, Toulouse School of Management

Audrey Rouzies, Toulouse School of Management

Satu Teerikangas, Turku University

Mergers and acquisitions serve as significant catalysts for organizational change, enabling leaders to reshape organizational boundaries and develop new capabilities. However, their implications extend far beyond the merging firms to affect employees, managers, customers, and communities. While M&A research has explored various themes and theoretical perspectives, most special issues have adopted narrow lenses focusing on single aspects like organizational culture or post-merger integration, leaving fundamental questions about how these large-scale transformations unfold.

M&As represent profound episodes of organizational change that disrupt established structures and challenge existing cultures. Yet research on M&As and change management has largely evolved separately, addressing similar questions about how people respond to uncertainty and how leaders enable adaptation without meaningful cross-fertilization. This special issue seeks to bridge these research communities, offering fresh perspectives on how actors at multiple levels shape M&A outcomes and navigate the tension between strategic ambition and human adaptability.

Appel publié par Journal of Change Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • M&As as continuous change: how firms handle deliberate design versus evolving circumstances, intended versus unintended change trajectories, and seizing opportunities while mitigating threats
  • Leadership and employee change agency in M&As: employees as sense makers, boundary spanners, and informal leaders; proactive versus passive roles in integration
  • Emotions and irrationality in M&As: hubris, anxiety, grief, excitement, overconfidence, and escalation of commitment in M&A decisions and integration
  • Changing relationships in M&As: renegotiating internal relationships among employees, teams, and leaders; external relationships with suppliers, customers, regulators, and communities; trust, social capital, and power dynamics
  • Digitalization and Technology in M&As: AI-driven analytics, ERP systems, collaboration software; digital capabilities as deal drivers; technology's impact on cultural dynamics and integration speed
  • M&As and Grand Challenges: role of M&As in addressing environmental degradation and global crises; economic and social sustainability; M&As as a force for good

Timeline

  • August 1, 2026: Submission starting date
  • October 31, 2026: Closing date

item.title: Oceans of Opportunity: Navigating a New Course for Coastal Tourism Planning and Development in Africa and Beyond
item.content:encoded:
Senija Causevic, Université Internationale de Rabat

Manuel Alector Ribeiro, University of Surrey

Aaron Yankholmes, Nottingham Trent University

Africa's coastal regions remain significantly underrepresented in global tourism research despite comprising 38 coastal nations with extensive marine biodiversity. The gap reflects both historical legacies of colonialism and contemporary academic inequities, leaving African coastal communities marginalized in planning and governance processes. This special issue seeks contributions that move beyond critique toward co-creating regenerative coastal tourism models grounded in vernacular knowledge and local spatial politics.

Coastal tourism planning currently privileges aesthetic conservation and tourist interests over equitable resource distribution and environmental sustainability, often resulting in economic leakage, spatial exclusion, and increased climate vulnerability for local communities. The special issue invites research on governance frameworks, community-led approaches, and planning instruments that address spatial injustices, strengthen local value chains, and balance competing coastal uses including fisheries, conservation, and port development.

Appel publié par Tourism Planning & Development. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Coastal tourism planning and development at the land–sea interface
  • Planning instruments for coastal tourism (zoning, development controls, permitting, enforcement, accountability)
  • Institutional coordination, planning capacity, and multi-level governance (local–regional–national)
  • Data gaps, indicators, and monitoring systems for coastal destination performance and carrying capacity
  • Cross-sector trade-offs in port and coastal cities (tourism–ports–fisheries–conservation–urban development)
  • Spatial justice in coastal tourism development (land tenure, coastal access, displacement, and enclosure)
  • Economic leakage, benefit-sharing, and strengthening local value chains (procurement, SMEs, labour linkages, etc.)
  • Investment, public-private partnership, ownership, and concession models (including FDI) and implications for local livelihoods
  • Financial planning for regenerative coastal tourism, i.e. public finance, climate finance, carbon markets
  • Climate risk, adaptation planning, and resilience for coastal tourism infrastructure, ecosystems, and livelihoods
  • Water security, resource pressures, and demand management in coastal and island destinations
  • Nature-based solutions and coastal ecosystem restoration linked to tourism development (mangroves, dunes, reefs, etc.)
  • Community participation, co-management, and community-led coastal governance innovations
  • Indigenous knowledge in tourism planning, monitoring, and coastal management
  • Tourism linkages with other sectors, i.e. fisheries, marine agriculture, etc. (livelihoods, resource conflicts, governance responses)
  • Coastal and maritime heritage tourism (interpretation, ethics, memory, community partnership, connected heritage landscapes, etc)
  • Destination diversification beyond enclave resort models (culture, conservation, science-based tourism, etc.)
  • Domestic, diaspora/VFR, and intra-African tourism mobilities and their implications for coastal destination planning
  • Relational and comparative research
  • Connected-place and relational coastal tourism development across sea basins (Africa–Europe, Western Indian Ocean, Africa–Middle East, Africa-West Indies, etc.)
  • Political conflict, power relations, and contested governance in coastal tourism development

item.title: Powering Household Portfolio: Digital Finance, Demographics, and Decisions
item.content:encoded:
Weixing Wu, Capital University of Economics and Business

Zhichao Yin, Capital University of Economics and Business

Susan Sunila Sharma, Deakin University

This special issue examines how three interconnected forces—digital finance, demographic shifts, and behavioral decision-making—are transforming household financial behavior. Digital finance technologies are lowering barriers to entry and enabling personalized services, while demographic changes such as aging populations and evolving family structures are reshaping household risk management. Understanding how households make financial decisions remains critical to comprehending financial markets and macroeconomic dynamics.

The issue welcomes research using high-quality micro-level datasets to investigate how household-level financial choices aggregate into market-wide and macroeconomic effects. Contributions should address the complexity and heterogeneity of household financial decision-making across consumption, investment, borrowing, and wealth management activities, drawing insights from economics, finance, behavioral science, and data science.

item.title: Psychology in the service of the disabled, the ill and the dying
item.content:encoded:
Ami Rokach, York University

This special issue addresses the psychological dimensions of disability, illness, and dying. Disability encompasses not only physical or cognitive impairments but also the social exclusion and discrimination that individuals experience. Illness creates significant psychological stress through pain, fatigue, and loss of control, with hospitalization triggering both immediate and lasting mental health effects. Dying represents an ultimate challenge that psychology must address through support for patients and their families.

The special issue welcomes empirical studies, reviews, theoretical manuscripts, and commentaries from psychologists across all specialties, healthcare professionals, and individuals who have experienced psychological support during illness or disability. Submissions should address how psychology can support individuals in navigating disability, managing illness-related stress, and confronting mortality with dignity.

Appel publié par The Journal of Psychology. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Adjusting to loss and navigating stigma among disabled individuals
  • Developing disability pride and addressing mental health disparities
  • Ableism and systematic discrimination against people with disabilities
  • Psychological impacts of disability, including emotional, mental, and social effects
  • Coping with illness as a major life stressor
  • Short-term and long-term psychological consequences of hospitalization
  • Perceived threat to life and uncontrollable nature of illness
  • Death and dying as areas of psychological specialization
  • Supporting families of the dying and preparing individuals for end-of-life
  • Grief and bereavement support

item.title: Relational pedagogies in an age of GenAI
item.content:encoded:
Karen Gravett, University of Surrey

Naomi Winstone, University of Surrey

Kieran Balloo, Southern Cross University

This special issue explores relational pedagogies—teaching practices emphasizing meaningful connections between teachers and students, and engagement with both human and nonhuman entities like digital technologies—within contemporary higher education contexts shaped by generative artificial intelligence. Relational pedagogies foster emotional and affective dimensions of education while challenging competitive individualistic approaches.

The rapid emergence of GenAI is fundamentally reshaping how educators and students interact, redefining educational practices politically, practically, and ideologically. The special issue seeks critical perspectives on how GenAI reconfigures relationality in higher education, addressing questions about student engagement with AI outside educator control, evolving assessment and feedback practices, care in digitalized contexts, equity implications, and the ethical and environmental concerns these technologies raise.

item.content:encoded:
Fernando Miramontes Forattini, Dublin City University

Regina Connolly, Dublin City University

This special issue examines how care ethics and relational approaches can advance responsible design and governance of AI-enabled systems. While contemporary AI ethics discourse has focused on fairness, transparency, and compliance frameworks, this call seeks to address the structural, relational, and institutional dimensions of how digital systems affect vulnerability, participation, and human agency.

The special issue invites empirical research, conceptual contributions, design science research, and interdisciplinary perspectives that move beyond procedural approaches to explore responsibility distribution across socio-technical arrangements. Submissions should examine relationships between technology, power, participation, exclusion, and accountability in digital environments, grounded in diverse epistemological and methodological traditions.

item.title: Robotics in Advertising and Marketing
item.content:encoded:
Mark Yi-Cheon Yim, University of Massachusetts Lowell

Esther Kang, University of Bristol

The rapidly evolving landscape of home robotics presents new opportunities for advertising and marketing. With advances in physical AI making robots more capable of interacting in everyday environments, and demographic shifts creating increased demand for in-home robotics, major technology companies are now commercializing robots for caregiving and other household functions. These robots offer a novel channel for brand engagement, as human-robot interactions can foster emotional connections that position robots as both companions and marketing agents.

This special issue seeks high-quality research examining the intersection of robotics, marketing, and advertising. The journal invites contributions exploring how consumers engage with robotic agents, how these interactions affect brand perception and consumer behavior, and how marketing strategies can effectively leverage robotic technologies. Research employing diverse methodologies and addressing topics ranging from human-robot interaction psychology to ethical and privacy considerations is welcome.

Appel publié par Journal of Interactive Advertising. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Human–Robot Interaction: Psychological effects of perceived vitality, animacy, and agency in brand-representative robots
  • Social and Relational Marketing: Use of social robots to build brand loyalty, foster parasocial relationships, and address consumer isolation through interactive engagement
  • Care Robotics: Roles of interactive robots in home and specialized contexts, including navigation, product recommendation, and customer service
  • Technology Adoption: Factors and mechanisms that influence consumer adoption of robots in domestic settings
  • Experiential and Event Marketing: Effectiveness of robotic installations in creating immersive brand experiences and interactive out-of-home (OOH) advertising
  • Ethical and Privacy Considerations: Issues of consumer trust, data privacy, and the ethical implications of autonomous data collection by robotic agents in advertising and marketing contexts
  • Measurement and Metrics: Development of frameworks for assessing ROI and consumer engagement in human–robot interactive advertising campaigns

item.title: Small Business and Entrepreneurship in Sparse Ecosystems: Immigrant Ventures, Innovation and Resilience in Peripheries
item.content:encoded:
Nafisa Yeasmin, University of Oulu

Anisur Faroque, University of Vaasa

Mohammad Osman Gani, University Canada West

Waliul Hasanat, University of Lapland

Hiran Roy, Canadian University

Arctic and remote peripheral regions face demographic decline and labour shortages alongside emerging economic opportunities. Immigrant entrepreneurs play a vital role in sustaining these communities through ventures in tourism, food, logistics, and digital services, yet this phenomenon remains understudied in mainstream entrepreneurship research focused on metropolitan areas.

This special issue examines how immigrant entrepreneurs develop ventures in sparse, geographically isolated, and institutionally thin environments where they navigate regulatory complexity and fragmented support systems. The issue integrates perspectives from entrepreneurship, migration studies, regional development, and sustainability to generate new theoretical insights into entrepreneurial ecosystems in peripheral and extreme contexts.

The special issue welcomes empirical, conceptual, comparative, and policy-oriented contributions exploring how immigrant enterprises mobilize resources, adapt to uncertainty, and shape Arctic and global peripheries. It seeks to expand understanding of entrepreneurial opportunity creation, resilience strategies, and the role of digitalization in these distinctive contexts.

item.title: Strategic Marketing and Regenerative Futures
item.content:encoded:
Ninh Nguyen, RMIT University

Ranjit Voola, The University of Sydney

M S Balaji, RMIT University

Dung Minh Nguyen, National Kaohsiung University of Science and Technology

Carolyn Strong, Cardiff University

This special issue examines how strategic marketing can advance regenerative futures. While sustainability remains important, regenerative approaches go beyond harm reduction and efficiency to actively restore social, ecological, and economic systems through business strategies, partnerships, and market practices. The issue seeks to understand how firms formulate regenerative marketing goals, develop and communicate regenerative strategies, and align commercial objectives with societal and ecological renewal.

The call invites both conceptual and empirical research exploring marketing's role in enabling restoration, renewal, resilience, and long-term stakeholder value creation. Diverse methodologies are welcome, including experiments, surveys, qualitative research, mixed methods, and multi-level or cross-cultural approaches. Papers should address strategic marketing capabilities, brand strategy, consumer behaviour, digital marketing, business models, stakeholder collaboration, and evaluation metrics related to regenerative transformation.

item.title: Strategic Marketing, Technology, and Societal Transformation: Ethics, Power, and Social Change
item.content:encoded:
Reem Khamis Hamdan, The University College of Bahrain

Marketing has evolved beyond economic value creation to encompass broader social impacts, particularly as digital technologies like artificial intelligence and big data become deeply embedded in society. These advancements enable marketing strategies that influence not only consumer behavior but also societal values and well-being, raising critical questions about ethical implications and power dynamics that remain underexplored in academic literature.

This special issue invites research examining how strategic marketing enabled by technology reshapes society and the accompanying ethical and power concerns. The editors seek both theoretical and empirical contributions that illuminate the relationship between marketing strategies and society, with particular emphasis on ethical issues, power imbalances, and societal consequences of marketing in digital environments.

item.content:encoded:

This special issue explores how global ESG pressures interact with local institutions and governance structures in Asia-Pacific economies. Most ESG frameworks are grounded in Western perspectives and often overlook the unique institutional features of APAC regions, including developmental states, government-linked companies, family-owned businesses, and concentrated ownership. The issue seeks research examining how firms interpret, adopt, and adapt global ESG standards within their specific institutional contexts.

The special issue welcomes diverse methodological approaches including qualitative, quantitative, comparative case studies, multi-country analyses, mixed-methods research, and policy-oriented studies. Submissions should address themes such as global ESG pressures and local translation, adaptation of reporting frameworks, investor and supply-chain influences, state-business relations, ownership structures, and corporate responses to sustainability challenges specific to Asia-Pacific contexts.

item.content:encoded:

As AI becomes increasingly integrated into marketing practice, educators must reconsider teaching approaches to prepare students for careers where human judgment and AI collaboration are central. item.title: The Changing Landscape of Influencer Advertising
item.content:encoded:
Jhih-Syuan (Elaine) Lin, National Chengchi University

Chen Lou, Nanyang Technological University

This special issue examines influencer advertising as an evolving interactive system shaped by technological advances, platform algorithms, and changing consumer expectations. The field has shifted from viewing influencers as isolated persuasion sources to understanding them as components within human-machine systems where outcomes emerge from interactions among influencers, platforms, algorithms, and audiences.

The special issue addresses both opportunities and risks in influencer advertising. While new technologies enable brand engagement, influencer advertising also presents boundary conditions and unintended consequences, including concerns about deceptive practices, consumer vulnerability, and well-being impacts, particularly within increasingly AI-mediated ecosystems.

The journal invites original research that theoretically and empirically examines how and when influencer advertising succeeds or fails, with particular emphasis on work integrating contemporary technological contexts and rigorous methodology across consumer behavior, technology innovation, industry development, negative effects, and global trends.

item.title: The crowdfunding of the future and the future of crowdfunding
item.content:encoded:

item.title: The politics of assessment
item.content:encoded:
Juuso Henrik Nieminen, Deakin University

Jan McArthur, Lancaster University

Tim Fawns, Monash University

Assessment profoundly shapes students' lives and identities through grades, examinations, scores, and metrics, yet scholarship has largely overlooked its political dimensions of power, equity, and social justice. This special issue invites critical examination of how assessment functions within higher education, challenging the prevailing view of assessment as neutral and objective.

The issue seeks both theoretical understanding and practical transformation of assessment practices toward greater justice and equity. Authors are invited to submit empirical studies, conceptual analyses, policy reviews, or research syntheses that adopt explicitly socio-political and critical approaches to assessment, engaging with themes such as agency, identity, inclusion, technology, and epistemic justice in assessment.

Submissions must clearly engage with socio-political perspectives while allowing diverse interpretations of what constitutes critical scholarship. Authors should reference the accompanying points of departure article and may engage with or critique its arguments.

Potential topics

  • Teacher and student agency: Who decides how and why assessment is done?
  • Identity, diversity and inclusion: How does assessment exclude and marginalise, and how can it be more equitable?
  • Grading and ungrading: How to disrupt the status quo?
  • Critical theory: How to challenge power and privilege in assessment?
  • Epistemic injustice and colonisation: What counts as legitimate knowledge in assessment?
  • Politics of technology: How does assessment take place in a digital world?

item.content:encoded:

This special issue explores how accounting and accountability can support the achievement of Sustainable Development Goal 11 on sustainable cities and communities. While SDG 11 addresses urban sustainability broadly, existing implementation has been criticised for its top-down orientation, often overlooking the capacity of local communities to inform behaviour change, generate local knowledge, and create participatory spaces. The special issue seeks to understand how accounting and accountability mechanisms can mobilise local capacities to advance a just transition toward SDG 11 that prioritises community voices and participation.

  • The extent to which emancipatory accounting and accountability approaches can shift power from city elites to marginalised communities in pursuit of sustainable cities and communities
  • How conflicts within cities impede sustainability goals achievement and whether accounting and accountability mechanisms can intervene to mediate or resolve such conflicts

item.content:encoded:

The digital economy has fundamentally restructured retail and consumer marketing, blurring boundaries between physical and virtual commerce while intensifying competitive pressures. Consumer expectations now center on personalization, authenticity, and social responsibility, with social media and mobile platforms playing critical roles in shaping purchasing decisions. This transformation presents both opportunities for businesses to strengthen customer relationships through digital tools and challenges related to technology access, market fragmentation, and legacy system integration.

This special issue invites research examining how businesses are adapting retail and marketing strategies to succeed in digital-transformed markets. The editors seek contributions that explore the theoretical foundations, empirical evidence, and practical insights regarding digital transformation in retailing, consumer engagement, distribution systems, and business strategy to guide practitioners, policymakers, and scholars navigating contemporary market shifts.

This special issue examines the intersection of embodiment and business ethics within organizational contexts. The call addresses how bodies are shaped by and through work, labor, and market systems, exploring the ethical implications of emotional labor, physical strain, commodification, and disciplinary practices. It seeks to move business ethics beyond abstract and conceptual frameworks toward understanding how embodied experiences and corporeal practices generate ethical dilemmas in organizational life.

The special issue welcomes diverse methodological approaches to investigating embodied labor across various industries including modeling, sports, healthcare, and entertainment. Contributions should interrogate how organizational norms regulate bodies in ways that reflect broader inequalities related to gender, race, and class, while also considering worker resistance and alternative theoretical frameworks such as feminist ethics and affect theory that center the lived body in ethical analysis.

item.title: Generative AI and New Methods of Inquiry in Information Systems Research
item.content:encoded:
Ahmed Abbasi, University of Notre Dame

Martin Bichler, Technical University of Munich

Ram Gopal, University of Warwick

Elena Karahanna, University of Georgia

Suprateek Sarker, University of Virginia

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping not only organizations, markets, and technologies, but also the practice of scientific research itself. Large language models, multimodal foundation models, and increasingly agentic AI systems now participate in activities such as literature discovery, theorizing, data analysis, simulation, coding, and writing.

This Special Issue seeks papers that push the boundaries of what can be achieved through innovative, rigorous, and responsible use of Generative AI in the information systems research process. Rather than focusing on GenAI solely as an object of empirical study, the SI emphasizes GenAI as a research collaborator, instrument, and infrastructure.

The ambition of the SI is twofold: to publish a small number of exemplary papers that demonstrate novel research capabilities enabled by GenAI, and to advance shared principles, frameworks, and practices that will shape how information systems research is conducted and reported in an era of human–AI collaboration.

Appel publié par Information Systems Research. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Hybrid human–AI workflows for coding, classification, or sensemaking

  • GenAI-supported survey design, sampling, and survey administration
  • GenAI-supported experimental design, treatment generation, and implementation
  • GenAI-supported computational theory construction
  • Simulation, agent-based modeling, or scenario generation
  • GenAI-enabled qualitative analysis, theory building, or inductive discovery
  • GenAI-assisted econometric modeling, estimation, or robustness analysis
  • AI-supported proof search, counterexample generation, or equilibrium exploration
  • Discovery or validation of analytical models using generative simulation
  • GenAI-assisted testing of operational utility and/or design validity
  • Design and evaluation of GenAI-based tools for IS research
  • Reproducible pipelines, benchmarks, and evaluation harnesses
  • Systems supporting transparency, provenance, and verification

item.title: Capturing Value in the Digital Era: Organizing for Innovation Protection and Information Security
item.content:encoded:
R&D Management has a rich publication history in research on appropriability, intellectual capital and capturing value from innovation. This special issue seeks to update and extend that tradition by explicitly bringing together two adjacent but typically separated conversations.

The first conversation conceptualizes protection of innovation in relation to appropriability mechanisms such as patents, trade secrecy, licensing, contracting, complementary assets, and ecosystem governance to investigate value capture potential.

The second conversation - so far mainly happening in information systems and engineering journals - conceptualizes protection of innovation as information security, such as the protection of R&D artifacts, risks of leakage and theft, industrial espionage, and applications of organizational secrecy for R&D purposes.

Appel publié par R and D Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Protection of R&D artifacts
  • Risks of leakage and theft in innovation
  • Industrial espionage
  • Organizational secrecy for R&D purposes
  • Information security in innovation management
  • Intellectual capital and capturing value from innovation

item.title: The Non-Human Innovator: Agentic AI, Physical AI, and the Transformation of R&D Management
item.content:encoded:
This Special Issue is explicitly positioned around a question that existing work on AI-enabled knowledge search, collaboration management, and general AI governance has not yet answered: what happens when AI ceases to be a mere instrument and becomes an agent of innovation? This distinction — between AI-as-tool and AI-as-innovator — defines the conceptual boundary of our four research themes, which address the optimal human–AI division of innovative labour, the architecture of autonomously populated innovation ecosystems, the reimagination of absorptive capacity for an agentic era, and the fundamental challenges to IP posed by non-human inventorship.

Appel publié par R and D Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Optimal human-AI division of innovative labour
  • Architecture of autonomously populated innovation ecosystems
  • Reimagination of absorptive capacity for an agentic era
  • Fundamental challenges to intellectual property posed by non-human inventorship

item.title: Bridging digitalisation, sustainability, and resilience through systems thinking tools: Integrated perspectives and collaborative practices for SMEs
item.content:encoded:
Rui Torres de Oliveira, Deakin University

Agnes Toth-Peter, University of Queensland

Martie-Louise Verreynne, University of Queensland

David Audretsch, Indiana University

Domenico Dentoni, MBS School of Business

Andrea Chiarini, University of Verona

This special issue explores how systems thinking tools and methodologies can address interconnected challenges of sustainability, digitalization, and resilience, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises. The collection seeks to move beyond superficial adoption of systems thinking toward genuine systemic change that integrates digital technologies, circular economy principles, and collaborative multi-stakeholder approaches to tackle complex, wicked problems.

The special issue invites theoretical and empirical research demonstrating real applications of systems thinking frameworks such as causal loop diagrams, system dynamics models, and participatory methods. Contributions should illuminate how holistic, systems-level perspectives can uncover hidden leverage points and foster innovative solutions that align digital transformation with sustainability goals while building organizational resilience.

Appel publié par Journal of Small Business Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Applications of systems thinking tools, such as causal loop diagrams, system archetypes, and system dynamics modeling, in addressing sustainability challenges
  • Development and validation of systems-level frameworks and methodologies for sustainable development
  • Case studies demonstrating the impact of systems thinking on real-world sustainability and/or digitalisation initiatives
  • Use of group model building and participatory system dynamics to support interdisciplinary and ecosystem solutions
  • Exploration of system archetypes and system dynamics models to identify leverage points for driving transformational change and to investigate levers in cross-boundary settings
  • The role of digital technologies, including IoT, AI, big data, and blockchain, in enabling systems-level insights and solutions in the circular economy and sustainability initiatives
  • Integration of digitalisation with circular economy strategies and Industry 5.0 principles and potentials
  • Innovative approaches to digital transformation that promote sustainable development
  • Cross-sectoral and interdisciplinary research to foster collaboration in bridging sustainability and digitalisation, using systems thinking
  • The role of ecosystems in sustainable business models and the boundaries of entrepreneurial ecosystems
  • Methodologies for recognising, assessing and addressing the interconnectedness of environmental, economic, and social systems
  • Open innovation in new sustainable businesses, considering distinct institutional contexts and economic systems, such as emerging and developed economies

Timeline

  • October 1, 2026: Rolling submissions open
  • May 31, 2027: Manuscript deadline

item.title: Reimagining Small Business Futures - AI, Inclusion, and Territorial Innovation
item.content:encoded:
Nicola Cucari, Sapienza University of Rome

Guanglei Zhang, Wuhan University of Technology

Jintao Lu, Shanxi University of Electronic Science and Technology

Hua Fan, Shanghai International Studies University

Eric Liguori, Florida State University

This special issue examines how artificial intelligence is transforming small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across three interconnected dimensions: technological transformation, inclusive innovation, and territorial ecosystem development. The special issue seeks to move beyond simple technology adoption perspectives to explore how AI reconfigures organizational capabilities, entrepreneurial cognition, stakeholder relationships, and value creation mechanisms in SMEs. The call welcomes both theoretical and empirical studies that provide novel insights into how SMEs can leverage AI to achieve sustainable growth while addressing challenges related to investment capacity, skills gaps, cybersecurity, and unequal access to digital infrastructure.

Appel publié par Journal of Small Business Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • AI-driven business model innovation in SMEs
  • Digital transformation pathways under technological turbulence
  • AI and sustainable competitive advantage in resource-constrained firms
  • AI-enabled work redesign and organizational reconfiguration in SMEs
  • Inclusive AI ecosystems for minority, women, migrant, and informal entrepreneurs
  • Algorithmic Bias and transparency in AI-assisted SMEs
  • AI-enabled territorial innovation and smart regional development
  • Public policies supporting equitable AI adoption among SMEs
  • AI, cybersecurity, and risk governance in small businesses
  • Human–AI collaboration and entrepreneurial decision-making
  • Data strategies and knowledge management in SMEs
  • Data ownership and territorial digital autonomy in AI-driven SME development
  • Ethical, social, and governance implications of AI adoption
  • AI platforms and SME participation in digital value chains
  • AI for local resilience, crisis response, and adaptive entrepreneurship

item.title: Artificial Intelligence–Enabled Production Systems: Empirical Evidence, Implementation Pipelines, and Industrial Applications
item.content:encoded:
Ruoqi Geng, Cardiff University

Di Li, Warwick University

Yang Cheng, Aalborg University

This special issue addresses how artificial intelligence is becoming embedded in production systems, moving beyond standalone analytics tools to operational capabilities that reshape real-time planning, control, and improvement. The key challenge lies in integrating point solutions—such as deep reinforcement learning for rescheduling or deep learning for predictive maintenance—into reliable end-to-end workflows validated across diverse industrial settings.

The special issue emphasizes empirically grounded research examining the complete AI implementation pipeline in production contexts. This includes business–AI alignment (translating production decisions into AI use cases), data readiness (governance, preparation, and integration), and deployment of AI into operational workflows. The focus is on understanding the enabling and constraining factors—data availability, organisational readiness, and human–AI interaction—that determine whether AI solutions succeed in real production environments.

Appel publié par Production Planning & Control. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • AI-Augmented Production Planning and Control
  • Business–AI Alignment and AI Readiness Pipeline for Production Systems
  • AI-enabled Quality and Process Control
  • Agentic and Workflow-Oriented Deployment in Production
  • AI-Enabled Cyber–Physical Production Systems and Digital Twins
  • AI and Additive Manufacturing
  • AI and Blockchain for Production Systems
  • Human–AI Interaction and Organisational Transformation
  • Empirical Innovations in Data, Measurement, and Evaluation

item.title: Enhancing Transparency and Replicability in Entrepreneurship Research with Preregistrations, Registered Reports, and Registered Revisions
item.content:encoded:
Katharina Fellnhofer, ETH Zurich

Karl Wennberg, Stockholm School of Economics

Thomas H. Allison, Texas Christian University

Pia Arenius, Emlyon Business School

Moren Lévesque, York University

J. Jeffrey Gish, Syracuse University

Jeffrey M. Pollack, NC State University

Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice (ETP) is committed to working alongside entrepreneurship scholars to advance transparency, replicability, credibility, and rigor in empirical research. This special issue encourages authors to preregister research plans, submit empirical studies as Registered Reports — papers that receive editorial decisions before empirical results are known — and engage with ETP's contemporary Registered Revision process. ETP is pleased to announce a virtual special issue featuring Registered Reports, supporting its longstanding dedication to methodological innovation.

A growing body of literature spanning multiple disciplines including entrepreneurship explores the importance of credibility and replicability in scientific inquiry and how scientific rigor can be improved. This call for papers reinforces these efforts in entrepreneurship research by specifically advocating for scholars to submit studies as Registered Reports. The Registered Report format has evolved rapidly from a niche innovation to a widely adopted practice. Since the introduction of the Registered Report format in 2013, more than 300 journals have embraced the approach.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Replication and Robustness in Entrepreneurship Research
  • New Ways to Collect Data for Entrepreneurship
  • Importance of Null Results
  • Boundary Conditions, Mechanisms, Mediators, and Contextual Sensitivity
  • Longitudinal and Panel-Based Studies (Using Secondary Data)
  • Field Experiments and Entrepreneurial Interventions
  • Theory-Driven Exploratory Studies and Qualitative Studies
  • Meta-Science and Methods in Entrepreneurship Research

  • December 22, 2026: Deadline for Registered Report submissions

item.title: Entrepreneurship Ex Machina: Transformative Artificial Intelligence for Theory and Practice
item.content:encoded:
Martin Obschonka, University of Amsterdam

Moren Lévesque, York University

Frédéric Ooms, HEC Liège

Jeffrey M. Pollack, NC State University

Denis A. Grégoire, HEC Montréal

Tara S. Behrend, Michigan State University

Boris Nikolaev, Colorado State University

Transformative Artificial Intelligence (AI) — that is, the use of AI tools that have such inherent capabilities that they could induce societal transitions similar to that of the agricultural or industrial revolutions — has become an omnipresent topic of interest. Because these tools offer order-of-magnitude efficiency improvements over prior ways of performing various human tasks, important research opportunities arise for better understanding their transformative impact.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Theorizing on algorithmic entrepreneurship
  • Mechanisms of external enablement of entrepreneurship via AI (e.g., generative AI)
  • Can AI help reduce the destructive aspects of entrepreneurship (e.g., societal and personal costs)?
  • Can AI create resource abundance, overcoming typical entrepreneurial resource scarcity and challenging leading startup methods (e.g., effectuation/bricolage, bootstrapping, lean startup)?
  • Do classic research findings and theories (e.g., on the role of knowledge and human and social capital in entrepreneurship) still hold in the new AI era?
  • How can AI impact entrepreneurial finance (e.g., AI-powered financial planning for entrepreneurs, VC investment portfolio management and decisions) and resource acquisition (e.g., entrepreneurs' pitch preparation, investors' due diligence, etc.)?
  • Does AI change the age curve associated with entrepreneurship (does it replace the advantage of industry experience, and do we therefore see an AI-empowered rise of youth entrepreneurs)?
  • How can AI contribute to equality and diversity (e.g., neurodiversity, closing the gender gap)?
  • Ethical and legal issues of algorithmic entrepreneurship and AI-supported research
  • How can AI support entrepreneurs' cognition, decision making, and psychological well-being?
  • Will the emerging AI economy of abundance replace entrepreneurship/human entrepreneurs?

Timeline

  • January 31, 2026: Final deadline for proposal submissions

item.title: Organizing Sustainably with Nature in the Global South
item.content:encoded:
Simone Barakat, Fundação Getulio Vargas

Maria Ehrnström-Fuentes, Hanken School of Economics

Seray Ergene, University of Rhode Island

Steffen Farny, Leuphana University Luneburg

Judy Muthuri, University of the West Indies

Contemporary sustainability challenges increasingly foreground organizations as embedded within complex social-ecological systems rather than operating independently from them. While ecological degradation and resource constraints affect organizations worldwide, these challenges are more immediate and structurally embedded in the operating environments of the Global South. These challenges are not just a background context to which organizations must adapt but an outcome of long-standing patterns of extraction, uneven development, and entrenched social inequalities that continue to shape what sustainability can mean in practice.

Appel publié par Organization & Environment. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Organizing for Environmental Sustainability across Communities and Regions - How do communities and organizations work together to govern natural resources and shared ecological commons?
  • How do sustainability standards, certifications, and supply-chain rules influence organizational practices across regions?
  • How do organizations manage environmental interdependencies across local and global contexts?
  • What challenges arise when local ecological priorities clash with global market or regulatory pressures, and how do organizations deal with these challenges in practice?
  • Organizing with Nature from a Global South perspective - How do organizations in the Global South manage their activities within the carrying ecological capacity of the planet (i.e., planetary boundaries), particularly under conditions of resource constraints and institutional fragility?
  • How do organizations in the Global South engage with degrowth, sufficiency, circular, or regenerative practices?
  • What tensions do organizations in the Global South face between economic survival and ecological realities, and how do they navigate these circumstances in practice?
  • How organizations in the Global South conceptualize and manage their embeddedness within social–ecological systems and attempt to develop a regenerative dynamic with nature?
  • Power, Inequality, and the Governance of Nature - What are the sources of environmental injustices currently in the global South? How are they experienced? What are some resistances to these injustices, and how do they unfold? What are some policy mechanisms (if any) to address these injustices?
  • How do power asymmetries manifest in sustainability governance and transnational regulations?
  • How do corporations influence environmental policy and access to natural resources?
  • How do resistance and counter-organizing emerge around contested environmental futures?
  • Stakeholders and Environmental Sustainability from a Global South Perspective - How do organizations in the Global South engage with stakeholders in relation to environmental sustainability?
  • How are the interests of diverse stakeholders, such as communities, governments, NGOs, and other stakeholders, navigated around environmental risks and resource use?
  • How do stakeholder relationships influence organizational decisions and practices related to environmental sustainability?
  • How do power asymmetries and dependency relations among stakeholders shape environmental outcomes and organizing processes?

Timeline

  • October 20, 2026: Paper Development Workshop
  • February 28, 2027: Full manuscript submission deadline

item.title: Reconceptualizing Careers in Disruptive Times
item.content:encoded:
Jos Akkermans, VU University

David G. Collings, Trinity College Dublin

Mila Lazarova, Simon Fraser University

Jennifer Tosti-Kharas, Babson College

Career theory has evolved over recent decades. Classic career theories were grounded in relatively stable organizational contexts with hierarchical career paths and a relatively stable external context. In the 1990s, there was increasing recognition of the emergence of more flexible, dynamic careers, driven by technological disruption, demographic shifts, and the rise of non-traditional work and career paths. This development is still often referred to as the 'new career' paradigm. Career theories (e.g., boundaryless career theory, protean career theory, and social cognitive career theory) and concepts (e.g., career orientations, career competencies, and career self-management) within that paradigm primarily emphasize theorizing how individuals can take charge and successfully navigate volatile career paths.

Appel publié par Organizational Psychology Review. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do ongoing social, technological, and geopolitical disruptions challenge existing assumptions embedded in dominant career theories?
  • How can new conceptual models better account for the relational and contextual aspects of career development in uncertain and changing environments?
  • How should we reconceptualize concepts such as career competencies and employability in labor markets characterized by volatility, automation, and shifting skill demands?
  • How can careers be reconceptualized in non-traditional work, including the gig economy, internal job deconstruction, and entrepreneurship?
  • How do new forms of digital, hybrid, or platform-mediated work reshape notions of career identity, career success, and career self-management?
  • What role does AI, including agentic AI, and the potential role of AI agents as co-workers play in how individuals' careers evolve?
  • How can career theories and concepts be adapted or renewed to capture the career experiences of underrepresented and marginalized groups?
  • How do organizational, institutional, and labor market structures shape individuals' capacity to construct meaningful and sustainable career paths during times of disruption?
  • How do global mobility patterns, migration, and geopolitical conflict reshape traditional narratives of career progression and mobility?
  • What new methodological or conceptual tools are needed to theorize non-linear, fragmented, or cyclical career patterns that increasingly deviate from traditional career models?

Timeline

  • Invalid DateTime: Expected finalization of the Special Issue
  • May 1, 2027: Full paper submission deadline

item.title: Time in Entrepreneurship: New Perspectives and Approaches
item.content:encoded:
Ludvig Levasseur, Indian Institute of Management Bangalore

Moren Lévesque, York University

Paul Spee, University of Queensland

Ute Stephan, King's College London

Matthew Wood, University of Oklahoma

This special issue seeks manuscripts advancing our understanding of time in entrepreneurship. Research on the duration, pace, timing, and speed of action calibration in entrepreneurial processes such as opportunity realization are key examples of the role temporal dynamics play in entrepreneurship. Time is equally critical when examining decisions about the timing of growth while managing external events and shocks alongside slowly or rapidly evolving industry trends and customer preferences. Further lines of inquiry concern the pace, timing, and speed of exit decisions, or decisions to pursue venturing activities over time. Entrepreneurs' subjective perceptions of time, and their own and their stakeholders' orientations towards the short- vs. long-term, the past, present or future shape how they navigate entrepreneurship.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do objective dimensions such as duration, pace, timing, speed, and window of opportunity impact the entrepreneurship process?
  • How do they shape links between entrepreneurs' subjective time perspective, their biological time (chronotype), and cognitive processes related to information scanning and learning?
  • How do entrepreneurs' subjective time perspectives relate to their cognitions including information scanning and search, entrepreneurial learning, information associations and connections, and opportunity evaluation and judgment?
  • How do time perspectives relate to informal investors' and venture capitalists' decision to provide funding?
  • How do investors' time perspectives shape who they invest in, and the timing and size of their investments?
  • With what pace and speed do failure consequences vary with institutional and cultural contexts?
  • How does the timing of these consequences vary across groups of entrepreneurs including minoritized groups and differently abled entrepreneurs?
  • When and how does time perspective lead to unhealthy persistence in entrepreneurship and undermine well-being?
  • How do entrepreneurs' perception of time and the temporal development of the business impact venture emergence, business sustainability, and social entrepreneurship?
  • Do we see variations in temporal profiles and differences across industries and cultures?
  • How do the pacing of external events and entrepreneurs' own time perspective relate to how they manage equity, diversity, decolonization, and inclusion within their ventures?

Timeline

  • September 30, 2027: Submission deadline

item.title: Advancing Management Research Through Theory Testing: A Special Issue of Replication and Reproducibility Studies
item.content:encoded:
William G. Obenauer, University of Maine

Robyn L. Brouer, University of South Alabama

Rachel Clapp-Smith, University of North Georgia

Ajay Rama Ponnapalli, Wayne State University

Andreas Schwab, Iowa State University
