item.title: Les TPE : vers de nouveaux modèles d'affaires ?
item.content:encoded:
Marion Polge, Université de Montpellier

Isabelle Calmé, Université de Tours

Colette Fourcade, Université de Montpellier

Les très petites entreprises (TPE) restent largement sous-étudiées malgré leur importance statistique et sociale. Ce numéro interroge si elles constituent des organisations singulières au-delà de simples PME réduites. Par leur légèreté structurelle, leurs interactions intenses et leur proximité territoriale, elles développent des modes d'ajustement innovants et des dynamiques entrepreneuriales spécifiques, plus sobres et résilientes que les organisations plus établies.

Depuis 2020, les mutations systémiques – crises sanitaires, défis écologiques, numérisation – transforment profondément les TPE. Le numéro explore comment elles réinventent la performance au-delà de la croissance, adoptant des approches multiformes axées sur l'équilibre, la durabilité et l'impact local. Les nouvelles technologies créent tant des opportunités que des vulnérabilités pour ces organisations.

Appel publié par Revue internationale P M E Économie et gestion de la petite et moyenne entreprise. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Trajectoires stratégiques atypiques et diversification des profils de dirigeants de TPE : profils, motivations, rapport au travail et au risque, bifurcations de parcours
  • Redéfinition de la performance dans les TPE : indicateurs alternatifs, refus de la croissance, équilibre de vie, ancrage territorial, relations au vivant
  • TPE, écologie et raréfaction des ressources : modèles économiques frugaux, économie circulaire, décroissance choisie, entreprise régénérative, impact écologique
  • TPE et technologies : appropriation, marginalisation ou résistance face à la numérisation, à l'intelligence artificielle, à l'ubérisation ou à la plate-forme-économie
  • Formes alternatives d'organisation et d'innovation : bricolage, mutualisation, coopération, hybridation des statuts, pratiques informelles ou hybrides
  • Rôle des TPE dans les transitions sociales et territoriales : résilience locale, dynamiques d'inclusion, réponses aux crises systémiques, justice économique
  • Méthodologies et épistémologies de recherche adaptées aux TPE : recherches partenariales, approches critiques, récits de vie, ethnographie entrepreneuriale

La revue Finance Contrôle Stratégie (FCS) est une revue en sciences de gestion consacrée aux recherches de pointe dans les domaines de la finance, de la comptabilité, du contrôle de gestion et de la stratégie. Elle vise à favoriser les échanges entre chercheurs de ces spécialités, en encourageant des approches transversales sur des thèmes d'actualité.

Dans un contexte international caractérisé par la recrudescence des conflits armés, l'exacerbation des tensions entre grandes puissances et le recours accru aux sanctions économiques et aux guerres commerciales, ainsi que par la persistance de déficits publics en Europe, les perturbations des chaînes d'approvisionnement et l'intensité des flux migratoires, les enjeux de souveraineté technologique et énergétique prennent une importance croissante.

item.title: Advancing towards a Responsible and Resilient Digital Future
item.content:encoded:
Imon Chakraborty, Indian Institute of Technology Madras

Saji K Mathew, Indian Institute of Technology Madras

Nargis Pervin, Indian Institute of Technology Madras

Viswanath Venkatesh, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University

Digital technologies like AI, platforms, and IoT are transforming organizations and society, creating both significant value and serious risks including algorithmic bias, privacy violations, and cybersecurity threats. This special issue seeks research on information systems that are simultaneously responsible—fair, transparent, ethical, and respectful of human rights—and resilient, able to withstand disruptions and recover from failures.

The research community needs theoretically grounded and empirically rigorous studies that move beyond simple technology adoption narratives to examine post-adoption use, value realization, human-machine collaboration, and the long-term impacts of digital systems. Information systems researchers are uniquely positioned to explore how responsibility and resilience interplay across individuals, organizations, institutions, and society.

The special issue welcomes submissions using various research methods that advance understanding of responsible and resilient digital futures in specific technological and organizational contexts. It is linked to the InCIS 2027 conference but is also open to all authors through direct submission.

Appel publié par Information Systems Frontiers. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Digital Trust, Privacy, and Cybersecurity

item.title: Creating, Measuring, and Managing Impact in Complex Service Systems
item.content:encoded:
A complex service system is an interdependent multi-actor system of service providers and users that jointly produce and deliver services, with outcomes emerging dynamically through interactions across contexts. Complex service systems such as healthcare, financial services, public administration, education, and social care significantly shape the wellbeing of individuals and societies by determining how essential services are delivered, which in turn directly affects people's daily lives and long-term outcomes. Innovation in these settings is often practice-driven rather than theory-driven. Professionals embedded within service delivery contexts are positioned at the interface of users and operational realities, where they continuously encounter emerging needs, service breakdowns, and contextual constraints. This enables them to generate need-based, practice-led innovations that directly reshape service processes and outcomes. Many studies offer theoretical advancements in identifying the factors and processes that may influence service performance within the system, yet they provide limited evidence of how research-based insights translate into tangible change in practice.

Appel publié par European Journal of Marketing. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • What frameworks and metrics can be used to assess behavioural, cognitive, relational, or systemic change resulting from research, and how can they capture impacts across the diverse stakeholders involved in complex service systems?
  • How can research impact in complex services be understood and assessed beyond financial metrics, including intellectual, professional, social, and personal development outcomes across diverse stakeholder groups?
  • How do the interdependencies, governance structures, and stakeholder relationships characteristic of complex service systems enable or inhibit research impact?
  • What common patterns or trajectories of impact emerge across complex service systems, particularly in relation to how value and impact are distributed among multiple stakeholders over time?
  • What mechanisms pathways enable the progression from awareness to engagement and ultimately to sustained change in generating research impact, and how are these shaped by the complexity of service systems and stakeholder interactions?
  • What forms of longitudinal or field-based evidence are needed to capture dynamic changes in stakeholder mindsets, behaviours, and systemic outcomes in complex service systems characterised by interdependence and co-evolution?
  • What roles do co-creation, stakeholder collaboration, and service design play in enabling research impact across multiple stakeholders, and how do these processes operate within complex service systems?
  • How do intervention-based or design-based research approaches produce and sustain measurable behavioural, organisational, and system-level outcomes in complex service systems characterised by interdependent actors and dynamic change?
  • In what ways have research insights informed and reshaped policy, professional practice, service design, or stakeholder decision-making in complex service systems characterised by interdependent actors and competing stakeholder priorities?
  • Under what conditions is research impact realised, scaled, sustained, or constrained within complex service systems characterised by interdependent actors, institutional complexity, and dynamic change?
  • How can researchers capture and evaluate both short-term and long-term impact in complex service systems characterised by interdependence, co-evolution, and evolving stakeholder relationships?
  • How can researchers identify both intended and unintended consequences of research impact in complex service systems characterised by interdependent actors and competing stakeholder interests?
  • What ethical considerations arise in the design, implementation, and measurement of research impact in complex service systems characterised by interdependent actors, power asymmetries, and potentially uneven distribution of benefits and harms?
  • How do power dynamics shape what is defined, recognised, and prioritised as "valuable" outcomes in evaluating research impact in complex service systems characterised by interdependent actors, institutional logics, and unequal stakeholder influence?
  • How are impacts of complex services experienced differently across stakeholder groups?
  • What stakeholder voices have been underrepresented in research in complex services?
  • How can organisations identify and manage unequal or unintended stakeholder impacts complex service systems in which actors are interdependent, influence is unevenly distributed, and outcomes are experienced differently across stakeholders?
  • How do professional, organisational, and societal interests align or conflict in complex service contexts?

Timeline

item.title: Reimagining Accounting for Inclusive Capitalism
item.content:encoded:
Charl de Villiers, University of Auckland

Ruth Dimes, The Open University

Anwar Halari, The Open University

Matteo Molinari, University of Bergamo

Capitalism remains the dominant framework for organising global economic life, yet its promises of prosperity and inclusion have increasingly come under scrutiny. Over the past few decades, the richest 1% have captured more than half of global wealth, while environmental degradation has accelerated at an alarming rate, threatening planetary boundaries. These outcomes have prompted growing calls for more inclusive and sustainable forms of capitalism, leading to the emergence of the concept of Inclusive Capitalism. Inclusive Capitalism seeks to reconcile profit-making with broader societal goals such as environmental stewardship, social justice and economic inclusion. However, its very emergence implies a failure of traditional neoliberal capitalism to deliver on its promises of inclusivity and prosperity. The push for Inclusive Capitalism thus reflects a growing recognition of capitalism's contradictions and the need to rethink how value is defined, measured and distributed.

Appel publié par Accounting, Auditing & Accountability Journal. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Historical and Conceptual Foundations: How has capitalism been historically conceptualised and what role has accounting played in shaping the boundaries of inclusion and exclusion in capitalist systems?
  • Accounting and the Language of Inclusion: How is capitalism linguistically constructed in corporate reports, policy documents, and the media? Why and how has the term 'capital' become associated more with financial capital than other forms of capital (natural, social, human, intellectual) and what are the implications of this? How do metaphors and anthropomorphic representations influence perceptions of accounting's role?
  • Accounting and Technology: How are emerging technologies shaping accounting practices that either widen or narrow inclusion? How might they entrench exclusion, concentrate power, or reinforce surveillance logics within capitalist systems? How is capitalism represented and contested in digital platforms and social media?
  • Critical Perspectives: How do accounting practices reflect and reproduce capitalist logics? What are the tensions between accountability, transparency, and inclusion in capitalist enterprises? Can alternative frameworks (e.g., feminist, indigenous, or social accounting) challenge dominant paradigms?
  • Institutional and Policy Dimensions: How can governments, regulators, and standard-setters use accounting to promote more inclusive and responsible capitalism? What are the implications of developments such as integrated reporting, sustainability standards, and ESG metrics?
  • Religion, Culture and Norms: How do religious organisations, cultural traditions and societal norms shape accounting practices and in what way do these practices create pathways that can support financial and social inclusion, or, conversely, undermine such goals?
  • Management Accounting Practices: How can management accounting systems incorporate multi-capital perspectives? What role do incentive structures and performance measurement play? How do managers change the way they think and act to reflect more integrated and inclusive ways of thinking about value creation?

Timeline

  • July 7, 2026: Workshop date in Bergamo, Italy
  • November 1, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions

item.title: Cold Cases: Revisiting founding myths, iconic cases, and forgotten stories in management
item.content:encoded:
Anaïs Boutru, Université Paris-Dauphine, PSL

Linda Rouleau, HEC Montréal

Géraldine Schmidt, Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne

Albéric Tellier, Université Paris-Dauphine, PSL

Management research has long been populated by celebrated cases that have achieved the status of founding myths. Cases such as IBM's blindness to personal computing, Xerox's strategic myopia toward the graphical user interface, Nokia's fall to smartphones, the Mann Gulch fire, and Elton Mayo's Hawthorne experiments have become ubiquitous in the field's collective memory. These 'cold cases', endlessly cited and taught, structure ways of thinking and provide a shared foundation of representations that are central to the construction of epistemic communities.

Despite their pervasive influence, few studies scrutinize the empirical robustness, theoretical validity, or performativity of these emblematic cases. In management research, particularly in qualitative research, the risk of circularity is significant. Researchers working with inevitably heterogeneous and incomplete material may, even unconsciously, select data that confirm their theoretical priors, set aside disconfirming evidence, and ultimately favor demonstrations of the 'as if' type.

Appel publié par M@n@gement. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Reexamination and reinterpretation of canonical management cases (IBM, Xerox, Nokia, Kodak, Enron, etc.)
  • Empirical robustness and theoretical validity of emblematic cases in management scholarship
  • Performativity of famous cases and their role as epistemic artifacts
  • Processes of canonization and erasure in disciplinary memory
  • Circularity in qualitative management research and issues of confirmation bias
  • Role of founding myths in structuring management thinking and epistemic communities
  • Halo effects and the stratification of knowledge in management research
  • Forgotten cases and alternative narratives in management history
  • Critical reexamination of the Hawthorne experiments and other foundational studies
  • Replication, falsification, and verification in management research
  • Archaeology of management knowledge and disciplinary self-reflexivity

item.title: Social change, backlash, and resistance in organizations
item.content:encoded:
Sarah Richard, Audencia Business School

Lucie Noury, Audencia Business School

Pauline de Becdelièvre, Université Paris Saclay

Céline Louche, Waikato Management School—University of Waikato

Stéphan Pezé, Université Toulouse Capitole

The production and dissemination of knowledge, particularly on inequalities, climate change, and biodiversity, are increasingly under attack. These attacks are reflected in some political and administrative decisions adopted across several national contexts, such as the measures taken by President Donald Trump since his return to power. Beyond the US, academic freedom is being directly or indirectly undermined in many countries. For example, in France, controversies surrounding 'Islamo-leftism' within universities, reignited by the Minister of Higher Education, have been accompanied by concrete attacks on several scientific institutions.

Appel publié par M@n@gement. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • What are the different forms of backlash affecting organizations? Are there 'invisible' forms of backlash?
  • How and to what extent does backlash contribute to the deinstitutionalization of established norms (e.g. ESG, DEI, climate)?
  • What forms of institutional work produce or hinder backlash?
  • What roles do different modes of governance and different forms of organization play in weakening or, conversely, protecting social progress? Are democratic organizations, in particular, more or less prone to backlash?
  • How do organizations respond, resist, protect themselves, and participate in backlash?
  • What are the risks, uncertainties, and tensions generated by backlash? How can they be managed?
  • What forms of collective response are organized to face backlash (e.g. meta-organizations, networks, lobbying)?
  • How do individuals participate in or resist backlash (e.g. through employee activism)?
  • What is the impact of backlash on individuals (identity, career paths, values, social representations, experience)?
  • How does backlash transform or disrupt individuals' relationships with work and the company?
  • What forms of individual and collective resistance to backlash can be observed? What are the conditions and effects of this resistance?
  • What is the role of researchers and what stance should they adopt in response to this phenomenon?
  • What methodological and epistemological approaches are best suited to studying backlash, its mechanisms, and its consequences? What methodological innovations are needed to better understand its contemporary forms?
  • How can organizational theory contribute to understanding the phenomenon of backlash?
  • What are the multi-level interactions between societal, organizational, and individual backlash?
  • How can backlash contribute to the emergence of other backlashes?

item.title: Anti-Environmentalism and the Future of Green Growth
item.content:encoded:
Anastasios Xepapadeas, Athens University of Economics and Business

Simone Marsiglio, University of Pisa

Luca Gori, University of Pisa

The special issue examines anti-environmentalism—opposition to environmental regulation, renewable energy expansion, and climate mitigation efforts—and its implications for achieving green growth and sustainable development. It addresses how public attitudes, political polarization, and institutional factors shape the feasibility and design of environmental policies in the context of escalating climate risks and planetary boundaries.

The collection seeks research across environmental economics, macroeconomics, political economy, and behavioral economics that explores the causes, dynamics, and consequences of anti-environmental movements for sustainable economic transitions. It welcomes diverse methodological approaches, with particular emphasis on studies that clarify the complex relationships between anti-environmentalism, economic incentives, and policy effectiveness in facilitating low-carbon development.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence, Affective Computing and Video Analytics for Intelligent Information Systems
item.content:encoded:
Andrea Generosi, Pegaso University

Luigi Gallo, Pegaso University

Valerio De Luca, Pegaso University

Maura Mengoni, Marche Polytechnic University

Josef Spjut, NVIDIA

Lucio De Paolis, University of Salento

This special issue addresses the intersection of video analytics and affective computing in intelligent information systems. With video data rapidly expanding across surveillance, retail, sports, and social platforms, combined with advances in deep learning and multimodal models, there is growing potential to extract emotional and social signals from visual content to enhance user engagement, recommendation systems, and decision-making processes.

The collection seeks original research, surveys, and perspectives on methods that fuse visual, auditory, and textual data to detect emotion, sentiment, engagement, and intent in real time. Topics include scalable video processing architectures, emotion recognition from video, multimodal analysis techniques, streaming-native AI systems, explainability and fairness in affective AI, and domain-specific applications in healthcare, finance, education, and smart environments.

Appel publié par Information Systems Frontiers. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Scalable video understanding: algorithms and architectures for analyzing large-scale video streams (e.g. in surveillance, social media or enterprise) to support decision-making and business analytics.
  • Emotion and sentiment analysis: detection of affective and engagement cues in video (e.g. customer-journey recordings, advertisement viewing, user-generated content).
  • Multimodal fusion: methods that combine vision with audio, text or other modalities to enrich social-media intelligence and contextual analysis.
  • Streaming-native AI and MLOps: online inference under tight latency budgets, stream processing/windowing, drift detection, A/B testing and safe rollouts, cost–latency–accuracy trade-offs, and end-to-end observability for production pipelines.
  • Video(-language) models for streaming: multimodal LLMs/VLMs, memory and token compression for long-horizon video, retrieval-augmented streaming.
  • Real-time and distributed architectures: edge/cloud or federated systems for real-time video analytics at scale, including considerations of latency, bandwidth and privacy.
  • Explainability, fairness and compliance: approaches to make affective video AI transparent and trustworthy, addressing ethical, legal and regulatory challenges.
  • Adaptive learning: techniques for domain adaptation, continual learning or few-shot learning to handle evolving video streams and reduce the need for large labeled datasets.
  • Case studies and applications: empirical studies in domains such as healthcare (e.g. remote patient monitoring), finance (e.g. behavioral analytics), education (e.g. XR/serious games environments), and smart environments.

item.title: Bibliometric Measures of Epistemic Change
item.content:encoded:
Bibliometrics has long sought to measure epistemic change through publication data, but current approaches are constrained by methodological conventions. Recent indicators attempting to measure novelty, originality, or disruptiveness in individual papers rely on three problematic assumptions: that epistemic change is a discrete event rather than a process, that it is fully contained in a single paper, and that quantifiable measures can replace detailed descriptions of the specific nature of changes.

The field faces fundamental challenges in validating bibliometric measures of epistemic change, including reliance on bibliographic metadata whose relationship to actual paper content remains unclear, the need for ground truths to test new methods, and questions about what information in metadata can support such measurement. This special collection brings together work from a series of workshops addressing how epistemic change can be properly conceptualized, operationalized, validated, and identified using both traditional bibliometric approaches and emerging computational methods.

Appel publié par Scientometrics. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Conceptualisation and operationalisation of epistemic change for bibliometric tracing
  • Construction of ground truths for developing and testing bibliometric methods
  • Metadata content relevant to epistemic change in bibliographic records
  • Validation of established bibliometric indicators against ground truths
  • Application of large language models to full texts for identifying epistemic change

Timeline

item.title: Building Digital Capabilities for Improved ESG Performance of Entrepreneurial Firms: Strategies for Tackling Challenges and Capitalizing on Opportunities
item.content:encoded:
Stefano Bresciani, University of Torino

Jawad Abbas, James Cook University

Fauzia Jabeen, Abu Dhabi University

Technological advancements require entrepreneurial firms to strategically develop digital capabilities to enhance their competitiveness, innovation capacity, and sustainable performance. This collection seeks to explore how such firms build digital capabilities to improve their environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance while addressing challenges in integrating digital solutions for sustainability.

The collection recognizes that entrepreneurial ventures, characterized by innovation and agility, play a critical role in advancing digital-driven sustainable business practices. Improved ESG performance is essential for managing environmental and social risks, enhancing corporate reputation, and meeting stakeholder expectations regarding ethical and responsible business conduct. The collection welcomes experimental, conceptual, theoretical, and empirical studies that examine the intersection of digital capabilities and ESG performance in entrepreneurial firms, illuminate obstacles, and propose practical solutions.

Potential topics

  • How do entrepreneurial ventures define and measure ESG performance in the digital era? What critical digital capabilities contribute to their improved ESG performance?
  • What challenges do entrepreneurial firms face in integrating digital solutions to enhance environmental sustainability? What could be the best practices for tackling those challenges?
  • What are the possible learning mechanisms and knowledge-sharing processes within entrepreneurial ecosystems that could foster development of digital capabilities for ESG goals?
  • What roles do leadership and organizational culture play in fostering digital capabilities for superior ESG performance in entrepreneurial firms?
  • How can entrepreneurial firms effectively utilize digital technologies to measure and improve their environmental performance within ESG frameworks?
  • How can digital capabilities be harnessed to address diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) challenges in entrepreneurial firms, contributing to improved social sustainability?
  • How do digitalization efforts impact the governance structures of entrepreneurial firms in the context of sustainability? What actions could be taken to improve it?
  • To what extent do regulatory frameworks influence the adoption of digital strategies for ESG compliance in entrepreneurial settings?
  • How do digital technologies facilitate transparency and accountability in ESG reporting for entrepreneurial firms?
  • How can entrepreneurial firms balance profitability goals with sustainable practices through digital transformations? Under this scenario, which opportunities and challenges could arise?

item.title: Behavioural Environmental Economics & Policy (BEEP): trends and reflections
item.content:encoded:
Sanchayan Banerjee, King's College London

Lory Barile, University of Warwick

This special issue focuses on Behavioural Environmental Economics & Policy (BEEP), which examines how departures from rational choice assumptions—such as bounded rationality and bounded willpower—affect environmental decision-making and policy effectiveness. The issue seeks to consolidate evidence on how behavioural insights can improve the design and evaluation of environmental policies to address urgent challenges including climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution.

The special issue welcomes conceptual, empirical, and policy-oriented contributions applying behavioural insights to environmental problems. Submissions may employ various methodologies including experiments, quasi-experimental designs, and literature reviews. The issue particularly values work that identifies both market and behavioural failures, designs and tests policies combining traditional instruments with behavioural tools, and evaluates their effectiveness and welfare impacts.

This is an invitation-only special issue in Environmental and Resource Economics.

Potential topics

  • Interactions between market failures and behavioural failures in environmental settings

  • Replication, meta-analysis, and open-science practices in this domain

item.title: Valuing health and longevity: Advances and innovations
item.content:encoded:
Lisa A. Robinson, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

Olof Bystrom, OECD

Ståle Navrud, Norwegian University of Life Sciences

This special issue focuses on the economic valuation of health risks and mortality in the context of environmental policy. Mortality risks dominate benefit estimates in environmental policies, but the value per statistical life literature contains significant gaps regarding how population and risk characteristics affect valuations. Similarly, nonfatal health impacts receive limited attention despite their substantial magnitude, and methodological challenges persist in synthesizing estimates across studies and applying them to new contexts.

The collection addresses recent advances in measuring individual willingness to pay for both mortality and morbidity risk reductions, improved techniques for combining and transferring results across research settings, and innovations in addressing practical questions such as how to handle co-occurring health effects and distributional equity concerns. The special issue brings together important contributions that serve as a reference for researchers and practitioners applying economic valuation methods to health and longevity improvements.

  • Approaches for combining and transferring valuation estimates
  • Addressing equity and distributional concerns in health valuation
  • Cost-benefit analysis methods for environmental and health policies
  • Best practice approaches to health and longevity valuation

item.title: Animals and Business Ethics: Reimagining Multispecies Co-existence In Business and Society
item.content:encoded:
Doris Schneeberger, Vienna University of Economics and Business

Linda Tallberg, University of Lapland

José-Carlos García-Rosell, University of Oulu

Astrid Huopalainen, Aalto University

Eline Jammaers, Hasselt University

Katherine Dashper, Leeds Beckett University

Helen Wadham, Manchester Metropolitan University

Whilst human treatment of animals has long been a subject of considerable debate within the ethics literature, it is only in more recent years that scholars in business have examined ethical issues around the tourism and food industries, innovation, business education, animal rights and business failure, posthumanism, art, work involving animals, multispecies space, animal protection work, and stakeholder theory. Such interest is to be welcomed. Nevertheless, the interest that business scholars have shown in animals remains piecemeal, and often seems unaware of non-Western or indigenous perspectives. Additionally, ongoing technological developments that have the potential to radically transform the moral demarcations we make between humans and animals have hitherto received limited attention. Such transformations could slow down, or potentially reverse, the exponential increase in human domination over animals that has been evidenced over the past two centuries, and could significantly impact producers who still depend on traditional ways of animal production.

Appel publié par Journal of Business Ethics. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Applying animal ethics theories to business ethics: Using specific animal ethics theories (e.g., rights-based, utilitarian, care ethics) to address business ethics issues
  • Corporate disclosure, CSR, and accounting for animals: Examining how businesses disclose and account for their impact on animals
  • Expanding business ethics frameworks to include animals: Discussing how stakeholder theory, corporate moral responsibility, or, for example, triple bottom line (TBL) approaches could incorporate animals
  • Non-Western and Indigenous ethical perspectives on multispecies organizations: Exploring how Indigenous and non-Western philosophies can inform business-ethics approaches to animals
  • Animals as workers: Investigating ethical concerns regarding animals used as workers in diverse settings, from agriculture to entertainment
  • Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) and the role of animals: Extending DEI discussions to consider nonhuman animals in business contexts
  • Multispecies inclusivity: Analyzing how businesses can integrate multispecies perspectives into ethical and operational frameworks
  • Animal tourism: Addressing ethical challenges and exploitation in wildlife tourism, zoos, and entertainment industries
  • Technological innovations and their impact on animals: Examining cultivated animal products, alternative proteins, AI, and digitalization in relation to animals
  • Farmed animals and emerging business models: Investigating ethical issues in new farming methods such as precision and regenerative agriculture
  • Hard-to-access animal-use industries: Exploring ethical concerns in medical research, pharmaceuticals, and laboratory testing

item.title: Ethics and Entrepreneurship: Foundations and Philosophical Perspectives

This special issue examines the ethical foundations of entrepreneurship, positioning ethics as central to entrepreneurial practice rather than a constraint on it. The issue brings together entrepreneurship studies and philosophical ethics to explore how venture creation, opportunity recognition, and stakeholder engagement involve fundamental questions about responsibility, justice, and human flourishing. It investigates the tension between entrepreneurship's capacity for creativity and disruption and concerns about commodification and self-optimization.

The special issue welcomes diverse methodological and disciplinary perspectives examining how philosophical traditions such as virtue ethics, phenomenology, pragmatism, and deontology illuminate entrepreneurial practice. It particularly emphasizes entrepreneurial decision-making under uncertainty and fluidity, where ethical judgment must balance competing stakeholder interests without reliance on established protocols. The issue seeks papers exploring how entrepreneurship and ethics can deepen each other's understanding through examining contingency, creativity, authenticity, care, and emerging futures.

item.title: The Ethics of Gender Paradoxes in Organizations
item.content:encoded:
Pauline Reinecke, Leuphana University Lüneburg

Ignas Bruder, Technische Universität Dresden

Tobias Hahn, Esade Business School

Olga Kokshagina, University of Sydney

Stephanie Schrage, Kiel University

Janina Sundermeier, Freie Universität Berlin

Gender paradoxes emerge from tensions embedded in organizations, where competing expectations generate not only managerial challenges but also fundamental ethical questions about inclusion, equality, and responsibility. While prior research has examined barriers such as the glass ceiling and pay inequality, less attention has been paid to how gender paradoxes subtly yet systematically shape organizational experiences and allocate moral responsibilities among actors.

Gender is approached as an institutionalized system of social practices for constituting people as two significantly different categories, men and women, and organizing social relations of inequality on the basis of that difference. At the same time, the special issue recognizes the lived realities of intersex, non-binary, genderfluid, and other gender-diverse individuals who navigate structures grounded in binary norms.

Appel publié par Journal of Business Ethics. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Systemic constraints: How ethical commitments to inclusion and equality clash with organizational systems optimized for efficiency – such as standardized evaluations, established management practices, or masculinized leadership norms
  • Competing values and moral ambiguity: How ideals such as fairness, meritocracy, and equity create ethical tensions and "tragic choices", where no option is without compromise
  • Limits of both/and thinking: How both/and strategies for navigating gender paradoxes can foster more inclusive responses, but may also obscure structural inequalities and shift responsibility to individuals
  • Symbolic inclusion and tokenism: How efforts such as diversity targets or flexible work arrangements may produce ethically problematic outcomes, including constrained agency, limited advancement, and superficial change
  • Stigma, visibility, and marginalization: How gender-diverse professionals experience and resist stigmatization within organizations, raising ethical questions about who bears the burden of representation

This special issue addresses how climate transition risks affect financial and operational systems, particularly through supply chain interconnections. The transition to a low-carbon economy creates uncertainty for firms, especially those in carbon-intensive sectors, requiring them to balance sustainability objectives with competitive performance and resilience to sudden shocks. Climate-related disruptions can propagate through global supply chains, amplifying operational risks across multiple tiers.

The integration of financial markets means that climate risks are transmitted through asset price movements, volatility, and liquidity effects, potentially leading to market instability. Recent work has begun exploring carbon pricing effects on asset values, portfolio realignment for low-carbon transitions, and investment horizons under uncertainty. The special issue seeks contributions that examine how financial institutions manage portfolio allocation and risk under evolving climate regulations and uncertain transition pathways.

This special issue investigates how collaborative intelligence—combining human expertise, artificial intelligence, and distributed problem-solving—can advance operations research to address modern decision-making challenges. Traditional OR methods struggle with the dynamic and interconnected nature of contemporary problems, from logistics to emergency response. The collection seeks contributions that demonstrate how human-AI collaboration can enhance decision-making, boost system resilience, and optimize complex operational environments.

The call invites theoretical, computational, and applied research on human-AI collaboration in OR models, optimization and game-theoretic approaches for multi-agent systems, adaptive and decentralized frameworks, and data-driven learning-based optimization. Modern operations research increasingly involves complex decision-making in data-rich environments where contextual information can significantly improve operational policies. This special issue focuses on integrating side information into optimization frameworks, combining advances from optimization, machine learning, and statistical learning. The challenge is to develop methods that go beyond historical averages to create adaptive, personalized solutions that effectively handle high-dimensional data, distribution shifts, and real-time computational demands.

The special issue welcomes contributions that develop novel theories, algorithms, and practical applications merging optimization with machine learning and data analytics. Priority is given to methods that address uncertainty while leveraging contextual information, with emphasis on improving actual decision quality and system performance rather than predictive accuracy alone.

This special issue focuses on reliability modeling and decision support for industrial engineering systems such as manufacturing, supply chains, logistics, energy, and transportation networks. While traditional reliability approaches rely on probabilistic analysis, advances in sensing technologies and data collection have enabled data-driven methods combining machine learning with classical reliability theory. The special issue seeks to bridge reliability analysis with practical decision-making for maintenance planning, resource allocation, and system optimization.

Research contributions should demonstrate both theoretical rigor and practical relevance to industrial applications. The issue welcomes papers on data-driven reliability modeling, machine learning approaches, decision support frameworks, predictive maintenance, and optimization informed by reliability performance. Submissions illustrating how data-driven analysis enhances system performance and decision outcomes are particularly encouraged.

This special section seeks to publish research that bridges data science and operations research, emphasizing both theoretical advances and practical organizational applications. The focus extends beyond technical innovation to address how analytics creates measurable value within organizations and drives necessary organizational change.

The collection invites contributions exploring the intersection of OR and analytics across multiple dimensions: ethical and governance considerations in data usage, challenges of applying OR techniques to big data and distributed systems, organizational barriers to analytics adoption, data quality and validation methods for large datasets, and the role of visualization and soft OR techniques in supporting data-driven decision making.

item.title: Development of the LIMB-QOL measurement system
item.content:encoded:
Jessica Roydhouse, Menzies Institute for Medical Research

Brittany Lapin, Cleveland Clinic

The Limb Injury Measurement Battery for Quality of Life (LIMB-QOL) measurement system is a multifaceted patient reported outcome system designed to measure several domains of functioning across physical, emotional, and social health for individuals with limb loss and other major extremity trauma.

The LIMB-QOL is the result of a large, collaborative project that was funded by the Congressionally Directed Medical Research Programs of the U.S. Department of Defense and overseen by the University of Delaware.

This special collection includes foundational manuscripts to introduce the LIMB-QOL measurement system to researchers and clinicians, including the development and implementation of this measurement system for individuals with major extremity injuries.

item.title: Digital Technologies for Combating Unethical Labour Practices and Promoting Human Rights
item.content:encoded:
Stefan Gold, Technical University of Munich

An estimated 50 million people worldwide experience unethical labour practices, with numbers expected to rise due to regional conflicts and restrictive migration policies. While digital technologies such as blockchain, AI, and cloud computing offer potential solutions for monitoring and addressing these practices, research in this area remains limited. This special issue seeks to understand how digital technologies can theoretically and empirically be deployed to monitor, detect, report, and remediate unethical labour practices.

The special issue welcomes original research using various methodologies that examines the relationship between digital technologies and unethical labour practices. Submissions should identify specific technologies examined and move beyond surface-level analysis to provide nuanced insights. The collection particularly encourages studies that challenge existing paradigms, explore underexamined aspects, or propose innovative frameworks for leveraging digital solutions to advance ethical and sustainable societies while informing policymakers, business leaders, and practitioners.

item.title: Enhancing Population Health Assessment: Key Papers from the EQ-DAPHNIE Project
item.content:encoded:
Brittany Lapin, Cleveland Clinic

Jessica Roydhouse, Menzies Institute for Medical Research

EQ-DAPHNIE represents a landmark endeavour in population health assessment and instrument evaluation, funded by the EuroQol Research Foundation. This initiative collected demographics, social determinants of health, as well as an extensive array of generic and symptom-specific patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) from 15 countries.

This special collection will include papers that delve into a myriad of research questions, including the establishment of population norms for various PROMs, cross-country comparisons, examination of health inequalities, assessment of instrument performance within and across countries, and specialized analyses focusing on self-reported health and the efficacy of different measures within the elderly population.

Appel publié par Quality of Life Research. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Establishment of population norms for various patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs)
  • Cross-country comparisons of health outcomes
  • Examination of health inequalities across populations
  • Assessment of instrument performance within and across countries
  • Self-reported health analyses
  • Efficacy of different measures within the elderly population
  • Generic and symptom-specific patient-reported outcome measures

item.title: Entrepreneurship and the Creation of Decent Work for All
item.content:encoded:
Societal changes, environment, political and financial crises inevitably affect labor markets and the quality of employment. Recent pandemic and global political changes have only demonstrated how quickly one's employment and workplace situation can change. Among other factors, entrepreneurship could play a crucial role in the creation of decent work, especially in a volatile environment.

Understanding the relationship between entrepreneurship and working conditions is crucial for supporting policies and instruments which aim at more productive, decent work, fair wages, better access to the labor market, and improved job opportunities for all.

In order to fully represent this multifaceted topic, we would like to gather a spectrum of current perspectives in a single Collection, facilitating a better understanding of possibilities and ways of striving toward the goal of 'achieving full and productive employment and decent work for all' (SDG 8 of the U.N.).

Appel publié par International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Equal pay for work of equal value
  • Gender discrimination in employment
  • Immigration and employment
  • Labor shortages after COVID-19
  • Modern slavery and child labor
  • Labor policy
  • Entrepreneurial enterprises, SMEs, and family businesses
  • Global entrepreneurial firms: organization design, emerging conceptions in entrepreneurship (i.e. born globals), globalization's challenges and opportunities, cultural differences
  • Remote work
  • Opportunity entrepreneurship as a direct way to generate high quality employment
  • Measuring and dealing with positive and negative externalities of new businesses

This Multi-Journal Collection is a cross-disciplinary resource for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers interested in entrepreneurship as a way to address paramount global issues, with an emphasis on the expected and realized changes as well as the implications related to entrepreneurship phenomena.

Papers featured in this collection investigate the impact of entrepreneurship with an eye toward how it can shape the future, utilizing micro, meso, and macro levels of analysis.

item.title: From Adoption to Impact: Post-Adoption, Value Realization, and Societal Transformation of ICT and AI
item.content:encoded:
Jyoti Choudrie, University of Hertfordshire

Sherah Kurnia, The University of Melbourne

Gabrielle Peko, University of Auckland

David Sundaram, University of Auckland

This special issue addresses the critical gap between technology adoption and actual value realization, focusing on how organizations and societies integrate, adapt, and leverage ICTs and AI beyond their initial implementation. While existing research emphasizes adoption decisions, there remains limited understanding of post-adoption dynamics, continued use, and the translation of technological investments into tangible organizational and societal benefits.

The issue welcomes research exploring post-adoption phenomena across individual, organizational, and societal levels, including technology assimilation, value creation, and transformation. It also addresses significant risks and ethical concerns arising from ICT and AI deployment, such as algorithmic bias, privacy threats, digital inequality, and unintended consequences that require scholarly attention.

Appel publié par Information Systems Frontiers. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Post-adoption behaviors: continued use, discontinuance, and switching

  • ICT-enabled institutional and governance transformation
  • Digital platforms, ecosystems, and network effects
  • Public sector and societal impacts of sustained technology use
  • Success and failure of digital transformation initiatives
  • Algorithmic bias, transparency, and accountability
  • Privacy, cybersecurity, and data governance challenges
  • Overuse, misuse, and unintended consequences of ICTs and AI
  • Environmental and societal externalities of digital technologies
  • Regulation and governance of AI and digital technologies
  • Organizational strategies for effective post-adoption management

It showcases recent developments in game theory alongside its diverse applications, with emphasis on interaction dynamics and collective decision-making through theoretical, practical, and interdisciplinary approaches.

The issue particularly welcomes expanded versions of papers presented at the European Meeting on Game Theory 2026 (SING21), though other relevant submissions are also encouraged. item.title: Global Supply Chain Reconfiguration Under Tariff Uncertainty
item.content:encoded:
Guoqing Zhang, University of Windsor

Jiaguo Liu, Dalian Maritime University

Hakan Yildiz, Wayne State University

This special issue addresses the urgent challenge of reconfiguring global supply chains in response to escalating tariff uncertainty and shifting trade policies. The unprecedented complexity of current tariff environments, characterized by high rates, retaliatory measures, and trade tensions, demands new decision-making approaches to support practical supply chain management.

The special issue seeks high-quality research that applies Operations Research and Artificial Intelligence methods to tackle these challenges. Contributions should include theoretical developments, methodological innovations, and applied modeling studies with real-world relevance, particularly those integrating OR, AI, supply chain management, and international economics.

The global entrepreneurial landscape is being reshaped by geopolitical tensions, realigning supply chains, technological disruption, digital progress, and long-term climate and demographic trends. This Collection aims to provide a platform for advancing theories, methodologies, and practices that enhance understanding of inclusive entrepreneurship in the region.

item.title: International Business in a Reconfiguring Southeast Asia
item.content:encoded:
S. Tamer Cavusgil, Georgia State University

Marleen Dieleman, IMD Business School

Md. Tareq Hossain, Thammasat University

Ruey-Jer "Bryan" Jean, National Taiwan University

Destan Kandemir, Georgia State University

Suntichai Kotcharin, Thammasat University

Hussain Rammal, Adelaide University

Southeast Asia represents a significant yet theoretically under-explored region in international business research. With ten ASEAN economies forming the world's fifth-largest economic bloc and attracting substantial foreign investment, the region presents unique phenomena including supply chain reconfiguration driven by China-plus-one strategies, the emergence of regional multinationals, and institutional diversity across countries with different political systems and development stages.

Despite its empirical importance, Southeast Asia remains underrepresented in leading international management journals, where research focuses predominantly on China and India. This special issue seeks contributions that treat Southeast Asian phenomena as theoretically generative rather than merely illustrative. It particularly encourages submissions from scholars based in the region and aims to develop international management theory beyond existing BRICS-centric frameworks by leveraging the region's distinctive features including family capitalism, ethnic-Chinese business networks, state-linked enterprises, and ASEAN-level institutional structures.

Appel publié par Management International Review. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • The rise and internationalization of Southeast Asian multinationals, including digital-native champions, conglomerate-based regional players, and state-linked enterprises
  • Supply-chain reconfiguration, maritime connectivity, and regional supply-chain governance in Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines
  • Cross-border trade, geopolitics, and strategies of Southeast Asian firms hedging between major power blocs
  • Indigenous theorizing and methodological innovation drawing on Southeast Asian intellectual traditions and fieldwork methods

item.title: Keeping Humans in the Loop in the AI-Driven Future of Information Security
item.content:encoded:
Laura Amo, University at Buffalo, State University of New York

Richard Baskerville, Georgia State University

Rui Chen, Iowa State University

Matthew Hashim, University of Arizona

Yaojie (William) Li, University of New Orleans

Yuan Li, University of Tennessee at Knoxville

As artificial intelligence increasingly dominates both offensive and defensive cybersecurity, this special issue emphasizes the critical importance of maintaining human involvement in security systems and decisions. The issue addresses concerns about AI-driven threats such as sophisticated phishing attacks, deepfakes, and behavioral data exploitation, while acknowledging that defensive reliance on AI-based threat detection creates cognitive challenges for practitioners.

Human-in-the-loop (HITL) is presented as a design principle that ensures human participation in system training, decision-making, and error mitigation, recognizing that fully automated security systems may be restrictive or dangerous. The special issue calls for behavioral information security research that balances AI's growing role with sustained focus on human behavior, cognition, and motivation in secure systems, training, and technologies.

Appel publié par Information Systems Frontiers. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Neurosecurity (NeuroIS) investigations of information security behavior
  • Behavioral analyses of design science treatments enhancing or balancing security and privacy tradeoffs
  • The behavioral intersection of cybersecurity/privacy research and AI/ML advancements
  • AI-enabled security awareness, training, nudging, and behavioral intervention systems
  • Human-AI collaboration in security decision-making, compliance, monitoring, and response
  • Behavioral security implications of generative AI, including phishing, social engineering, misinformation, insider threats, and user overreliance on AI tools
  • Design science approaches to developing, evaluating, and theorizing intelligent security artifacts with behavioral implications
  • Adaptive, personalized, and context-aware security interventions enabled by AI and analytics
  • Theoretical extensions or reconceptualizations of established behavioral security theories in AI-mediated environments

item.title: Multiple Objective Programming and Goal Programming: Artificial Intelligence for Decision Making in Economic and Social Sciences
item.content:encoded:
Matteo Rocca, University of Insubria

Davide La Torre, Skema Business School

Constantin Zopounidis, Technical University of Crete

This special issue brings together research at the intersection of multiple objective optimization, goal programming, and artificial intelligence to address complex decision-making problems in economic and social sciences. By combining structured methods for evaluating conflicting objectives with machine learning approaches that process large datasets, the issue seeks to advance both theoretical understanding and practical applications of these integrated methodologies.

The special issue welcomes original research papers, including substantially extended versions of presentations from the 16th International Conference on Multiple Objective Programming and Goal Programming (MOPGP'25, held July 1-3, 2025, in Varese, Italy), as well as papers not presented at the conference. Contributions should address theory or applications of multiple objective programming, goal programming, or artificial intelligence with relevance to economic or social decision-making contexts.

item.title: OR for Sustainability in Supply Chain Management
item.content:encoded:
Kannan Govindan, University of Southern Denmark

This special section addresses the integration of sustainable development goals (SDGs) into supply chain management using advanced operations research methods. Organizations face mounting pressure to balance economic growth with resource conservation and environmental protection, making this research area crucial for achieving the UN's 2030 sustainability agenda.

The special section seeks research applying optimization models, algorithms, and decision-making techniques such as multi-attribute and multi-objective decision making to design and implement sustainable supply chains. Contributions should explore how operations research can support stakeholder engagement in sustainability policymaking, innovative practices for resource management, and mechanisms for monitoring progress toward SDG targets across different economic contexts.

Appel publié par Annals of Operations Research. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Designing and policymaking in SDGs through stakeholder support: to provide examples of sustainable policy and design making with multi-stakeholder perspectives and to define how sustainability is considered in framing policies and enumerating success factors and challenges on supply chain management
  • Implementing SDGs in supply chains through innovative strategies and practices: to identify the sustainable goals, indicators, and practices related to the implementation of sustainable supply chain management and to explore how this knowledge may be used to effectively manage and conserve resources with less environmental and societal impact
  • Monitoring supply chain governance and implications with a focus on SDGs: to elaborate practices and supporting mechanisms in measuring, monitoring, and reporting progress toward achieving targets, and to further emphasize various challenges related to the implementation of SDGs in supply chain management in different applications/context/economies

item.content:encoded:
Eva K. Lee, Georgia Institute of Technology

This special section seeks research that applies optimization and computational methods to medical and biological problems. The initiative recognizes that healthcare complexity and data-rich biological systems require rigorous mathematical and algorithmic approaches to advance treatment and prevention strategies.

Contributions should address theoretical or methodological developments in optimization models and algorithms, including continuous, integer, combinatorial, and stochastic methods, with direct applications to healthcare delivery, disease management, medical imaging, and biological research. The special section welcomes partnerships between operations research and medical communities to solve problems benefiting public health.

item.title: Patient experience data in regulatory and health technology assessment
item.content:encoded:
Wen-Hung Chen, AstraZeneca

Lori D. McLeod, RTI Health Solutions

Regulatory and health technology assessment bodies increasingly recognize the value of incorporating patient perspectives during product development and evaluation. Patient experience data encompass patient-reported outcomes, clinical outcome assessments, and patient preference information. However, there is inconsistency in how decision-makers collect, evaluate, and utilize these data, highlighting the need to understand different stakeholders' approaches to ensure patients' voices meaningfully influence healthcare decisions.

This collection invites submissions addressing how patient experience data—encompassing preferences, symptoms, and quality of life—can better inform regulatory and HTA processes. The collection welcomes original research, reviews, and discussion papers on recent developments in the field, as well as work exploring innovative applications such as artificial intelligence and digital health technologies in patient experience research.

Appel publié par Quality of Life Research. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.content:encoded:

Alexander Pflaum, University of Bamberg

Haozhe Chen, Iowa State University

Marcel Papert, University of Bamberg

Modern supply chains face unprecedented disruptions while simultaneously confronting environmental limits and resource scarcity. This requires a fundamental transformation toward more responsive and circular systems. Digital technologies including IoT, AI, digital twins, and blockchain are critical enablers for building resilient supply chains that adapt quickly to change while reducing resource consumption and closing material loops.

The special issue seeks papers demonstrating how digital and data-driven solutions implement these responsive and circular supply chains, along with their associated business models. Contributions should explore digital technologies across multiple supply chain tiers, with particular emphasis on industry-specific applications and the integration of responsiveness, servitization, and sustainability goals.

item.content:encoded:

Danae Manika, Brunel University of London

Babak Taheri, Texas A&M University

This special issue seeks to advance understanding of how artificial intelligence can be designed and deployed responsibly and trustworthily within tourism and hospitality sectors. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in service delivery, marketing, operations, and guest experiences, the sector faces both opportunities for innovation and significant ethical challenges regarding fairness, accountability, transparency, and consumer trust.

The special issue invites interdisciplinary research examining the technical, managerial, legal, and societal dimensions of responsible AI adoption. Submissions should explore the design, governance, and impacts of AI-enabled platforms and systems, addressing topics such as algorithmic bias, consumer trust, sustainable AI applications, ethical frameworks, digital transformation, and labor implications within tourism and hospitality contexts.

item.title: Strategizing in a Fractured World: MNE Responses to Fragmented Stakeholder and Institutional Pressures
item.content:encoded:

Vera Kunczer, Copenhagen Business School

Jonas Puck, Vienna University of Economics and Business

Harald Puhr, Universität Innsbruck

Michael Wolfesberger, Vienna University of Economics and Business

This focused issue addresses how multinational enterprises navigate environments characterized by fragmented, conflicting, and overlapping institutional and stakeholder pressures arising from national security concerns, populist movements, and societal disruptions. The call recognizes that while international institutions like the UN SDGs and Paris Agreement shape MNE decision-making, domestic resistance in some countries creates institutional conflicts that MNEs must resolve through their strategic choices.

The issue seeks contributions exploring four main areas: the factors exposing MNEs to institutional fragmentation; how firms combine market and non-market strategies to respond to these pressures; how MNEs orchestrate responses across multiple jurisdictions; and how macro-level tensions affect internal organizational dynamics. The editors welcome conceptual and empirical papers using various methodologies, along with interdisciplinary work that incorporates political science perspectives.

Appel publié par Management International Review. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • What drives the exposure of MNEs to institutional fragmentation and fracturing?

  • How do institutional fragmentation and geopolitical tensions shape interactions within firms?
  • MNE strategy in response to fragmentation and conflicting institutional pressures
  • Interdisciplinary approaches complementing business perspectives with political science

item.title: Techno-Nationalism, State Strategy, and Corporate Innovation in the Asia-Pacific
item.content:encoded:
Siah Hwee Ang, Victoria University of Wellington

Di (David) Fan, RMIT University

Jiatao Li, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

Wei Liu, Qingdao University

In today's highly digitalized and knowledge-driven global economy, technology has come to signify far more than traditional notions of productivity and efficiency. Its strategic importance has risen to the level of a critical determinant of national competitiveness, institutional security, and social stability. Against this backdrop, the emergence of techno-nationalism represents a salient new trend. Investigating how techno-nationalism reshapes corporate innovation and strategy can not only fill the theoretical gap in existing IB research between macro-level politics and micro-level firm practices, but also provide new insights into the resilience-building and innovation pathways of Asia-Pacific firms in this new normal.

Appel publié par Asia Pacific Journal of Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

This special collection seeks submissions that investigate technology transfer, entrepreneurship, and innovation through partnerships between academic researchers and external stakeholders such as practitioners and policymakers. The editors recognize that meaningful research in this field often benefits from close collaboration across disciplinary and sectoral boundaries, providing access to emerging phenomena and underexplored mechanisms that traditional approaches might miss.

The collection particularly welcomes papers co-authored by academics and non-academic partners including technology transfer professionals, policymakers, entrepreneurs, investors, and innovation intermediaries. Such collaborative work is expected to generate unique insights, improve data access, broaden empirical scope, and tackle fundamental questions from diverse perspectives while maintaining rigorous academic standards.

Digital platforms and their ecosystems have become central to value creation in the global economy, but their concentrated power raises significant concerns about societal impacts. These platforms now mediate how people work, communicate, access information, and engage in public discourse, making it crucial to understand their design, governance, and regulation.

This special issue seeks scholarly contributions examining critical questions about digital platform ecosystems, addressing both their innovative potential and their societal risks. Contributions should address governance mechanisms, market power, content moderation, platform regulation, protection of vulnerable users, and the socio-economic development implications of platform-mediated activities across different contexts.

The Topical Collection on Artificial Intelligence-based Assistants and Platforms focuses on assistant systems (e.g. chatbots, recommenders) that are based on artificial intelligence and the interaction with users via declarative natural-language interfaces. They are present in various forms as well as industries and often assume a platform logic when services and devices from different providers are included.

The Topical Collection relates to a minitrack at the Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS) and comprises research on novel methods, models, processes, and approaches related to the design, implementation, deployment, operation, and optimization of AI-based assistants and platforms for the digital economy.

item.title: Contemporary research in financial technology (Fintech)
item.content:encoded:
Rainer Alt, Leipzig University

Rob Gleasure, Copenhagen Business School

Ke-Wei Huang, National University of Singapore

Mingfeng Lin, Georgia Institute of Technology

De Liu, University of Minnesota

Liudmila Zavolokina, University of Lausanne

FinTech emerged as a disruptive force in the financial industry around 2010, introducing innovative applications and business models. Now an established sector, FinTech has revolutionized payment, financing, lending, and insurance through platform-based, customer-oriented, and crowd-based processes. On the one hand, FinTech solutions have reached a maturity, which is characterized by well-adopted solutions that have reached a critical mass as well as by a growing degree of regulation. In practice, investments in FinTech start-up ventures have decreased and much research has also been published with four special issues in the Electronic Markets journal alone. On the other hand, ongoing technological advancements like agentic and generative artificial intelligence, blockchain/distributed ledger technologies, and quantum computing are driving further innovations.

Appel publié par Electronic Markets. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Interaction and integration between FinTech and traditional financial institutions (e.g., traditional banks, central banks, and central bank digital currencies)
  • Study of segments of FinTech (InsurTech, PropTech, RegTech, Green FinTech and sustainable finance)
  • Research on innovation processes in FinTech and analysis of (new) business models (e.g., crowd-based, digital platforms, decentralized business models)
  • Upcoming concepts in Fintech (e.g., embedded, contextual, silent, open and ubiquitous finance and banking)
  • Use of centralized (e.g., core banking/insurance systems) and decentralized digital platforms (e.g., blockchain and distributed ledger technology) for financial services
  • Research on cryptocurrencies, crypto exchanges, and digital assets (e.g., tokenization, Initial Coin and Securitized Token Offerings (ICO/STO))
  • Emerging standards in the financial industry (e.g., data/process standards and application programming interfaces) and regulations like PSD in Europe
  • Adoption and business value of FinTech models and applications (e.g., financial inclusion and literacy, regulation and governance, diffusion and network effects)
  • Emerging FinTech topics and applications (e.g., quantum computing, metaverse, Internet of Things, Agentic and Generative AI)
  • Studies of innovative applications in FinTech (e.g., robo-advising, algorithmic trading, portfolio management, market making, and social trading)
  • Innovative payment models and systems (e.g., payment networks, micropayments, mobile payments)

item.title: Digital Transformation and Service
item.content:encoded:
Christian Bartelheimer, University of Göttingen

Daniel Beverungen, Paderborn University

Sara Hofmann, University of Agder

Lysanne Lessard, University of Ottawa

This topical collection examines how digital transformation and service shape contemporary information systems, particularly focusing on value creation across organizational boundaries through digital technologies, platforms, and ecosystems. The collection seeks theoretically grounded research that goes beyond broad claims about digital transformation to instead examine how IT artifacts are designed and applied to enable value co-creation in service contexts.

The collection prioritizes submissions that explicitly analyze IT artifacts rather than treating them as black boxes, showing how these artifacts shape and are shaped by organizational digital transformation. Research should be grounded in IS literature and address relevant gaps for both theory and practice, with particular interest in inter-organizational and platform-based service scenarios relevant to Electronic Markets.

item.title: Transformative Marketing Strategies: Embracing the Future
item.content:encoded:
V. Kumar, Brock University

The use of new-age tools for transformative marketing strategies is an emerging area with several unexplored dimensions. While prior research has established a conceptual foundation, significant gaps remain unaddressed. Existing studies primarily focus on theoretical frameworks or conceptual models, lacking sufficient empirical validation of how these technologies influence consumer attitudes, decision-making, and purchasing behavior.

Furthermore, there is a lack of empirical research quantifying the return on investment (ROI) of integrating these advanced technologies into marketing campaigns. Previous research has also not thoroughly examined the tension between hyper-personalized marketing enabled by GAI and consumer privacy concerns, particularly in the context of Blockchain's ability to ensure data traceability.

This special issue aims to encourage researchers to explore these critical issues and bridge the existing research gaps.

Appel publié par Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Use of new-age tools for transformative marketing strategies

  • Return on investment (ROI) of integrating advanced technologies into marketing campaigns
  • Tension between hyper-personalized marketing and consumer privacy concerns
  • Blockchain's ability to ensure data traceability in marketing contexts
  • Generative AI (GAI) applications in marketing

Timeline

item.content:encoded:

Digital technologies are fundamentally reshaping how both private and public organizations—including universities, hospitals, and local administrations—conceive strategy, innovate, and compete. However, scholarly understanding remains fragmented regarding how digitalization operates across different functional areas and organizational levels, and literature has not fully clarified the mechanisms through which technological adoption generates performance gains or the conditions under which it falters.

item.title: Wildfires in a Changing Climate: Impacts, Adaptation, and Policy
item.content:encoded:
Sarah Meier, ETH Zurich

Eric Strobl, University of Bern

Robert J. R. Elliott, University of Birmingham

Wildfires are becoming more frequent and intense in many regions, driven by climate change, land-use shifts, and expanding human settlements in fire-prone areas. These changes have transformed wildfires into systemic economic and ecological risks. The economic impacts are substantial and multifaceted, extending beyond direct suppression costs to include disruptions to supply chains, labour productivity losses, effects on tourism and housing markets, and significant public health burdens from smoke exposure.

This special issue seeks empirical research that quantifies the economic consequences of wildfires and smoke, and evaluates the effectiveness of policy responses and adaptation strategies. The journal welcomes applied environmental and resource economics studies using innovative data sources and identification methods, as well as interdisciplinary work that strengthens economic understanding of wildfire impacts and informs policy decisions. The issue particularly encourages cross-regional comparisons to facilitate knowledge exchange between regions with established fire experience and those facing emerging vulnerabilities.

Appel publié par Environmental and Resource Economics. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Labour productivity, sectoral employment shifts, and worker mobility
  • Housing markets, mortgage risk, and migration and other behavioural responses to wildfire risk and exposure
  • Natural capital and ecosystem service valuation, including impacts on biodiversity, recreation, and forest asset pricing
  • Inequality, information access, and distributional impacts of exposure and monitoring technologies
  • Public finance, insurance markets, and the fiscal consequences for local and regional governments
  • Institutions, governance, and risk-sharing arrangements, including coordination across jurisdictions, public-private roles, and firm responses to wildfire risk
  • Prevention, suppression, and adaptation strategies, including land-use planning, prescribed burning, indigenous fire stewardship, and advanced monitoring and management technologies
  • Welfare losses from smoke exposure, including physical and mental health outcomes and associated human capital effects

Timeline

  • September 30, 2026: Submission deadline
