item.title: Backfiring Effects of Social Psychological Interventions
item.content:encoded:
Journal of Experimental Social Psychology,

Social psychological interventions aim to change thoughts, feelings, and behaviors in beneficial ways. However, accumulating evidence suggests that such interventions sometimes backfire, producing effects opposite to those intended. This special issue seeks to advance our understanding of when, why, and for whom social psychological interventions produce unintended negative consequences.

Appel publié par Journal of Experimental Social Psychology. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Boomerang effects and unintended consequences of social psychological interventions
  • Reactance and psychological resistance to intervention attempts
  • Individual differences in susceptibility to intervention backfiring
  • Temporal dynamics of intervention effects (delayed backfiring)
  • Mechanisms underlying when and why interventions backfire
  • Cross-cultural variation in intervention effectiveness and backfiring
  • Interventions targeting attitudes, behaviors, beliefs, or social norms that produce opposite-to-intended effects
  • Meta-analyses or systematic reviews of intervention failures
  • Novel theoretical frameworks explaining intervention backfiring
  • Practical implications for improving intervention design and implementation

Timeline

item.title: Extended Reality (XR) for Enhanced Decision Making and Organizational Transformation
item.content:encoded:
This special issue focuses on the transformative potential of Extended Reality (XR) technologies—including Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), and Mixed Reality (MR)—in enhancing decision-making processes and driving organizational transformation. As organizations increasingly face complex challenges requiring rapid, data-driven decisions, XR technologies offer innovative approaches to visualize information, simulate scenarios, and facilitate collaborative problem-solving in immersive environments.

The special issue welcomes original research contributions that explore how XR can improve decision support systems across various organizational contexts. We are interested in studies examining the effectiveness of immersive technologies in enhancing situational awareness, reducing decision-making time, improving decision quality, and fostering organizational innovation. Both theoretical frameworks and practical implementations are encouraged.

Appel publié par Decision Support Systems. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Applications of XR technologies in decision support systems
  • Immersive visualization for complex data analysis
  • VR/AR/MR interfaces for business intelligence
  • XR-based training and knowledge transfer for organizational learning
  • Human-computer interaction in extended reality environments
  • User experience and usability in XR decision support applications
  • Integration of XR with artificial intelligence and machine learning
  • Real-time collaboration in virtual/mixed reality spaces
  • XR applications in crisis management and emergency response
  • Organizational change management through XR adoption

item.title: Higher-Order Network Representations and Modeling Methods for Transportation Resilience
item.content:encoded:
This special issue focuses on the development and application of higher-order network representations and advanced modeling methods to enhance our understanding of transportation resilience. Traditional transportation network models often fail to capture the complex, multi-way interactions and higher-order dependencies that characterize modern transportation systems. This special issue invites contributions that leverage higher-order network approaches, such as hypergraphs and simplicial complexes, to better represent the intricate relationships between transportation components and improve resilience analysis and management.

We welcome papers that present novel theoretical frameworks, empirical studies, computational methods, and practical applications of higher-order network representations in transportation contexts. Contributions may address how these advanced representations can help identify vulnerabilities, enhance system robustness, and support decision-making for more resilient transportation infrastructure.

Appel publié par Transportation Research Part B: Methodological. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Higher-order network representations (e.g., hypergraphs, simplicial complexes) for transportation systems
  • Modeling methods that capture complex interactions and dependencies in transportation networks
  • Applications of higher-order networks to transportation resilience
  • Resilience assessment and enhancement strategies using advanced network representations
  • Interdependencies between transportation and other critical infrastructure networks
  • Temporal and dynamic aspects of higher-order transportation networks
  • Data collection and empirical studies on higher-order structures in transportation systems
  • Computational methods and algorithms for analyzing higher-order transportation networks

Timeline

This special issue seeks to explore how Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming methodological approaches in technology management research. We invite submissions that demonstrate innovative applications of LLMs as research tools, methodological enhancers, and theoretical instruments for advancing our understanding of technology management, innovation, and organizational change.

Contributions should address both the opportunities and challenges of incorporating LLMs into research practice, including questions of validity, reliability, ethical considerations, and the development of new theoretical frameworks that account for LLM capabilities and limitations in research contexts.

Potential topics

  • Applications of LLMs in technology management research
  • LLMs for data analysis and pattern recognition in technology studies
  • Novel methodological approaches enabled by LLMs
  • Theoretical frameworks for understanding LLM capabilities and limitations in research contexts
  • LLMs for literature review and synthesis
  • LLM-assisted qualitative and quantitative research methods
  • Validation and reliability of LLM-based research findings
  • Ethical considerations in using LLMs for academic research
  • LLMs for forecasting technological trends
  • Integration of LLMs with traditional research methodologies

item.title: Market-Based Measures for Port and Shipping Emissions Mitigation
item.content:encoded:
This special issue focuses on market-based measures and economic instruments designed to mitigate emissions from ports and the shipping industry. The collection seeks to advance understanding of how market mechanisms can effectively reduce environmental impacts while maintaining economic competitiveness in the maritime sector.

The issue welcomes contributions exploring various market-based approaches including carbon pricing, emission trading systems, green bonds, subsidies for clean technologies, and other economic instruments. Papers may examine these mechanisms from theoretical, empirical, or policy perspectives, with particular interest in their effectiveness, design, implementation challenges, and real-world outcomes.

item.title: Mathematical Foundations for Trustworthy AI Applications in Transportation Systems
item.content:encoded:
This special issue focuses on the mathematical and computational foundations necessary for developing trustworthy artificial intelligence applications in transportation systems. As AI increasingly influences critical transportation decisions affecting safety, efficiency, and equity, there is an urgent need for rigorous mathematical frameworks that ensure these systems are reliable, interpretable, and accountable.

The special issue welcomes contributions that advance the theoretical understanding and practical implementation of trustworthy AI in transportation. This includes work on mathematical models that enhance transparency, ensure robustness against adversarial attacks, quantify uncertainties, and address fairness concerns in transportation algorithms and systems.

Submissions should demonstrate how mathematical and computational approaches contribute to building trustworthy AI systems that stakeholders can understand, verify, and depend upon for critical transportation applications.

Appel publié par Transportation Research Part B: Methodological. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Mathematical frameworks for explainability and interpretability in transportation AI
  • Formal verification and validation methods for autonomous vehicles
  • Trustworthy machine learning algorithms for traffic prediction and management
  • Robustness and adversarial resilience in transportation systems
  • Uncertainty quantification in AI-based transportation applications
  • Fairness and bias mitigation in transportation decision-making systems
  • Privacy-preserving techniques in transportation data analytics
  • Game-theoretic approaches to multi-agent transportation systems
  • Causal inference methods for transportation research
  • Probabilistic and Bayesian methods in transportation AI

Timeline

  • December 1, 2026: Full paper submission deadline

item.title: MNEs and exogenous shocks: Learning from pandemics and other major disruptions
item.content:encoded:
,

Multinational enterprises (MNEs) face unprecedented challenges from exogenous shocks such as pandemics, natural disasters, geopolitical tensions, and supply chain disruptions. These major disruptions test the resilience and adaptability of global business operations and require strategic responses that span multiple countries and business units.

The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the vulnerabilities and opportunities within global value chains and MNE operations. Understanding how MNEs learn from and adapt to such major disruptions is critical for both theory and practice in international business.

This special issue seeks to advance our understanding of how MNEs respond to, learn from, and build resilience against exogenous shocks. We welcome empirical and theoretical contributions that examine MNE adaptation strategies, organizational changes, and the factors that influence their ability to navigate major disruptions.

Appel publié par Journal of World Business. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How have MNEs adapted their global value chains in response to exogenous shocks?
  • What organizational and strategic changes have MNEs implemented to build resilience?
  • How has the pandemic affected MNE subsidiary autonomy, mandates, and roles?
  • What is the role of digital transformation in MNE adaptation to exogenous shocks?
  • How do institutional contexts shape MNE responses to major disruptions?
  • What are the short-term and long-term implications of exogenous shocks for MNE competitiveness?
  • How have MNEs managed stakeholder relationships during major disruptions?
  • What lessons can be learned from MNE responses to past crises?

item.title: Sustainable Maritime Transportation: New Insights from Artificial Intelligence
item.content:encoded:
This special issue focuses on the intersection of sustainable maritime transportation and artificial intelligence technologies. Maritime transportation plays a crucial role in global commerce and logistics, accounting for a significant portion of international trade. However, the shipping industry faces considerable environmental challenges, including greenhouse gas emissions, fuel consumption, and pollution. Artificial intelligence and machine learning offer promising opportunities to address these sustainability challenges while improving operational efficiency.

The special issue welcomes contributions that explore innovative AI-based solutions for enhancing sustainability in maritime transportation. This includes research on optimizing vessel performance, reducing carbon footprints, improving safety protocols, and developing intelligent systems for port and logistics management. We are particularly interested in studies that demonstrate practical applications of AI technologies in real-world maritime contexts.

item.title: The evolution of decision-making and reasoning from childhood to adulthood
item.content:encoded:
,

,

This special issue examines how decision-making processes, choice behavior, and reasoning capabilities evolve from childhood through adulthood. Understanding the developmental trajectory of these fundamental cognitive and behavioral processes provides insight into the mechanisms that underlie human judgment and decision-making across the lifespan.

The collection seeks to integrate perspectives from developmental psychology, behavioral economics, cognitive science, and neuroscience to explore how individuals acquire, refine, and modify their decision-making strategies as they mature. Contributions may address the biological, cognitive, social, and environmental factors that shape the development of choice behavior and reasoning abilities.

Empirical studies, theoretical frameworks, and methodological approaches that advance our understanding of developmental decision-making are welcome. This includes research examining both normative development and individual variation in how people learn to make choices and engage in reasoning from early childhood through adulthood.

Appel publié par Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Economics. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Developmental changes in decision-making and choice behavior across the lifespan
  • Cognitive mechanisms underlying reasoning development
  • Economic decision-making in children and adolescents
  • The role of emotions and affect in developing choice behavior
  • Neural and biological substrates of reasoning development
  • Individual differences in decision-making trajectories
  • The impact of education and experience on choice behavior
  • Temporal and risk preferences across development
  • Social influences on reasoning and decision-making
  • Irrational choice patterns and their developmental origins

item.title: Registered Reports
item.content:encoded:
In cases in which results, whether present or not, may have important theoretical or practical implications, scholars are encouraged to submit a Registered Report. In this type of submission, authors submit the introduction, methods, measurement info, and analysis plan (but not the results) of a completed or planned study.

This abbreviated paper is then evaluated on the basis of the importance of the topic, the merit of the selected analytic approach, methodological rigor and quality, and potential for impacting down-the-road theorizing and/or practice/policy. As results are not included in the registered report, what was or is likely to be found has no bearing on the outcome of the evaluation. This is in line with the journal's willingness to publish papers reporting negligible or non-effects.

Appel publié par Academy of Management Discoveries. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Empirical studies with important theoretical or practical implications
  • Research with rigorous methodological design
  • Studies reporting null or negligible effects
  • Organizational and management research

item.title: Rethinking Business School Structures, Standards, and Success for Neuroinclusive Management Learning and Education
item.content:encoded:
Miriam Moeller, University of Queensland

Dana L. Ott, University of Otago

Matevž Rašković, University of Technology Auckland

Sophie Hennekam, Audencia Business School

Timothy J. Vogus, Vanderbilt University

Joy E. Beatty, Eastern Michigan University

Judith Clair, Boston College

Business schools around the world are undergoing rapid transformation, reflecting questions about their social license, legitimacy and identity, changing student demographics, technological developments, and evolving understandings of social justice, equity, inclusion, and belonging. Amid this period of re-evaluation and change, recognition is growing that an estimated 15-20% of the global population is neurodivergent. With more than half of Gen Z now identifying as neurodivergent, it underscores the urgency of advancing theoretical, empirical, and pedagogical conversations about whom business school systems of teaching, assessment, and professional formation are designed to serve – and how they might evolve to achieve greater neuroinclusion.

Appel publié par Academy of Management Learning and Education. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How does neurodiversity help reimagine social justice and DEI in business schools?
  • What tensions emerge between performance metrics and inclusion for neurodivergent students, academic and professional staff, and how are such trade-offs effectively managed?
  • How do policies on reasonable accommodations align (or conflict) with institutional objectives and wider institutional logics?
  • How is neurodiversity effectively addressed in non-WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic) environments and institutional settings in higher education contexts?
  • How does a country's legal context shape the expectations, obligations, and opportunities for business schools to develop and deliver more neuroinclusive pedagogy?
  • How can existing practices and processes within business schools be adjusted and/or redesigned to be more neuroinclusive (e.g., recruiting and selection, onboarding, networking, and organizational culture)?
  • How can business schools attract and retain neurodivergent talent (learners, academics and professional staff)?
  • How can business schools support neurodivergent academic and professional staff and challenge ableism as an organizational paradigm?
  • How do business schools address the neurodiversity of learners, academic, and professional staff at different levels (i.e., undergraduate, postgraduate, executive education) and in different cultural and institutional contexts?
  • How do neurodivergent learners, academic and professional staff experience management learning processes differently and what unique challenges do they face?
  • What are the experiences of learners and academic and professional staff with intersectional social identities involving neurodiversity?
  • What is the role of institutional logics/culture, pedagogy, peer learners, and academic and professional staff in the way neurodivergent individuals and groups experience and navigate their management education, including from an intersectionality perspective?
  • What insights can be gleaned from the experiences of neurodivergent learners and academic and professional staff regarding neurotypical norms in management education? What role do visibility and representation specifically play in this?
  • How can cross-neurotype (between neurodivergent and neurotypical individuals) collaboration and connection be fostered and leveraged in the classroom and outside it (i.e., bridging the double empathy problem)?
  • How do neurodiverse groups of learners (i.e., those with neurotypical and neurodivergent members) work together (e.g., the biases experienced or avoided, the interpersonal challenges) and perform (e.g., task performance, creativity)?
  • How do neurodivergent individuals experience the transition into the workforce as well as from secondary school into management education? What practices, supports, and tools aid more successful transitions? How do these transitional practices vary across global cultures?
  • What role does executive functioning, sensory processing, or divergent social cognition play in shaping reflection and feedback loops within learning processes?
  • In what ways can experiential learning or study abroad be adapted for neurodivergent learners and educators?
  • How does neurodiversity inform alternative models of learner identity and transformation?
  • What is the impact of educational support on academic achievements and the employability of neurodivergent individuals?
  • What role do internships and mentoring play in the academic achievements and work-readiness of neurodivergent management learners?
  • How can business schools foster neuro-inclusion as a leadership and management capability?
  • How can universal design for learning and inclusive pedagogy reshape management education?
  • How can constructive alignment more effectively incorporate the needs and experiences of neurodivergent learners and educators across different levels and contexts?
  • What can we learn from neuro-inclusive education in other fields? What best practices, policies, and procedures can be identified?
  • How do assessment and participation norms impact neurodivergent learners' educational outcomes?
  • How does neurodiversity intersect with other (potentially) stigmatizing attributes or sources of social identities, such as gender, age, race, ethnicity, sexual orientation, or other disabilities among management learners?
  • How do individuals with multiple co-occurring neurocognitive conditions navigate higher management education?
  • What teaching innovations have emerged in neurodiversity-informed business courses and programs?
  • How important is visibility and representation among academic and professional staff?
  • How may internalized ableism and embodied pedagogy affect neurodivergent academic and professional staff?
  • How do inclusive pedagogies engage with issues of masking, disclosure, and psychological safety?
  • How can technology, and in particular artificial intelligence, be meaningfully leveraged to support neurodivergent learners in management education? How can such technologies be used to enhance cross-neurotype collaborations and relationships?
  • How are higher education institutions and educators adapting AI-driven educational technologies to support neurodivergent learners in management programs?

  • May 13, 2026: Deadline for submitting 3,000-word proposal (including references) for optional professional development workshop in May 2026
  • November 1, 2026: Special issue submission window opens
  • December 14, 2026: Full paper submission deadline

item.title: Managing Under Political Turbulence
item.content:encoded:
Jonathan Doh, Villanova University

Srividya Jandhyala, ESSEC Business School

Yadong Luo, University of Miami

Grazia D. Santangelo, Copenhagen Business School

Political turbulence is on the rise, as evidenced most dramatically in violent conflicts (e.g., wars, terrorism attacks), volatile political transitions (e.g., dramatic regime change, cuts to government employees, new geopolitical alliances, coups), and geopolitical tensions (e.g., trade wars, democratic backsliding, sanctions). This escalated political turbulence exacerbates geopolitical risks for organizations and their stakeholders.

Whether anticipatory (e.g., fear of cyberattacks) or actual (e.g., ongoing trade wars, competition over territories), rising geopolitical risks affect organizations in many ways. The rise of techno-nationalism, driven by national security and ideological concerns, challenges the resilience of global technology supply chains. With the rapid development of AI comes misinformation and disinformation that further aggravate political tensions and ideologies. Tariffs, sanctions, and protectionist trade restrictions bring escalating compliance risks. Rising populist sentiment drives immigration restrictions and is creating a shortage of high-skill talent for MNEs.

Appel publié par Academy of Management Perspectives. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Managing Stakeholder Nationalism
  • The Role of New Technologies
  • Managing Corporate Innovation
  • Navigating the Race for Talent

item.title: Turning Implications Into Evidence: Actionable Solutions to Real-World Problems of Practice and Policy Based on Prior Academy of Management Publications
item.content:encoded:
Julian Birkinshaw, Western University

Thomas P. Lyon, University of Michigan

Denise M. Rousseau, Carnegie Mellon University

Majken Schultz, Copenhagen Business School

Mo Wang, University of Florida

Amid rising concern about the relevance of their contents, many scholarly journals mandate inclusion of a managerial implications section. This section may be relegated to a few paragraphs at the end of an article and comprised of speculative statements loosely connected to the paper's empirical or theoretical content. And there these unvalidated implications tend to remain, largely unaddressed in future research studies and having little relevance to practice or policy.

This special issue calls for original research that develops actionable solutions from previously published managerial implications. By developing actionable insights from underdeveloped or dormant implications, this special issue furthers the core function of any science: the development of a corpus of valid and reliable knowledge. An applied science has the added demand that knowledge be usable outside of academia.

Appel publié par Academy of Management Perspectives. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Developing actionable solutions from previously published managerial implications
  • Novel empirical or conceptual analysis of practice and policy implications
  • Real-world problems of practice and policy overlooked in managerial implications sections
  • Robust analysis providing specific guidance for practitioners and policy makers
  • Building on theory developed in Academy of Management journals to enrich and reveal nuances of their usefulness

Timeline

  • January 1, 2026: Call for papers opens
  • January 31, 2027: Submission deadline at 23:59 ET

Associate editors

  • Michael L. Barnett, Rutgers University

item.title: Open Call for Papers
item.content:encoded:
Academy of Management Perspectives (AMP) publishes papers that matter to managers. The journal seeks to realize the field's long-standing call for managerially relevant work. AMP papers must be managerially driven from the start, not theory-driven papers with managerial implications added as an afterthought. Papers rejected from theory-focused journals are not suitable for AMP unless they are fundamentally reoriented toward managerial relevance.

AMP papers must meet three core criteria: they must be RELEVANT, RIGOROUS, and READABLE. Relevant papers inform an issue of evident importance to managerial practice and/or policy. Rigorous papers engage in rigorous and original conceptual or empirical analysis. Readable papers concisely and clearly convey key ideas to a non-specialized audience. All three criteria must be satisfied.

Appel publié par Academy of Management Perspectives. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Papers that inform managerial practice and policy
  • Work addressing issues of evident importance to managerial practice and/or policy
  • Rigorous and original conceptual or empirical analysis
  • Papers accessible to non-specialized audiences and practitioners
  • Work grounded in evidence or robust conceptual frameworks
  • Papers offering actionable insights for managers and policymakers

Timeline

item.title: Agency in the Age of AI
item.content:encoded:
Paul Leonardi, .pop

Alex Murray, .pop

Frank Nagle, .pop

Nelson Phillips, .pop

Juliana Schroeder, .pop

Paula Ungureanu, .pop

Elisa Villani, .pop

Agency is central to organizational sciences and heavily debated. Assumptions about who can act, what acting requires, and who is answerable for results underlie theories of motivation, leadership, decision making, control, value creation, careers, institutions, and technological change. These views largely developed before intelligent technologies began participating in organizational action. As analytic, generative, and agentic AI increasingly participate in organizational action, intention, execution, and consequence—traditionally assumed to reside in a single human actor—are coming apart, and with them our settled sense of who exercises agency.

item.title: AI-Enabled Frontiers in Organizational Science
item.content:encoded:
Claudine Gartenberg, .pop

Sharique Hasan, .pop

Lamar Pierce, .pop

Christopher Bail, .pop

Hengchen Dai, .pop

Oliver Hauser, .pop

Hatim Rahman, .pop

Dennis Zhang, .pop

This special issue asks a fundamental question about artificial intelligence and social science: do we want it to produce faster, cheaper versions of what we already do, or do we want fundamentally new science? Returning to Organization Science's founding mission—Daft and Lewin's 1990 call to break out of the "normal science straitjacket" and March's "exploration of new possibilities"—we want to shift our focus to how AI is changing the production of science and how it can expand our knowledge, rather than merely increasing the number of papers through efficiency and reduced labor.

In this call for science, we seek contributions that reimagine what a social science research contribution is in an AI-enabled world, encouraging wild ideas and radical innovation over obvious incremental improvement. We are not looking for conventional full-length papers with AI-related content, nor "AI slop"—we want the innovative applications themselves.

Appel publié par Organization Science. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Synthetic social systems
  • New approaches to established research designs
  • Critical or boundary-setting work on the limits of AI-enabled science
  • Reimagining social science research contributions in an AI-enabled world

item.title: A Decade (2015-2025) of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): Trends, Reflections, and Realignments in Hospitality and Tourism Research
item.content:encoded:
Edmund Goh, Abu Dhabi Hospitality Academy, Les Roches

This special issue marks the tenth anniversary of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals by examining how hospitality and tourism research has engaged with the SDG framework since 2015. Although tourism encompasses all 17 SDGs either directly or indirectly, a significant research gap remains: many studies investigate sustainability themes without explicitly aligning their work to specific SDG targets or omit the SDG lens entirely. This disconnect hampers the sector's ability to measure progress and influence policy.

Appel publié par Current Issues in Tourism. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Reflecting on the First Decade (2015–2025) of SDG achievements and gaps in hospitality and tourism
  • Critical reviews of how research references SDGs and where conceptual or methodological gaps persist
  • Evaluating tourism and hospitality's contribution to all 17 SDGs, including SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) through community tourism, local sourcing, and food redistribution
  • Examining progress toward SDG 3 (Good Health and Wellbeing) through wellness tourism, workplace health initiatives, and traveller safety
  • Assessing SDG 4 (Quality Education) via tourism and hospitality curriculum transformation, sustainability literacy, and lifelong learning
  • Policy coherence and alignment of tourism strategies with SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions), focusing on governance, transparency, and ethical practices
  • Reviewing the role of SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure) in sustainable destination design, transport systems, and smart tourism
  • Integrating SDG 8 (Decent Work), SDG 5 (Gender Equality), and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) through inclusive recruitment, fair wages, and leadership opportunities
  • Advancing SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) via food waste management, circular hospitality systems, and sustainable event management
  • Strengthening SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) by aligning urban tourism, heritage conservation, and destination capacity management
  • Building SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals) through cross-sector collaborations among government, academia, and private enterprises
  • Linking SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) and SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) to energy-efficient hotel design, water conservation, and waste-water reuse
  • Exploring SDG 13 (Climate Action), SDG 14 (Life Below Water), and SDG 15 (Life on Land) through carbon-neutral travel, biodiversity protection, and eco-restoration tourism
  • Applying SDG 9 (Innovation and Infrastructure) and SDG 16 (Institutions) in AI-driven sustainability measurement, blockchain transparency, and smart destination governance
  • Embedding SDG 3 (Health) and SDG 11 (Communities) in wellness, resilience, and crisis recovery frameworks
  • Integrating ethical, cultural, and spiritual perspectives on sustainability to support SDG 4 (Education) and SDG 17 (Partnerships)
  • Reimagining the Future Beyond 2030: Regenerative, Technological, and Ethical Horizons
  • Conceptualising post-SDG paradigms such as regenerative tourism, circular hospitality
  • Examining the intersections of sustainability with digital transformation, big data, and tourism intelligence systems
  • Developing cross-SDG frameworks and metrics to capture interlinkages
  • Big data analytics, AI, and social media mining for SDG progress tracking and destination reporting
  • Comparative cross-national or longitudinal studies assessing tourism's SDG impact

item.title: A Decade After Brexit: Navigating the New Age of Barriers in European Finance Issues
item.content:encoded:
Steven Ongena, University of Zurich

Nam Vu, Miami University

Kiet Tuan Duong, University of York

Luu Duc Toan Huynh, Queen Mary University of London

A decade after the Brexit referendum, the financial landscape has transformed dramatically with increased protectionism, geopolitical tensions, and global economic fragmentation. This special issue examines how the UK's departure from the European Union reflects broader trends toward economic nationalism and regional separation, and how financial institutions are adapting to this new environment of barriers and reduced international integration.

The special issue seeks contributions exploring the long-term financial effects of Brexit on markets and services, the impact of recent trade policies on international finance, and how overlapping trade barriers affect equity and debt markets. Additional focus areas include regional financial inequalities, industrial policy effectiveness, institutional responses to fragmentation, syndicated lending disparities, regulatory approaches, fintech diffusion challenges, household financial behavior, and corporate governance changes among British and European firms.

Appel publié par The European Journal of Finance. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • The long-term effects of Brexit on UK and EU financial markets and financial services a decade after withdrawal
  • The macro-financial implications of Trump 2.0 trade policies for the UK, particularly in the context of renewed tariff regimes affecting British exports and imports and their global financial spillovers
  • The broader impact of overlapping trade barriers—including economic sanctions and retaliatory trade measures—on equity and debt markets
  • Regional disparities and financial inequalities in credit access and banking systems are exacerbated by trade and financial fragmentation
  • The resurgence of industrial policy and its effectiveness in promoting financial resilience under conditions of reduced international integration
  • Institutional responses and the capacity of international and regional organisations to mediate and stabilise an increasingly fragmented economic and financial order
  • Disparities in syndicated lending between UK and European lenders and borrowers, with particular attention to sustainable finance
  • The role of regulation and policymaking in reconnecting, or further decoupling, British and European financial systems
  • Barriers to financial technology diffusion following Brexit and the practical implementation of Brexit since 2020
  • Financial behaviour and household finance (e.g., financial flows, savings, investment decisions, overreactions, and reversal effects) ten years after Brexit
  • Changes in corporate governance among British and/or European firms, particularly shifts in board composition and the associated financial consequences

Timeline

  • March 1, 2026: Submissions open
  • September 30, 2026: Manuscript deadline

item.title: Addressing Ultra-Low Fertility and Workforce Shrinkage: A Human-Centered HRM Response to the Demographic Crisis
item.content:encoded:
Ingyu Oh, Kansai Gaidai University

Jie Wu, University of Aberdeen

Ho Kwong Kwan, China Europe International Business School

Hyun Jeong Kim, Inha University

Ultra-low fertility, defined as a total fertility rate of 1.3 or lower, is becoming a critical global challenge affecting human resource management across diverse regions including East Asia, Southern and Eastern Europe, and increasingly North America and Oceania. This demographic crisis is transforming HRM into a strategic imperative as organizations face risks of workforce shrinkage, declining productivity, and increased costs for talent acquisition and retention. The crisis requires rethinking foundational HRM frameworks and developing innovative strategies to build sustainable and resilient workforces.

This special issue seeks research that examines how organizations are responding to demographic scarcity through human-centered HRM innovations. It invites scholars to contribute work extending core theories such as the Resource-Based View, Institutional Theory, and Human Capital Theory to address labor market challenges, while exploring practical strategies including expanded parental leave, work-life balance initiatives, AI-enabled workforce planning, and inclusive hiring practices that integrate women, older workers, and immigrants.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Work-life balance challenges and family-friendly HRM policies
  • Gender inequality and its impact on fertility decisions
  • Cultural expectations and traditional gender roles influencing fertility rates
  • Flexible work policies including remote work and parental leave
  • Upskilling and reskilling programs addressing workforce shrinkage
  • Inclusive benefits such as childcare and fertility treatment support
  • Diversity and inclusion strategies utilizing underutilized labor pools
  • Innovative recruitment strategies and international talent acquisition
  • Human-centered AI solutions for workforce management
  • AI-assisted work-life balance and personalized employee support

item.title: Advertising Narratives: Transportation, Imagination, and Brand Storytelling
item.content:encoded:
Eunjin (Anna) Kim, University of Southern California

Robert Kozinets, University of Southern California

The proliferation of AI tools and digital platforms is transforming advertising storytelling into an adaptive, multi-authored process where narratives are created, circulated, and remixed across humans, algorithms, and channels. This raises critical questions about how stories function as persuasive and cultural resources when they are fragmented, personalized, and constantly recombined by algorithms and influencers. The special issue addresses gaps in understanding what makes advertising narratives compelling in this evolving landscape.

While established psychological mechanisms like transportation, empathy, and identification explain narrative effectiveness, these mechanisms are being tested in environments of short-form content, emerging formats, and AI-generated narratives. Simultaneously, cultural and ethical dimensions remain underexplored—including the role of authenticity, the risks of manipulation, the tension between entertainment and persuasion, and how algorithmic storytelling interacts with human creativity and consumer meaning-making.

Appel publié par International Journal of Advertising. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • (Re-)Conceptualizing advertising storytelling in contemporary contexts
  • Exploring AI-generated content that circulates alongside human imaginaries and narratives
  • Moving beyond 'do narratives work in advertising?' toward 'how do they work in contemporary media environments?'
  • Investigating the craft of advertising storytelling from the creator's perspective
  • Revisiting narrative advertising persuasion mechanisms such as transportation, empathy, identification, and mental simulation in fragmented and multi-platform environments
  • Comparing effectiveness of narrative versus non-narrative advertising approaches
  • Investigating questions about authorship, coherence, authenticity, and credibility when campaigns function as adaptive or transmedia flows
  • Examining how algorithmic and human-authored narratives interact to create or fracture meanings for consumers
  • Brand storytelling strategies where advertising narratives function as cultural resources
  • Researching the human craft of advertising storytelling built on relationships
  • The role of retro-narratives, nostalgia, and other human and cultural elements in advertising
  • Micro-narratives in TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts: narrative advertising strategies for persuasion in seconds
  • Examining forms, structures, and impacts of influencer storytelling around the globe
  • Cross-device coherence in narrative advertising across TV, mobile, and digital formats
  • Algorithmic sequencing and recombination of story fragments and implications for narrative coherence and persuasion
  • Brand integration challenges in short-form storytelling advertising and risks of the 'vampire effect'
  • Tensions between advertising messages and social and political issues
  • Exploring the dialectical relationship between brand storytelling and consumer resistance, skepticism, or counter-narratives
  • Story fatigue and manipulation: consumer overexposure, cynicism, and narrative distrust
  • Dark narratives: how persuasive stories may normalize harmful stereotypes or glamorize risky behaviors
  • Ethics of AI-augmented storytelling and deepfake narratives
  • Gap between brand narrative promises and reality in terms of truthfulness and accountability
  • How storytelling in advertising creates context for identity, authenticity, and the quest for the 'real'

item.title: AI and the Future of Advertising Creativity
item.content:encoded:
Yung Kyun Choi, Dongguk University

Tae Hyun Baek, Sungkyunkwan University

This special issue examines how generative AI is transforming advertising creativity. Generative tools are shifting creative work from slow, expensive human-led processes to rapid, scalable production of copy, images, video, and message variants. This technological shift raises fundamental questions about how advertising creativity is imagined, produced, evaluated, and valued in an industry where creative advantage has long been central to competitive success.

The papers sought will investigate how AI affects each stage of creative work, from idea generation through asset production to personalization and variant creation. Beyond the mechanics of creative production, the issue addresses how agencies, brands, and platforms are reorganizing creative labor, which roles and skills remain valuable, and how business models built on production fees are being reshaped as marginal costs approach zero.

Appel publié par Journal of Advertising Research. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How does AI change the way creative ideas are generated, selected, and refined, and where in that process is human judgment most valuable?
  • When does AI assistance widen the range of creative directions a team explores, and when does it narrow it?
  • How should briefs, brainstorming, and creative workflows be redesigned around generative tools?
  • What is the most effective division of labor between human creatives and AI across ideation, drafting, and refinement?
  • How does near-zero marginal cost production change what advertising creative gets made, and how much of it?
  • What is gained and lost when finished assets are generated rather than crafted?
  • How does AI-produced creative compare with human-produced work on effectiveness, quality, and cost (for example, click-through, attention, and brand lift)?
  • How does production at scale change media planning, creative testing, and iteration?
  • How does generative AI change dynamic creative optimization and one-to-one message tailoring?
  • How can brands produce thousands of variants without eroding distinctiveness and brand consistency?
  • When does personalized AI creative outperform a single strong idea, and when does it not?
  • How do consumers respond to creative that is visibly machine-tailored to them?
  • How are agencies, in-house teams, and platforms reorganizing creative labor around AI?
  • Which creative roles and skills are being automated, augmented, or newly created?
  • How does AI reshape the agency and client relationship, the pitch process, and value capture?
  • What happens to agency business models when the cost of production approaches zero?
  • Does AI change how creativity is defined, judged, and rewarded in advertising?
  • How should originality, distinctiveness, and craft be valued when execution becomes commoditized?
  • Does widespread AI use homogenize advertising creative, and how can brands resist sameness?
  • How should creative awards, evaluation standards, and quality benchmarks adapt?
  • What methods (field experiments, computational and multimodal analysis, large-scale A/B testing) best capture the effect of AI on creative outcomes?
  • How can creativity itself be measured at scale across large volumes of AI-generated work?
  • How can researchers study homogenization, distinctiveness, and the diversity of creative output?
  • When does AI-generated creative help or hurt brand building and long-term equity, and what guardrails keep it on-brand and effective?

  • September 1, 2027: Special issue submission window opens
  • October 15, 2027: Special issue manuscript deadline

item.title: AI-Driven Decision Making under Uncertain Environments: Theory, Methods, and Industrial Applications
item.content:encoded:

This special issue addresses decision-making in complex industrial systems facing dynamic uncertainty through artificial intelligence and optimization techniques. The issue seeks research combining AI methods such as reinforcement learning, generative AI, and digital twins with operations research and optimization approaches to manage manufacturing, supply chains, healthcare, and other sectors dealing with demand fluctuations and disruptions.

The special issue welcomes both theoretical and practical contributions demonstrating how AI-driven methodologies can improve decision-making under uncertainty. Particular emphasis is placed on interdisciplinary research with clear industrial applicability and the adoption of open science practices including data and code sharing to enhance reproducibility.

item.title: Beyond AI: HRM and the Work of the Future
item.content:encoded:
Sandra Fisher, FH Münster

Janet Marler, University at Albany - SUNY

This special issue examines how artificial intelligence and related technologies are transforming human resource management practices and the future of work. Building on two decades of e-HRM research, the collection seeks to understand how AI differs from previous technological advances, what new capabilities it offers for HRM, and what challenges or limitations need to be addressed. The issue welcomes both papers presented at the 10th e-HRM Conference in Muenster (June 2026) and submissions from researchers unable to attend.

The collection addresses critical questions about which HRM processes should be automated versus augmented through AI, how to mitigate concerns about bias and inequality, and how to maintain human agency and trust in AI-enabled systems. It emphasizes the role of academic research in providing evidence-based guidance on responsible AI implementation in organizations, ensuring benefits for all stakeholders including employees, managers, and organizations.

item.title: Beyond the Westminster model: a myth that needs constant refreshing?
item.content:encoded:
Leighton Andrews, Cardiff University

Matthew Collins, Cardiff University

The special issue examines the relationship between ministers and civil servants within Westminster model governance systems. It addresses growing tensions between political and bureaucratic cultures, where ministers increasingly prioritize electoral cycles and party interests while civil servants maintain institutional norms of impartiality. The breakdown of traditional constitutional conventions has led to public blame attribution, demands for personal accountability of officials, and increased risk aversion among civil servants, with significant implications for policy quality and governance.

The issue invites both theoretical and empirical research exploring how the minister-official relationship affects policy-making and delivery. Contributors may focus on either side of the relationship or the relationship itself, using qualitative, quantitative, mixed-methods, or conceptual approaches. While emphasizing the Westminster model, comparative studies engaging with other jurisdictions and broader public administration frameworks are welcomed.

Appel publié par Public Money & Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • The nature and dynamics of trust between ministers and civil servants.
  • The politicization of advice and its consequences for advisory quality.
  • Risk aversion, deference, and the suppression of honesty.
  • Ethical and conduct standards.
  • The role of special advisors in mediating the minister-official relationship.
  • The consequences of ministerial turnover for policy continuity.
  • The impact of organizational or departmental culture.
  • Parliamentary accountability and the personal exposure of named officials.
  • The constitutional position of ministers and/or civil servants.
  • Historical perspectives on the cycle of strain and reform in the minister-official relationship, particularly those that reflect the impact of crises.

item.title: Brand Activism at a Crossroads: New Theoretical and Empirical Horizons in Marketing and Society
item.content:encoded:
Antonella Cammarota, International University of Monaco

Jessica Vredenburg, Auckland University of Technology

Benjamin Rosenthal, Getulio Vargas Foundation

Brand activism has evolved into a mainstream corporate practice where companies and executives publicly engage with controversial socio-political issues. While existing literature has explored authenticity, ideology, and corporate strategies in brand activism, there remains a significant gap regarding its broader social and transformative impacts. The phenomenon has expanded across diverse contexts including non-profits, universities, CEOs, and consumers, and is studied in B2B markets, the luxury sector, and globally.

Recent developments suggest that brand activism is undergoing significant transformation. Since late 2024, many major corporations have withdrawn from diversity and inclusion commitments, scaled back activist visibility on social media, and reduced socio-political content. This shift, driven by rising populism, geopolitical conflicts, and societal polarisation, highlights a critical disconnect between existing theoretical frameworks and evolving real-world practices that scholars struggle to capture adequately.

Appel publié par Journal of Marketing Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Changes in Brand Activism Strategies – Is brand activism taking a new form? Are we witnessing the rise of less visible, more strategic, or quieter modes of activism? How do activist brands act in the current landscape?
  • Emerging Brand Activist Contexts – How, and to what extent, does brand activism manifest across different political, cultural, and geographical contexts? Particular attention is invited to the Global South and emerging markets, where civil liberties, media pluralism, or legal protections for civil rights may be limited or contested.
  • Institutional Actors as Activist Agents – What happens when universities, public institutions, public figures, or cultural organisations engage in activist practices? How do these actors influence public discourse, shape political debate, or redefine the boundaries of market responsibility?
  • The Transformative Effect of Brand Activism – Can marketing-driven activism lead to lasting social change, or is it ultimately limited to symbolic gestures and market-oriented performance goals?
  • International and Transnational Dimensions of Activism – How does activism unfold across national borders, global supply chains, and international institutions? What new conditions arise when brand activism is framed as a systemic, transnational commitment?
  • Backlash, Culture War, and Polarisation – How brand activism is affected when social and institutional risks emerge, corporate activism provokes ideological resistance, public fatigue, or consumer boycotts? How has the context of rising populism affected the conditions for brand activism?
  • Consumer Activism and Spaces of Expression – Has consumer activism changed? If so, how do activist consumers influence brand strategies, communication, and positioning? How do new forms of digital and/or offline spaces affect how consumer activists express their demands, critiques, or support? Are there changes in the relationships between brands and consumer activists?
  • Authenticity and Consumer Activism - How can we critically differentiate between authentic brand activism and opportunistic appropriation of activist discourse? Have consumers' understandings of authentic brand activism changed amid current shifts in the sociocultural context?
  • Artificial Intelligence and Activist Contents – How is artificial intelligence transforming the creation, personalisation, and dissemination of activist messages? What ethical, moral, and authenticity-related concerns arise when activism is mediated by machine-created content?
  • Shifting Channels of Activist Communication – To what extent has sociopolitical pressure prompted a shift in activist communication from open, accessible platforms - such as social media - to more niche, closed (not public) or offline spaces? What are the implications of this relocation of activism visibility and audience engagement regarding brand activism practices and social impact?
  • Activism and the Depoliticisation of Society – What are the potential connections between brand activism and the depoliticisation of society? Does brand activism foster genuine political engagement and collective mobilisation, or does it risk causing activism fatigue, depoliticising conflict and reinforcing dominant ideologies? How can we critically assess the boundaries between symbolic engagement and meaningful transformation?
  • Measuring Systemic Impact – How can we assess the broader societal effects of brand activism beyond corporate performance indicators or consumer responses? What critical or participatory methodologies are needed to evaluate systemic change?

Timeline

  • September 30, 2026: Manuscript deadline

item.title: Business and Cities in the Global Economy
item.content:encoded:
Valeria Giacomin, Bocconi University

Youssef Cassis, European University Institute

Jan Logemann, University of Göttingen

Chinmay Tumbe, Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad

This special issue examines cities as central agents in global capitalism and business expansion. Rather than treating cities as passive backdrops, the issue positions them as active institutional and infrastructural foundations that shaped how businesses, capital, and people circulated globally. The collection seeks to integrate perspectives from business history, urban history, and global studies to understand how cities mediated commerce, finance, manufacturing, and investment across regions and centuries.

Contributors are invited to explore how urban environments structured business globalization through various mechanisms: financial centers and trading networks, real estate and property investment, infrastructure development like ports and warehouses, informal and migrant-led trade circuits, and urban adaptation to crises and environmental change. The issue welcomes comparative work across world regions, with particular interest in underrepresented areas such as Japan, Southeast Asia, Africa, and Latin America, drawing on primary evidence and rigorous historical methodology.

Appel publié par Business History. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Cities as Nodes of Global Finance, Trade and Manufacturing: How did businesses use cities as hubs of commerce, credit, and investment in globalizing economies? What role did stock exchanges, banks, trading houses, and merchant guilds play in embedding global capital within specific urban contexts?
  • Cities, Real Estate, and Global Investment: How did property markets and urban real estate development become globalized? From colonial land concessions and foreign-owned plantations to the rise of multinational property firms, how did investment in land and real estate shape the growth, form, and business dynamics of cities?
  • Urban Infrastructures of Globalization: Ports, warehouses, transport corridors, and communication systems were often financed, managed, or operated by businesses. How did firms shape, invest in, and benefit from urban infrastructures that connected production and consumption across continents?
  • Migration, Informality, and Urban Globalization: How did informal markets, migrant entrepreneurs, and diasporic communities leverage urban density, mobility, and transnational connections to build alternative circuits of trade, credit, and labor?
  • Resilient Cities: Crisis, Adaptation, and Environmental Change: How did wars, revolutions, financial crises, pandemics, or deindustrialization reshape urban hierarchies? What does a long-term perspective reveal about the intertwined dynamics of crisis, resilience, and ecological transformation in shaping global urban capitalism?

Timeline

  • November 1, 2026: Manuscript deadline

item.title: Celebrating the 75th Birthday of Professor Kathryn E. Stecke
item.content:encoded:
Bernie F. Quiroga, West Virginia University

This special issue honors Professor Kathryn E. Stecke's 75th birthday by showcasing research that builds upon her substantial contributions to production research, flexible manufacturing systems, supply chain management, and the interface between production and marketing. The issue seeks to curate cutting-edge articles in active and emerging areas that reflect her legacy and influence.

The special issue welcomes high-quality submissions including empirical studies, analytical models, simulation-based research, case analyses, and conceptual papers. Manuscripts should demonstrate rigorous, impactful research with comprehensive literature reviews, novel decision-aid models, comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, discussions of real-life applications, and managerial insights.

Appel publié par International Journal of Production Research. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Advances in flexible manufacturing systems (FMSs), including machine grouping, loading policies, and production ratio optimization for enhanced utilization
  • Interfaces between production and marketing, including focal points such as advance selling strategies, pre-order mechanisms considering consumer behavior (e.g., loss aversion), lead time and price quotation modes, production-transportation integration in make-to-order systems, and competition/coordination in online marketplaces
  • Reconfigurable production systems, such as Seru, for improving responsiveness and adaptability in volatile environments
  • Supply chain resilience strategies, including adaptive ordering, disruption mitigation, and multi-echelon network design amid geopolitical and operational uncertainties

item.title: Centering the societal impacts of AI, social media, and emerging technologies in advertising
item.content:encoded:
Linda Tuncay Zayer, Loyola University Chicago

Jing Yang, Boston University

Shu-Chuan (Kelly) Chu, DePaul University

With the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence, social media algorithms, robotic interfaces, and immersive technologies such as virtual and augmented reality (VR/AR), the boundaries between technology, persuasive influence, and human activities have blurred. In this evolving landscape, the individual and collective well-being of consumers, as well as society at large, is increasingly at risk and warrants critical scholarly attention.

Consumer well-being is a multidimensional concept that encompasses individual and shared experiences, which can be manifested through cognitive, affective, and psychophysical states. Moreover, well-being is contextualized, with advertising holding the potential to enhance or diminish well-being at various micro, meso, and macro levels. At a broader level, societal well-being extends these concerns to collective equity, inclusion, and information integrity, highlighting how advertising technologies shape civic life, cultural representation, and public trust.

item.title: Creating value for citizens in public service ecosystems
item.content:encoded:
Paula Rossi, University of Vaasa

This special issue examines how public services can create value for citizens within public service ecosystems (PSEs), moving beyond traditional service-user and organization-centric perspectives to encompass the complex interplay of multiple actors, political contexts, and non-living elements. The PSE framework emphasizes systemic, relational, and context-dependent nature of value creation, recognizing how administrative and political governance shapes what is possible in public service environments.

The call seeks contributions that explore both societal value for communities and individual value for service users, addressing the dynamics and conditions that enable or hinder value creation across individual, organizational, and institutional levels. Submissions should advance understanding of public administration and management theory and practice, with both theoretical and empirical approaches welcome, including research articles, debate pieces, and new development articles.

  • Exploring the implications of understanding place-based public services from a PSE and value creation perspective

item.title: Creativity and copyright in the shadow of GenAI: Managing and organizing creative content in the digitalization frenzy
item.content:encoded:
Konstantin Hondros, Helmut Schmidt University/University of the Armed Forces Hamburg

Leonhard Dobusch, University of Innsbruck

Astrid Mager, Austrian Academy of Sciences Vienna

Patricia Aufderheide, American University Washington

Patrick Cohendet, HEC Montréal

This special issue addresses the intersection of creativity, copyright, and generative AI within organizational and management contexts. As GenAI technology rapidly generates novel content across various forms, it raises critical questions about copyright management, ownership rights, and creative practices that have previously remained underexplored in management and organizational literature. The call seeks to examine how regulatory uncertainty and rapid technological development create both opportunities and challenges for creative work.

The editors invite empirical and conceptual research exploring how organizations navigate copyright and creativity amid GenAI adoption. Contributions are welcome from diverse disciplines including management, media studies, cultural studies, sociology, and science and technology studies, and from various fields potentially affected by GenAI such as creative industries, journalism, digital platforms, and scientific research. The special issue aims to make copyright a more accessible research topic and foster an interdisciplinary community examining creativity management in the context of emerging digitalization.

Appel publié par Innovation. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Creativity in the shadow of GenAI: How does GenAI affect the creation and management of creative content? How do creative and artistic practices change through GenAI use? What role does copyright play in creative transformations?
  • Doing copyright: How does GenAI foster copyright-related practices within and across organizations? Who are the actors and actants doing copyright in GenAI contexts? How are these practices shaping the organization of creativity? How is emerging GenAI regulation affecting organizations and creativity?
  • Conflicts over copyright: How do conflicts over copyright foster or impede creativity? What is the role of digitization in these conflicts and their evolution with GenAI? How do these conflicts affect organizational creativity and technological innovation management?
  • Inequality and copyright: How does GenAI affect access to knowledge within and across organizations? Who owns copyright and how does GenAI influence ownership structures? What are the consequences of copyright inequality for creativity?
  • Alternatives to copyright: What are alternatives to exclusive copyright regimes in GenAI contexts? How do commons-based and knowledge-sharing approaches challenge or facilitate the management and organization of creativity?
  • Researching copyright: What are methodologically promising ways to investigate the interrelation between copyright and creativity in organization and management? What are specific obstacles in the GenAI context?

Timeline

item.title: Cultural organizations in transition—rethinking management, governance, and organizational change
item.content:encoded:
Lorenzo Mizzau, University of Genoa

Leticia Labaronne, Zurich University of Applied Sciences

Katja Lindqvist, Lund University

Yeşim Tonga, IMT School for Advanced Studies Lucca

Cultural organizations—including museums, theaters, festivals, and media production houses—serve crucial public missions by preserving and distributing cultural value. These institutions face mounting pressures from volatile funding frameworks, shifting government support models, and rising accountability expectations. Digital transformation and AI technologies are fundamentally changing how culture is produced and experienced, forcing organizations to reconsider their traditional management and governance approaches.

The special issue investigates how cultural organizations can maintain their public mission while adapting to organizational, technological, and sustainability challenges. It welcomes research examining innovative managerial practices, organizational structures, and governance frameworks that help cultural institutions navigate digital transformation, workforce changes, and evolving policy environments while pursuing their cultural and public value missions.

item.title: Data Intelligence Drives Innovation in E-Commerce Enterprises
item.content:encoded:

This special issue examines how data intelligence and advanced technologies are transforming e-commerce enterprises. The rapid integration of big data analytics and AI with e-commerce has enabled innovations such as dynamic pricing, personalized recommendations, and optimized supply chains. However, challenges remain in handling massive data volumes, processing both structured and unstructured data, and differentiating competitive offerings through algorithms.

The special issue seeks research addressing current bottlenecks in data-driven e-commerce, including operational efficiency improvements, data processing complexity, and reducing over-reliance on historical data. Contributions should explore how emerging technologies like AI and generative AI can enhance recommendation systems, marketing strategies, and cross-channel retail integration while overcoming algorithm homogenization issues.

This special issue examines Indigenous-led enterprises as drivers of sustainable regional development. Indigenous entrepreneurs worldwide create ventures that blend economic ambition with cultural stewardship, community well-being, and sustainability, often emerging from contexts of historical marginalization and systemic exclusion. The issue broadens geographic scope beyond Anglophone regions to include insights from Latin America, Asia, Africa, and beyond, recognizing Indigenous entrepreneurship as a global phenomenon.

The special issue situates Indigenous entrepreneurship at the intersection of place-based enterprise, sustainability, and regional development. Indigenous ventures are deeply embedded in specific lands, ecosystems, and social networks, operating as collective processes that integrate cultural values with business strategy. Many pursue triple bottom-line objectives combining economic, social, and environmental goals, challenging mainstream entrepreneurship paradigms to adopt more inclusive, community-centric frameworks.

item.title: Digital Nomadism and the Future of HRM: Rethinking Work, Workforce, and Workplace
item.content:encoded:

Stefanie Reissner, Durham University

Brian Harney, Dublin City University

Digital nomadism represents location-independent work performed with geographic mobility, raising significant questions for human resource management regarding how organizations manage workers with fluid employment relationships and changing work locations. This special issue seeks scholarship that examines digital nomadism as both a distinctive research context and a lens for reconsidering fundamental HRM concepts in the context of distributed, fragmented, and fluid work arrangements.

The issue addresses a gap in HRM research by bringing together topics often studied separately—remote work, global mobility, platform work, and transnational employment regulation. Contributors are encouraged to develop theory-driven research that demonstrates implications for HRM phenomena, systems, and practices, moving beyond descriptive accounts of digital nomads as a lifestyle group to examine organizational and institutional dimensions.

item.title: Digital Visibility: Design, Management, & Impacts
item.content:encoded:

Digital visibility—making oneself or others visible through digital technologies—has become central to modern organizing, yet remains theoretically fragmented. Algorithmic systems and digital infrastructures increasingly determine how individuals and collectives become visible, valued, or excluded, fundamentally reshaping coordination, communication, and collaboration. The special issue addresses how visibility has shifted from a secondary organizational feature to a primary mechanism through which strategy, power, identity, and modes of organizing are constructed.

item.title: Educational Immersion for All: Accessibility and Inclusion in eXtended Reality
item.content:encoded:

This special issue explores how immersive technologies such as Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality, and Mixed Reality can be designed and implemented to create equitable educational experiences that serve all learners. While immersive technologies offer significant potential for engaging students through interactive, embodied learning, many current applications lack adequate accessibility and inclusive design considerations, potentially creating new digital divides.

The special issue welcomes interdisciplinary research integrating perspectives from human-computer interaction, educational technology, accessibility research, and learning sciences. It seeks contributions investigating how immersive technologies can support diverse learners, including students with disabilities, neurodivergent learners, and individuals from varied cultural and socio-economic backgrounds.

Original research articles, empirical studies, case studies, and evidence-based methodological analyses addressing accessibility challenges, design frameworks, adaptive systems, evaluation methods, and inclusive practices in XR educational environments are invited for submission.

item.title: From emergency response to inclusive resilient governance in an era of crises
item.content:encoded:
Paresh Wankhade, Edge Hill University Business School

Giles McClelland, Edge Hill University Business School

This special issue examines how public organizations are shifting from traditional emergency response approaches toward more inclusive and resilient governance frameworks. It addresses the complex challenges posed by modern disasters, pandemics, and crises that require coordination across professional and organizational boundaries, while emphasizing the importance of trust, legitimacy, learning, and community engagement.

The issue seeks contributions that bridge disaster management, emergency services, and public administration scholarship, with particular interest in governance capacity, collaborative networks, and the role of individual job crafting in workforce resilience. It also recognizes that crisis experiences are shaped by social inequalities, identity relations, and uneven distributions of power and resources.

Submissions may be research articles, new development pieces, or debate articles that explore topics including multi-level coordination, leadership, organizational learning, digital transformation in emergency management, and the contributions of communities and civil society to building resilience.

Appel publié par Public Money & Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • How do emergency services balance centralized command with local discretion, improvisation and community knowledge?

  • What role do leaders and managers play in influencing the job crafting behaviours of teams and individuals?
  • How do public organizations maintain trust, legitimacy and accountability during and after crises?
  • What role do identities such as women and gender-diverse actors play in community resilience, mutual aid and local crisis leadership?
  • How do inequalities shape exposure to disaster risk, access to emergency services and recovery outcomes?
  • What role do communities, civil society organizations, volunteers and private actors play in building resilience?
  • How do governments and emergency services learn or fail to learn from inquiries, reviews and past disasters?
  • How are digital technologies, data analytics, AI, early warning systems and crisis communication platforms transforming emergency management?

item.title: From Shallow Waters to Deep Dives: Indigenous Theorizing on Chinese Family Enterprises
item.content:encoded:
Bingbing Ge, Lancaster University Management School

Hanqing Fang, Missouri University of Science and Technology

Alfredo De Massis, D'Annunzio University of Chieti-Pescara

Junsheng Dou, Zhejiang University

Winnie Qian Peng, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

This Special Issue aims to advance theoretical and empirical discussions on Chinese family businesses and entrepreneurial families by diving deep into them as contexts that challenge prevailing Western theories and as generative contexts for indigenous theorizing in family entrepreneurship. Scholarship has increasingly highlighted the importance of context in shaping entrepreneurial phenomena and emphasized entrepreneurship as a socially constructed process. Yet dominant frameworks in family business and family entrepreneurship—such as socioemotional wealth (SEW), agency theory, stewardship, and the resource-based view (RBV)—were largely developed in Western institutional and cultural environments characterized by individualism, contractual governance, and relatively liberal market economies. When these frameworks are applied to Chinese family enterprises, their underlying assumptions about self-interest, agency costs, governance logics, and resource valuation often prove misaligned, producing puzzling or contradictory findings.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship & Regional Development. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Indigenous Theorizing and Concept Development: Building indigenous theories rooted in Chinese cultural, institutional, and geopolitical conditions, drawing from Confucian ethics, guanxi logics, or dynastic continuity as explanatory mechanisms
  • Entrepreneurship as Constraint and Renewal: Exploring how institutional and cultural elements such as filial obligation, demographic legacies, and social perceptions shape entrepreneurial succession
  • History-informed research: Taking a history-informed perspective to understand entrepreneurship and family business practices, including innovation through tradition
  • Regional Heterogeneity: Incorporating regional institutional heterogeneity as a central explanatory factor in family entrepreneurship across China's varied development models and cultural norms
  • Purpose in Chinese Business Families: Theorizing Chinese family offices and their approaches to transgenerational wealth through multi-enterprise portfolios and informal arrangements
  • Gender and Patriarchal Paradoxes: Theorizing gendered pathways of leadership specific to the Chinese context and female successors' roles in patriarchal traditions
  • Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG), Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and Communal Orientation: Understanding how cultural embeddedness shapes responsibility, CSR, and legitimacy in Chinese family firms
  • Geopolitical Turbulence as Institutional Hybridity: Theorizing how family firms navigate global turbulence under conditions of institutional hybridity and restricted learning opportunities
