This special issue examines how gender diversity influences governance and public service outcomes. While private sector research on gender diversity is extensive, its role in public administration and state-owned enterprises remains underexplored despite its significance for equitable and accountable governance. The call seeks contributions exploring how gender-diverse teams improve decision-making quality, reduce groupthink, and strengthen public sector performance.

Governments worldwide have implemented reforms to increase female representation in public institutions, including quota systems and legal mandates. However, significant implementation gaps persist, with uneven progress in developing talent pipelines and achieving executive-level representation. This special issue investigates the actual impact of these policies on organizational outcomes and identifies barriers and enablers of women's advancement in public organizations.

This special issue examines how Generative AI and Large Language Models are transforming financial modelling and applications. It welcomes research that explores AI's impact on traditional finance areas including asset pricing, financial intermediation, markets and investment, behavioral finance, banking, accounting, and insurance. The editors are particularly interested in work addressing ethical implications, financial inclusion benefits, and regulatory changes driven by these technologies.

The rapid adoption of tools like ChatGPT has sparked renewed interest in AI applications within finance. While Generative AI shows promise for enhancing data generation, analysis, decision-making, and risk management, research on its modelling and applications remains nascent. item.title: Hétérodoxie logistique : explorer des chemins de traverse
item.content:encoded:
Adèle Fouché, Université de Tours

François Fulconis, Avignon Université

Gilles Paché, Aix-Marseille Université

La logistique et le supply chain management sont actuellement dominés par des approches normatives et techniques privilégiant l'optimisation de la performance. Cette normalisation risque de rendre invisibles certaines pratiques, acteurs et dynamiques fondamentalement logistiques. Le numéro spécial propose d'explorer une hétérodoxie logistique : une démarche scientifique interrogeant les angles morts du champ, déplaçant les cadres d'analyse existants et ouvrant de nouvelles perspectives pour appréhender la logistique comme fait social traversé par des enjeux historiques, politiques et culturels.

Cette approche envisage la logistique au-delà de la gestion des flux licites et visibles, incluant les terrains « sensibles » ou « hors normes » : économies informelles, réseaux parallèles, circulations illicites et systèmes clandestins. Ces contextes offrent des espaces empiriques pour comprendre la matérialité des flux, les formes alternatives de coordination et les logiques de pouvoir structurant les chaînes logistiques.

Appel publié par Logistique & Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Logistique dans les contextes informels, illégaux ou clandestins

  • Repenser les concepts classiques du supply chain management (performance, résilience, coordination, visibilité) à travers des configurations non-normatives
  • Continuités entre logistiques historiques (esclavage, colonisation) et systèmes contemporains
  • Organisation des flux dans des environnements contraints, incertains ou hostiles
  • Rôle des infrastructures, institutions et technologies dans les systèmes alternatifs
  • Modèles post-COVID-19 au-delà du juste-à-temps
  • Souveraineté et relocalisation industrielle
  • Circuits courts et logistique alternative
  • Construction et recomposition des frontières entre licite et illicite dans les chaînes logistiques
  • Implications éthiques, politiques et sociétales de l'hétérodoxie logistique
  • Renouvellement des cadres théoriques et méthodologiques en logistique
  • Logistique militaire et logistique des crises humanitaires
  • Histoire longue des infrastructures logistiques

Waseem Ul Hameed, Universiti Utara Malaysia

This special issue examines how artificial intelligence systems are transforming workplace interactions, employee behavior, and organizational dynamics. While prior research has focused on AI adoption and performance outcomes, this collection addresses the human-centered dimensions of AI at work, including how employees develop trust in intelligent systems, experience AI-mediated processes, adapt their behaviors, and navigate issues such as technostress, autonomy, and cognitive load.

The special issue prioritizes behavioral, cognitive, and psychological perspectives on human-AI interaction in organizational settings. It seeks contributions that explore employee experiences with intelligent technologies, design of user-centered AI systems, transparency mechanisms, and the creation of psychologically sustainable digital work environments. The collection welcomes empirical, theoretical, and design-oriented research across quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-method approaches.

item.title: Hybrid Human-AI Collaborative Networks
item.content:encoded:
Rosanna Fornasiero, CNR IEIIT

Luis M. Camarinha-Matos, NOVA University Lisbon

Xavier Boucher, Mines Saint-Étienne

Angel Ortiz, Universitat Politècnica de València

Hybrid Collaborative Networks combining human and artificial intelligence actors are becoming fundamental to value creation in digitally distributed ecosystems. These networks integrate diverse actors such as organizations, individuals, intelligent systems, and platforms operating across physical, digital, and organizational boundaries. Understanding their dynamics is essential for ensuring effective design, management, resilience, and sustained performance in changing environments.

This special issue addresses the scientific challenges of managing the life cycle of hybrid human-AI collaborative networks, including how such structures emerge, evolve, adapt, and dissolve. It calls for innovative design methods, adaptive governance models, and frameworks that integrate technological solutions with socio-human and managerial approaches to ensure effective human-AI integration, trust, and scalability.

item.title: Implementing the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive: Challenges, Opportunities, and Emerging Practices
item.content:encoded:
Diogenis Baboukardos, Audencia Business School

Begoña Giner, Universitat de València

Ronita Ram, University of Reading

Frank Schiemann, University of Bamberg

The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), adopted by the European Union in 2022, represents a major transformation in corporate sustainability disclosure regulation. The directive expands the scope of affected companies, introduces European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) covering environmental, social, and governance topics, and mandates third-party assurance. However, these changes present significant implementation challenges for companies, assurance providers, and information users. In 2025, the EU proposed amendments through an 'Omnibus' package aiming to simplify reporting requirements and reduce compliance burdens, though these changes have created uncertainty and raised concerns about potentially weakening the EU's sustainability leadership.

Appel publié par Accounting in Europe. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • The role of CSRD/ESRS to fulfil investors and other stakeholders' needs and be a strategic mechanism to enhance Europe's competitiveness, resilience, and capacity for innovation
  • Implementation challenges: Practical hurdles or burdens faced by companies in adopting CSRD/ESRS, including data collection, stakeholder engagement, and materiality assessment
  • Benefits of the EU transparency disclosure framework: The economic, operational, and reputational effects of CSRD/ESRS implementation
  • Interactions and alignment between ESRS and global frameworks: How ESRS aligns (or conflicts) with other frameworks, such as GRI or IFRS S1 & S2, and the implications, especially for multinational companies
  • Regulatory, institutional, and political dynamics: Institutional and political forces impacting the CSRD's evolution, including the role of EFRAG and EU member states
  • Sector-specific disclosure challenges: Unique hurdles and burdens faced by different sectors, such as finance, energy, manufacturing, or technology, in meeting CSRD requirements
  • Implications of CSRD for audit firms and assurance providers: The evolving role of auditors, the requirements for the development of assurance standards, and the impacts of the CSRD/Omnibus on the capacity of the assurance market to meet demand
  • Implications of CSRD for small and medium-sized enterprises and non-European companies: Direct and indirect effects of the CSRD/Omnibus on small and medium-sized enterprises and non-EU firms operating in or trading with the EU
  • Comparative perspectives: Variations in CSRD implementation across EU member states, including differences in national enforcement
  • Critical perspectives: Risks of greenwashing, standard overload, and compliance-driven reporting, as well as (threats to) the potential for the CSRD to drive meaningful sustainability outcomes
  • CSRD impact beyond the EU: CSRD's influence on sustainability reporting regulation and practices in non-EU countries and its role in shaping global standards

The Physical Internet is transitioning from theoretical concept to practical implementation through pilots, demonstrators and large-scale initiatives. This special issue seeks rigorous, empirically grounded research that offers actionable insights for managers, policymakers and supply chain stakeholders on how PI principles can be implemented, governed and scaled.

The call welcomes empirical studies, case studies, pilots and industry-driven innovations that address real implementation challenges. While conceptual contributions are considered, they must be strongly connected to practical implications and managerial relevance. Research should demonstrate sound scientific methodology while providing clear lessons learned for practitioners.

item.title: Indigenous entrepreneurship under colonialism and beyond: institutional negotiation, exclusion and resilience
item.content:encoded:
Himadri Roy Chaudhuri, Xavier School of Business (XLRI)

Mark Tadajewski, University of York

Andrew Perchard, Otago Business School, University of Otago

Zoi Pittaki, University of Dundee School of Business

This special issue examines Indigenous entrepreneurial agency under colonial rule, treating colonial institutions as both economic constraints and sociopolitical structures that shaped market access, legal standing and accumulation strategies.

It invites business historical accounts of how entrepreneurs in colonised societies navigated, contested and reworked the rules of commerce, especially where access to courts, licensing, property rights, banking and credit markets was restricted or selectively enforced.

Contributions drawing on primary sources such as company records, court records, licensing files, banking archives, trading accounts, petitions, newspapers and vernacular-language materials are particularly encouraged.

Appel publié par Business History. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Entrepreneurship under legal and financial exclusion: responses to constraints in courts, licensing, taxation, banking, property rights, labour regimes and credit markets.
  • Institutional negotiation and boundary work: how entrepreneurial actors exploited institutional gaps, navigated plural legal orders, reinterpreted colonial rules and mobilised intermediaries or brokers.
  • Resilience as strategy: cooperative, mutual-aid and associational forms; diasporic, kinship and inter-regional networks; and late-colonial economic nationalism and early decolonisation as sites of institutional reconfiguration.
  • Innovation as resistance: technology adoption and adaptation through which entrepreneurs offered alternatives that subverted or circumvented colonial hegemony.
  • Comparative or connected histories that use the shared conceptual lens across cases.
  • Submissions may use archival research, oral history, biography, microhistory, and comparative or connected history, and may engage postcolonial scholarship, subaltern studies, and critical perspectives on firms, markets and institutions.

item.title: Innovation intermediaries and capability-building: institutional, economic and social change in regional innovation systems
item.content:encoded:

Federica Rossi, Università degli Studi di Modena e Reggio Emilia

Elvira Uyarra, University of Manchester

Regional innovation systems face significant challenges from digital transformation, decarbonization needs, and economic crises. Governments increasingly fund innovation intermediaries—organizations like research centres, incubators, and technology organizations—to coordinate stakeholders and bridge gaps in innovation cycles. These intermediaries shape regional development through knowledge transfer and institutional adaptation.

This special issue seeks contributions examining how innovation intermediaries interact with regional economic change and institutional evolution. The editors welcome conceptual, empirical, and policy-focused papers employing interdisciplinary approaches and diverse methodologies, spanning economic geography, innovation studies, and public policy. Contributions should address how intermediaries foster diversification, support sustainability transitions, facilitate skills development, and shape emerging markets within regional contexts.

item.title: Innovation, Security, and Resilience: Firm Strategy and Industrial Dynamics amid Critical Infrastructure Disruption
item.content:encoded:

Dong Yang, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University

This special issue addresses how firms and innovation systems navigate security challenges facing critical infrastructure systems such as energy, transportation, telecommunications, and water. As infrastructure disruptions increasingly cascade through supply chains and threaten economic competitiveness, the intersection of innovation and security has become central to industrial dynamics and firm strategy. The call seeks contributions examining how technological, organizational, regulatory, and strategic innovations build infrastructure resilience while contending with geopolitical tensions, cyber threats, environmental pressures, and dual-use technology dilemmas.

The special issue examines innovation processes across multiple levels: firm-level adaptations to infrastructure vulnerabilities, sectoral coordination among heterogeneous actors, and policy frameworks managing tensions between openness and security controls. Contributions should explore how organizational innovations developed in response to infrastructure threats subsequently reshape infrastructure provision and adjacent sectors, and how innovation systems balance knowledge networking with security governance.

item.title: Innovations in Production Planning: Emerging Problems and Modern Solution Paradigms
item.content:encoded:
Mirco Peron, NEOMA Business School

Ibrahim Kucukkoc, Balikesir University

Daniel Alejandro Rossit, Universidad Nacional del Sur

Ilkyeong Moon, Seoul National University

Olga Battaïa, KEDGE Business School

Michael Pinedo, Stern School of Business, New York University

Production planning has long been central to operations management, with classical problems like scheduling and capacity planning addressed through mathematical programming and heuristics. However, emerging technologies—cyber-physical systems, IoT, digital twins, additive manufacturing, and AI—are fundamentally transforming both the problems planners face and the methods available to solve them.

These technological shifts have introduced new planning challenges: digital twin-driven real-time optimization, hybrid conventional-additive manufacturing systems, reconfigurable production topologies, circular economy objectives, and resilience under global disruptions. Concurrently, solution approaches have evolved from traditional optimization to data-driven methods including reinforcement learning, hybrid metaheuristics, simulation-optimization frameworks, and multi-agent systems.

Appel publié par International Journal of Production Research. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Digital twin–enabled planning and real-time adaptive scheduling
  • Production planning under sustainability, circular economy, emissions or carbon goals
  • Resilience-oriented planning under uncertainty, disruptions, and volatility
  • Advanced optimization methods: decomposition, robust/stochastic models, metaheuristics
  • Machine learning, reinforcement learning, hybrid AI–optimization for planning
  • Simulation–optimization frameworks and surrogate modeling
  • Production Planning problems associated with customized environments (engineering-to-order, make-to-order, mass customization)

item.title: Insights on the future of search-related advertising and artificial intelligence
item.content:encoded:
Kirsten Cowan, University of Edinburgh

Yang Feng, University of Florida

Seth Ketron, University of St. Thomas

Aidin Namin, Loyola Marymount University

Generative AI is fundamentally transforming how consumers search for and interact with product information and brands. Traditional search dominated by Google and SEO strategies is giving way to AI-generated summaries and zero-click searches, disrupting conventional advertising approaches and forcing the industry to adapt. This special issue seeks research exploring how advertising evolves within this transformed search landscape.

As AI mediates search experiences, three major shifts are occurring: search may transition from a pull activity initiated by consumers to AI-led experiences without explicit human initiation; search tasks are being delegated to AI, potentially bypassing traditional consumer journey stages; and AI interactions are expanding beyond functional, utilitarian purposes toward experiential and social dimensions. These changes raise critical questions about how advertisers reach consumers, the role of transparency and bias in AI-driven recommendations, and the balance between personalization and privacy.

Appel publié par Journal of Advertising Research. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How advertisers can effectively leverage AI-generated content and zero-click searches to reach their target audiences

  • The evolution of SEO strategies in response to AI-driven search algorithms
  • The role of AI in shaping consumer journeys and experiential marketing
  • How AI has shifted and/or will shift psychological mechanisms in search, including but not limited to empowerment, attention, memory, processing styles, and cognitive bias
  • How social, cultural, and other contextual differences might lead different consumer segments or markets to react to and utilize AI differently in search
  • The role of AI in relation to marketer-controlled vs. nonmarketer-controlled sources of information (e.g., ads or website content vs. customer reviews or social media) and consumers' relative reliance on each
  • The effects of AI on speed, locus of control, and effort in consumer search
  • The potential for AI-driven advertising to enhance or undermine consumer trust and brand loyalty
  • The impact of AI on ad pricing and revenue models, including the potential for more nuanced and contextual pricing strategies
  • The role of AI in facilitating more personalized and relevant advertising search experiences, and the potential trade-offs with consumer privacy
  • The need for new metrics and benchmarks to measure the effectiveness of AI-driven advertising campaigns, and the potential for AI to provide more granular and actionable insights into consumer behavior and preferences
  • The potential for AI to create more intimate and human-like interactions with consumers
  • The ethical implications of AI-driven search and advertising practices
  • The future of search interfaces, including voice-activated, image-based, and multimodal search
  • The interplay between AI-generated search experiences and consumer autonomy
  • The implications of AI-driven search ecosystems for market competition and brand visibility
  • The role of AI transparency and explainability in consumer trust and regulatory compliance
  • The sustainability and environmental impact of AI-driven search and advertising ecosystems

  • How the reduced visibility of paid versus organic influence in conversational AI affects consumer understanding, disclosure, and trust in recommendations
  • How the growing tendency to treat AI systems as social or companion-like partners might reshape the value of impressions, expectations of authenticity, and marketplace pricing for AI-mediated advertising interactions

item.title: Intelligent Knowledge Management Systems: Integrating Human and AI Cognition for Organizational Innovation
item.content:encoded:

Francesco Santarsiero, Università della Basilicata

Dagmara Lewicka, AGH University of Science and Technology

The intersection of Knowledge Management (KM) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming how organizations create, share, and apply knowledge to pursue sustainability. In this context, 'intelligent knowledge' refers to the management of knowledge systems that dynamically combine human cognitive capacities with advanced AI-driven tools and models to facilitate ethical, inclusive, and purpose-driven innovation. This Special Issue examines how intelligent knowledge management systems can enhance organizations' innovation capacity and align their efforts with environmental, social, and governance (ESG) commitments and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

item.title: Just sustainability transitions in tourism
item.content:encoded:
Raymond Rastegar, Griffith University

Rami K. Isaac, Bethlehem University

Andrew Mzembe, Breda University of Applied Sciences

Lisa Ruhanen, The University of Queensland

The tourism sector faces profound sustainability challenges including climate crises, socioeconomic inequalities, and biodiversity loss. While green transitions and net-zero initiatives have gained prominence, they often remain focused on technical solutions rather than addressing the political dimensions of change. This special issue seeks work that critically examines who benefits from transitions, who bears the burdens, and whose voices are included in governance processes.

The special issue advances the concept of Just Sustainability Transition (JST) to move beyond narrow carbon and labour-focused agendas toward interrogating fundamental questions about power, equity, and historical context. It recognizes that sustainability transitions in tourism are embedded in structural inequalities and shaped by global power asymmetries. The issue welcomes theoretical, conceptual, and empirical contributions using intersectional, decolonial, ecological, feminist, Indigenous, and multispecies justice perspectives to illuminate tensions and transformative potentials in sectoral transitions.

Appel publié par Journal of Sustainable Tourism. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.content:encoded:

Organizations in resource-constrained and institutionally weak contexts face significant challenges in maintaining competitiveness and innovation amid political uncertainty and technological change. This special issue addresses the underexamined role of knowledge management in enabling these organizations—including SMEs, NGOs, and entities in developing regions—to overcome financial constraints, limited technological access, and skilled workforce shortages.

Knowledge management has demonstrated capacity to enhance innovation, strengthen organizational resilience, and foster learning even under severe resource limitations. While empirical evidence from emerging economies supports these benefits, research remains concentrated on stable, well-developed environments, leaving underrepresented contexts insufficiently studied despite their numerical significance and potential for theoretical contribution.

item.title: Leader Behaviours and their Perception across Organizational Levels
item.content:encoded:
Iris K. Gauglitz, University of Bamberg

Peter Harms, University of Alabama's Culverhouse College of Business

Urszula Lagowska, NEOMA Business School

Birgit Schyns, NEOMA Business School

Kimberley Breevaart, Erasmus University Rotterdam

Leadership research increasingly recognizes the importance of examining both leader behaviours and their interpretations across organizational levels. Rather than treating behaviour and perception as competing perspectives, this special issue seeks to integrate them and explore how different organizational actors understand and react to leader actions in complex, modern workplaces.

The issue addresses gaps in current understanding, including how leader behaviours and their perceptions vary outside the leader-follower dyad, discrepancies between leader intentions and follower interpretations, and the effectiveness of leadership development programs. Contributors are encouraged to employ multilevel analytical approaches and diverse methodologies to capture the complexity of leadership dynamics.

Research submissions are invited across multiple areas: theoretical development of multilevel leadership models, investigation of underlying processes and contextual factors affecting behaviour perception, examination of interactions between organizational actors, and methodological innovations in measuring leader behaviour and perceptual biases.

Appel publié par European Journal of Work and Organizational Psychology. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Theoretical models proposing new or conceptually advanced configurations of leader behaviour and its perceptions, which consider the role of new working contexts in shaping leader behaviours and their perceptions
  • Multi-level conceptualizations of the impact of leader behaviour at multiple levels of organizations with a view to understand how and why perceptions across levels differ
  • Studies including models that explain why and under which conditions leader behaviour and its perceptions affect workplace outcomes, notably when leaders and others differ in their perceptions/(perceived) intentions or when behaviour is perceived as inconsistent or ambivalent
  • Research that investigates polarisation in follower perceptions—why perceptions of the same behaviour may diverge significantly
  • Studies looking at leader and follower behaviour and their interaction, such as how behaviours from one party trigger behavioural reactions of the other party and what that means for an effective collaboration
  • Studies considering the role of organisational hierarchy in how leaders behave and how their behaviour is perceived
  • Contributions considering interactions between personality traits (e.g., leader–follower trait congruence) in shaping behavioural expressions and perceptual accuracy; team outcomes of leader behaviour, for example, perception differences between team members and how this affects outcomes; and relative leader behaviour, that is, perceptions of how one follower is treated compared to others
  • Studies that develop and validate new measures of leader behaviour (e.g., behavioural indicators)
  • Studies that develop new measures that allow for the measurement of perceptual biases in leadership ratings and studies using advanced statistical approaches (e.g., polynomial regression analyses, multilevel modelling, pattern approaches)

item.title: Low-Altitude Logistics: Theoretical Frameworks, Underlying Mechanisms and Scenario-Based Applications
item.content:encoded:
Weihua Liu, Tianjin University

Lei Xu, Civil Aviation University of China

Kannan Govindan, Adelaide University

Yang Cheng, Aalborg University

Low-altitude logistics, enabled by drones and digital platforms integrated with ground transportation systems, represents an emerging frontier in logistics and supply chain management. While existing research has explored drone-assisted delivery and truck-drone coordination, significant gaps remain between rapid real-world experimentation and fragmented academic understanding. The special issue addresses critical questions about adoption barriers, network integration, stakeholder acceptance, business model viability, and sustainability implications of low-altitude logistics systems.

The journal invites empirically grounded studies that develop theoretical frameworks, uncover underlying mechanisms, and examine scenario-based applications of low-altitude logistics. Research should explain how organizations adopt and govern these systems, how they reshape logistics networks and service processes, and how they affect operational efficiency, resilience, sustainability, and public value. The special issue seeks to establish a coherent research agenda moving beyond isolated technological applications.

Appel publié par International Journal of Logistics Research and Applications. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Managing the digitally-savvy workforce: Human Resource Management in an evolving digital landscape
item.content:encoded:
Sanjay Singh, University of Dundee

Sateesh Shet, Northumbria University

Tanya Bondarouk, The University of Twente

Paresha Sinha, University of Waikato

James Duggan, Cork University Business School

This special issue addresses how Human Resource Management must evolve to effectively manage a workforce that is digitally fluent, technology-enabled, and deeply embedded in digital ecosystems. As organizations undergo digital transformation, a new type of employee has emerged with distinct expectations around flexibility, autonomy, continuous learning, and meaningful digital interactions. The integration of emerging technologies like AI, machine learning, and HR analytics is reshaping traditional HR functions including recruitment, performance management, and employee development.

The special issue identifies critical gaps in understanding how HRM can strategically align with and support digitally-savvy employees while addressing emerging challenges. Key concerns include digital wellbeing and burnout, ethical surveillance, algorithmic fairness, and digital inequality. The editors seek research that explores workforce planning for digital roles, work design for technology-mediated environments, and HRM frameworks that balance technological innovation with human-centric values.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Work design for digital flexibility, autonomy, and remote/hybrid work arrangements

  • Talent acquisition and employer branding for digitally-savvy employees
  • Performance management in tech-driven environments and algorithmic evaluation
  • Employee engagement and experience in digital workspaces
  • Digital fatigue, techno-stress, and well-being challenges
  • Ethics, privacy, and surveillance in digital HR practices

item.title: Marketing in a Divisive World: The Role of Political Forces in Shaping Marketing and Consumption
item.content:encoded:
Hanna Reinikainen, University of Helsinki

Essi Pöyry, University of Helsinki

Jason Weismueller, University of Western Australia

Rory Mulcahy, University of the Sunshine Coast

Political divisions are reshaping marketing and consumption as brands face mounting pressure to respond to geopolitical conflicts, populist movements, and ideological tensions. Divisive politics no longer remains confined to formal institutions but permeates lifestyle choices, cultural narratives and consumption practices, compelling brands to navigate scrutiny not only for what they communicate but also for what they remain silent about.

Multiple pathways allow political forces to influence marketing systems, including brand activism and consumer responses to sociopolitical positioning, political ideology affecting consumer preferences and attachment, and boycott or buycott movements impacting marketplace outcomes. Digital infrastructures and social media influencers increasingly amplify political signals while spreading misinformation, creating complex dynamics where brand silence itself becomes a political statement carrying strategic risks.

Appel publié par Journal of Marketing Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Political ideologies, identities and lifestyle politics: How do political forces shape consumption choices, brand perceptions, media use and information processing?
  • Explicit political stances, silence and neutrality in brand communication: When, why, and how does taking a political stance, or the refusal to engage in such, generate support, scepticism, backlash or disengagement?
  • Consumer activism, boycotts, buycotts and cancel culture: How do consumers mobilise for or against brands, and what determines escalation, forgiveness or longer-term market consequences?
  • Influencers, creators and political-commercial hybrids: How do influencers, celebrities, and other intermediaries blur the boundaries between promotion, identity politics, advocacy and civic participation?
  • Digital platforms, algorithms and misinformation: How do platform design, governance, recommendation systems and mis/disinformation shape exposure to and responses to political marketplace content?
  • Race, nationalism, populism and anti-DEI movements: How do contested political projects reshape inclusion, exclusion, legitimacy and representation in markets?
  • Ethics, responsibility and governance: What normative, regulatory and strategic questions arise when market actors seek to leverage political issues or influence public discourse?
  • Methodological and theoretical innovation: What new concepts, frameworks and methods are needed to study politics in contemporary marketing and consumption?

item.content:encoded:

This special issue addresses the challenge of developing new theoretical frameworks to explain unprecedented digital phenomena reshaping organizations and society. The call emphasizes the need for native IS theories that combine new concepts with existing theoretical foundations to explain the "why" behind digital phenomena, moving beyond descriptive accounts to deeper theoretical understanding.

The issue welcomes both articles that critically engage with existing theories to demonstrate their limitations in explaining contemporary digital phenomena, and articles proposing novel native IS theories grounded in the IS discourse. Theories should contain logically interconnected propositions and address specific "why" questions about emerging phenomena like surveillance capitalism, artificial intelligence, social media impacts, and other disruptions requiring explanation.

item.title: Net-Zero Pathways in Logistics, Transportation, and Supply Chain Management
item.content:encoded:
Paul Tae-Woo Lee, Zhejiang University

International organizations have implemented regulations requiring decarbonization of transportation and logistics industries. The special issue addresses net-zero emissions implementation through multimodal transport networks, where major cargo owners and stakeholders have committed to zero-emission transportation. AI and big data technologies are identified as catalysts for digital transformation and carbon reduction optimization.

The special issue aims to fill research gaps concerning net-zero pathway implementation, particularly around three key challenges: direct emissions reduction, higher capital and operating costs for green technologies, and establishing sustainable green energy supply chains. The collection seeks comprehensive and integrated approaches to enable logistics and transportation industries to achieve carbon reduction and multimodal network sustainability.

Researchers are invited to explore how AI, digitalization, new technologies, and policy mechanisms can support decarbonization. The special issue targets the research community and practitioners in transport, logistics, and supply chains to provide managerial insights and expand literature on net-zero pathways.

Appel publié par International Journal of Logistics Research and Applications. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Neurophysiological Foundations and Effects of Contemporary Digital Technologies
item.content:encoded:
René Riedl, University of Applied Sciences Upper Austria & Johannes Kepler University Linz

Jan vom Brocke, University of Münster

Jella Pfeiffer, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology

Robert Gleasure, Copenhagen Business School

The advent of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence systems (e.g., large language models such as ChatGPT, diffusion models, graph neural networks, or vision transformers used in healthcare, manufacturing, software development or finance), together with other contemporary digital technologies (e.g., autonomous cars, immersive worlds, and neuroadaptive interfaces), has fundamentally reshaped human interaction with information systems. As these technologies become embedded in work, consumption, private life, and society in general, the ways in which they affect human cognition, emotion, and social interaction remain poorly understood.

Appel publié par European Journal of Information Systems. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How does sustained interaction with AI-enabled systems (e.g., LLMs) and other advanced digital tools reshape neural networks associated with language, reasoning, and memory?
  • Does reliance on AI systems and other forms of automation/digital decision support alter attentional control, working memory, metacognition, or problem-solving processes at the neurophysiological and behavioral levels?
  • What are the implications of digitally augmented cognition for neuroplasticity, skill acquisition, and expertise development over time?
  • How can integrated neurophysiological and behavioral measures provide a fuller picture of technology-mediated cognitive processes?
  • How do individuals' brains respond to empathetic or anthropomorphic cues exhibited by conversational AI and other interactive systems?
  • What neurophysiological correlates underlie trust, reliance, distrust, or skepticism toward AI systems and other algorithmic or platform-based systems?
  • How does emotional regulation change when decision-making is mediated by AI support, algorithmic decision aids, or digital nudges?
  • What are the neurophysiological mechanisms of stress, fatigue, or overload in contexts of AI-assisted work and other digitally intensified work settings?
  • How does technological mediation in team collaboration influence the neurophysiological foundations of social coordination, empathy, and shared attention?
  • What neural mechanisms underlie shifts in authority, leadership, and influence when AI becomes a co-decision-maker?
  • How do cultural differences modulate neurophysiological responses to AI and other digitally mediated collaboration settings?
  • How do gender, age, or personality differences modulate neurophysiological responses to IS artifacts?
  • How might AI-driven systems and other algorithmic/persuasive designs reinforce or mitigate cognitive biases?
  • What neural signatures accompany ethical dilemmas and moral decision-making in AI-mediated contexts and broader digital governance settings?
  • How does long-term use of AI and other digitally intensive work systems shape neurophysiological well-being, stress, or mental health at the workplace?
  • How can neurophysiological insights inform the design of AI systems and other digital systems that are more intuitive and aligned with human cognitive limits?
  • What are the neurophysiological underpinnings of productivity, efficiency, or value creation in digitally mediated economic interactions?
  • How can genetic and neurophysiological approaches together explain individual differences in the adoption and use of digital systems?
  • Which neurophysiological tools are best suited for investigating contemporary IS phenomena?
  • How can hybrid approaches combining neurophysiology with computational methods enrich IS theory development?
  • How can multi-level research designs integrate genetic, neurophysiological, behavioral, self-report, and organizational data to address IS phenomena more holistically?

item.title: New Developments in Luxury Advertising: Artificial Intelligence, New Technologies, Sustainability, and Influencers
item.content:encoded:

The luxury sector is undergoing a profound transformation, marked by complexity, volatility, and new societal and technological challenges. Traditional growth models show signs of fatigue, while institutional pressures push brands toward more authentic commitments to sustainability, ethics, and inclusion. Simultaneously, luxury brands face a rapidly shifting competitive landscape, with changes in global markets, consumer expectations, and technological innovation.

item.title: New Directions in Influencer Research
item.content:encoded:
Veronica L. Thomas, Old Dominion University

Kendra Fowler, Youngstown State University

Influencer marketing has become central to brand communication strategies, but the field now stands at a critical juncture. Rapid technological changes including generative AI, synthetic influencers, evolving platform structures, and creator professionalization are fundamentally transforming the landscape, making many previously established assumptions potentially obsolete.

This special issue seeks research that transcends incremental contributions and instead examines how influence operates in contemporary contexts. The call invites scholars to adopt new theoretical frameworks, explore how technological and cultural shifts have altered influencer dynamics, and investigate emerging managerial challenges that will shape future advertising strategies.

Contributions should critically revisit core assumptions while avoiding simple replications of well-established findings. The journal welcomes theoretically grounded and methodologically rigorous work addressing evolving ecosystems, influencers as entrepreneurs, strategic implications, measurement innovation, and fundamental reconceptualizations of influencer theory.

Appel publié par Journal of Advertising Research. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How are deepfakes and synthetic media altering how consumers process and engage with influencer marketing?

  • How has the influencer ecosystem changed, or how does it need to change, to address increased opportunities for influence beyond social media platforms or the use of AI tools to facilitate content creation?
  • How is influence extending beyond traditional social media into commerce, entertainment, education, and hybrid digital physical spaces?
  • How do influencers function as brands, entrepreneurs, and marketing organizations rather than merely as endorsers?
  • What competitive threats do influencers face from other creators, platforms, AI generated content, or brand owned media?
  • How do influencers adapt, reposition, or professionalize as their audiences, technologies, and revenue models evolve?
  • How can influencers themselves be protected from exploitation, burnout, harassment, or reputational harm?

  • How can researchers capture spillover effects, halo effects, and cross-platform influence in influencer campaigns?
  • What new metrics or analytical approaches are needed to study influence at scale and over time?
  • How should advertisers select influencers to fit their specific strategic needs?
  • Are existing influencer typologies still relevant, or are new classification frameworks needed?
  • Where do existing theories of persuasion, social influence, and communication fall short in explaining consumer–influencer relationships today?

item.title: New Perspectives on Advertising and Promotion in Food and Beverage Marketing
item.content:encoded:
Kacy Kim, Bryant University

Junghoon Moon, Seoul National University

Lamberto Zollo, University of Milan

Riccardo Rialti, University of Siena

Food and beverage advertising has long emphasized nourishment, affordability, and convenience. Yet this perspective no longer captures contemporary consumption trends or the complex role of advertising. Many consumers adopt dietary regimes—even without medical necessity—as expressions of identity and self-esteem. Advertising reflects this shift by positioning consumption of "healthier" options such as gluten-free snacks, keto-friendly products, vegan substitutes, or diet beverages as lifestyle choices tied to self-image. Campaigns for plant-based milk, for example, highlight wellness and modernity, appealing to aspirational goals beyond nutrition. Beyond individual identity, advertising also conveys cultural and social values: halal- and kosher-certified products underscore cultural continuity, while fine wines, gourmet chocolates, and craft spirits are framed as markers of refinement and status. Increasingly, campaigns link food to place-based identity, such as agritourism promotions that emphasize heritage, authenticity, and local cuisine.

Appel publié par International Journal of Advertising. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Data privacy, trust, and consumer acceptance of AI-driven food advertising

  • Immersive and experiential food advertising (e.g., AR/VR tasting, hybrid in-store activations, branded pop-ups)
  • Sensory and symbolic persuasion (e.g., ASMR, soundscapes, anthropomorphism, emojis, playful cues)

item.title: Open Innovation in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Reshaping Knowledge Search, Collaboration, and Governance
item.content:encoded:
Saverio Barabuffi, Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna

Giulio Ferrigno, Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna

Letizia Mortara, University of Cambridge

Yogesh K. Dwivedi, King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals

Innovation increasingly depends on collaboration among diverse actors who combine and recombine their knowledge. While organizations traditionally select partners based on complementary knowledge structures, the emergence of large volumes of structured and unstructured data alongside artificial intelligence technologies has fundamentally altered how firms search for external knowledge, identify complementarities, and govern collaborative innovation. Recent advances in AI, particularly Large Language Models, enable systematic analysis of millions of documents to map technological trajectories and detect emerging knowledge fields, potentially reshaping the scope and modalities of knowledge search.

Despite growing interest in AI and innovation, understanding of how AI technologies influence open innovation processes remains fragmented. There is limited evidence on how AI affects partner selection, reconfigures knowledge search strategies, and alters coordination mechanisms within innovation ecosystems. While AI-driven tools promise expanded collaboration opportunities, they also raise challenges including transparency, algorithmic bias, and unequal access to computational capabilities.

Appel publié par Industry and Innovation. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • AI and Inbound Open Innovation: Partner Search and Knowledge Scouting
  • How do AI-based tools reshape the classic trade-off between search breadth and depth in open innovation? Can algorithmic scouting explore distant knowledge domains more efficiently than traditional methods?
  • To what extent can AI overcome local search biases, revealing latent complementarities across industries, regions, or technologies that human managers may overlook?
  • Can AI-powered analysis of diverse data sources democratize access to innovation ecosystems, or does it favor incumbents with larger digital footprints?
  • Orchestration & Governance of Innovation Networks
  • How do AI tools enable algorithmic governance of knowledge flows in multi-partner networks?
  • How can AI help coordinate heterogeneous actors, including firms, universities, NGOs, and governments, within mission-oriented innovation systems?
  • How are platforms leveraging AI-tools to shape technological trajectories and orchestrate complementors in ecosystems?
  • What are the implications of AI-mediated orchestration for value capture, appropriation, and transparency in collaborative innovation?
  • Knowledge Flows, Spillovers and Innovation Mapping
  • How do generative AI and Natural Language Processing techniques uncover tacit knowledge flows and early-stage spillovers invisible to traditional patent- or publication-based metrics?
  • How do AI tools improve the mapping of technological landscapes, identify "white spaces", and detect emerging trajectories to inform strategic decisions such as make, buy, or ally?
  • What methods best integrate multiple data streams to track cross-sectoral and cross-regional knowledge diffusion enabled by AI?
  • AI-Enabled Absorptive Capacity and Human AI interaction
  • How should absorptive capacity be reconceptualized when AI tools, such as LLMs, assist in the recognition of external knowledge?
  • What is the optimal division of labor between AI systems and human R&D managers in scanning, interpreting, and assimilating external knowledge?
  • How can AI support organizational learning while mitigating barriers such as the "Not Invented Here" syndrome, especially when AI identifies previously unknown sources of innovation?

item.title: Parenthood and Entrepreneurship: A New Research Agenda
item.content:encoded:
Shuang Lu Frost, Aarhus University

Magdalena Markowska, King's College London

Kai Roland Green, Aarhus University

Kimberly Eddleston, Northeastern University

Alisa Jno-Charles, Babson College

Haibo Zhou, University of Nottingham Ningbo China

Ulla Hytti, University of Turku

Nearly half of early-stage entrepreneurs globally are raising children, yet the intersection of parenthood and entrepreneurship remains underexplored in research. Parent-entrepreneurs face unique tensions between childcare demands and business pressures at individual, family, and societal levels, while entrepreneurship often intensifies rather than resolves work-family conflict. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for developing effective support systems and policy frameworks that recognize the dual roles many founders navigate.

The special issue seeks both explanatory and interpretive research examining how parenthood shapes and is shaped by entrepreneurial activity across diverse family forms, parental roles, and regional contexts. Key areas include motherhood and entrepreneurship (beyond work-family balance), underexplored topics such as fatherhood, single parenthood, and LGBTQ+ parenting, household dynamics between partners and across generations, and how institutional frameworks and welfare policies influence parent-entrepreneurs differently across regions.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship & Regional Development. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Performance extra-financière et transformation des supply chains : enjeux réglementaires, innovations et défis opérationnels
item.content:encoded:
Elizabeth Couzineau-Zegwaard, PPA Business School

Nathalie Fabbe-Costes, Aix-Marseille Université

Olivier Meier, Université Paris-Est Créteil

This special issue examines how supply chains are being transformed by regulatory pressures and sustainability imperatives. The convergence of resource scarcity, climate urgency, and increasingly stringent European regulations—including CSRD, CSDDD, and the Digital Product Passport—requires companies to integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance into their supply chain strategies. However, this integration raises significant methodological and operational challenges around impact measurement, traceability, and inter-organizational coordination.

The call seeks contributions exploring the tensions and synergies between extra-financial performance requirements and supply chain management from academic, regulatory, and managerial perspectives. Recent regulatory uncertainty, including the proposed Omnibus simplification package, creates new research questions around regulatory path dependency, stranded costs, and the trade-offs between anticipatory compliance and operational greenwashing versus greenhushing strategies.

Appel publié par Logistique & Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Sustainable regulations and supply chain management strategies: impacts of CSRD, CSDDD, and European taxonomy on supply chain structuring and logistics choices (relocation, supplier diversification), integration of ESRS in extra-financial reporting, compliance tools and methodologies
  • Circular economy and innovation: circular business models (reuse, repair, recycling), eco-design levers, contribution of digital technologies (blockchain, AI, IoT) to transition toward more sustainable or regenerative supply chains
  • Measurement, transparency and risks: impact assessment indicators and methodologies (Scope 3, biodiversity, human rights), comparative uses of GRI, SASB and ESRS frameworks, identification of greenwashing signals and best practices for credibilizing ESG commitments, disclosure strategy for objectives versus results in supply chain extra-financial performance
  • Extra-financial performance measurement and supply chain management: impact of extra-financial performance measurement on supply chain design and decisions, trade-offs between cost control, profitability and value creation beyond financial returns, does work on measuring and improving extra-financial performance stimulate logistics innovations?

item.title: Place-Based Strategy Design for Value Creation
item.content:encoded:
Carmine Bianchi, University of Palermo

Greta Nasi, Bocconi University

Bin Chen, Baruch College

Gabriela Lotta, FGV-São Paulo School of Business Administration

Public administrations confront increasingly multifaceted challenges such as social inequality, climate change, and digital transformation that standard management approaches struggle to address. The call invites examination of how place-based strategy design can foster sustainable value creation by integrating organizational capabilities with local ecosystemic contexts, moving beyond traditional linear and centralized planning models toward adaptive, collaborative approaches grounded in specific spatial, cultural, and institutional conditions.

The special issue seeks contributions that advance understanding of how public value emerges from interactions between internal strategic intent and external community demands, mediated by place-specific factors termed locus and habitus. It emphasizes the need for performance management systems sensitive to local diversity, collaborative governance platforms, and methods that balance inside-out organizational perspectives with outside-in ecosystem thinking to address wicked problems effectively.

Appel publié par Public Management Review. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Frameworks for place-sensitive strategic planning in public services
  • How public value emerges within complex, nested ecosystems shaped by spatial and cultural dimensions of place
  • Methods for enhancing collaborative policy design and implementation in place-based ecosystems
  • The role of local knowledge, culture, and beliefs in shaping strategy
  • Interactions between inside-out (organizational) and outside-in (contextual) strategy perspectives
  • Synergies and tensions between internal capabilities and external demands in co-design of public service strategies
  • Adaptive and intelligent performance management systems
  • Indicators and metrics for value-in-context and value-in-society
  • The role of citizen perception in evaluating public service outcomes
  • How collaborative policymaking can generate value outcomes aligned with equity, accountability, transparency, trust, and social cohesion
  • The dynamics of value destruction in public service ecosystems
  • Collaborative platforms for cross-sector governance
  • Orchestration of theme-focused ecosystems for modular place development
  • Meta-governance and boundary-spanning leadership
  • Governance responses to turbulence and building robust place-based public services
  • Interplay of formal and informal knowledge in ecosystem adaptation

item.title: Populism and Public Management
item.content:encoded:
Zoe Radnor, Aston University

David Walker, Oxford Health NHS Foundation Trust

This special issue examines the intersection of populism and public management, inviting cross-disciplinary perspectives from law, social sciences, politics and public administration. The rise of populist movements worldwide, spanning both left and right of the political spectrum, raises fundamental questions about how public managers and administrators navigate their responsibilities when faced with politicians whose values may conflict with liberal democratic principles and established governance standards.

The issue seeks contributions that explore critical tensions in public administration under populism: whether public managers have ethical obligations to defend democratic institutions, how they balance political responsiveness with professional integrity, and whether existing accountability frameworks adequately address challenges posed by populist policies. Contributors are encouraged to consider international comparisons and examine how different governmental structures and civil service frameworks respond to populist pressures.

Appel publié par Public Money & Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Are we facing the limits of traditional thinking in public management? Do public managers have a 'moral personality' with value commitment to liberal democracy and/or state continuity?
  • Does populism create a challenge for public managers to abide by good governance principles?
  • Are public managers obliged to defend the state from attack, rhetorical or actual?
  • Have public managers traditionally lacked 'voice' within the political–administrative interface and what challenges do they face with the rise of populism?
  • Is there a problem facing public managers if they are becoming answerable to politicians with antagonistic value sets or who may break the law?
  • How anachronistic are Weberian doctrines of 'responsiveness' in the face of populism?
  • What is 'extremism'/populism and can it be defined ex ante?
  • Do public managers observe/answer to a code that protects them against orders?
  • How far do existing doctrines of accountability accommodate answerability for extremist policies?
  • Do public managers have ethical commitments that equip them to resist political directives that might subvert constitutional order?
  • What lessons could public managers learn from international and comparative perspectives on populism?
  • Is the UK a special case with its uncodified constitutional system?

Timeline

  • January 31, 2027: Submission deadline for research articles and new development pieces
  • March 31, 2027: Submission deadline for debate pieces

item.title: Rethinking Regional Skills: Place-Based Capabilities and Economic Transformation
item.content:encoded:
David Morris, University of Nottingham

Carlo Corradini, University of Reading

Lisa De Propris, University of Birmingham

Duygu Buyukyazici, London School of Economics and Political Science

This special issue examines how regional skills function as place-based capabilities that shape labour markets, industrial development, and regional economic trajectories. While skills are fundamental to regional development, they remain underexplored theoretically and are frequently confused with education or human capital. Contemporary challenges like technological change, digitalisation, and green transitions are fundamentally altering regional skill demands and exacerbating regional disparities.

The special issue invites conceptual, theoretical, methodological, and empirical research investigating how regional skills are developed, adapted, and deployed to support economic transformation and regional development. It welcomes submissions from researchers examining advanced, emerging, and developing economies at various geographic scales, including contributions from early-career scholars and researchers from underrepresented regions.

Appel publié par Regional Studies. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • The nature and dynamics of regional skills formation and transformation due to technological change (skills creation, resilience, obsolescence, disappearance)
  • The links between education, skills transformation and job dynamics in the green and digital transitions of regional economies
  • The drivers and barriers of a regional skills transition for the innovation, growth and resilience of regional economies
  • The regional skill mismatch and skill formation in new labour spaces, e.g. green jobs, remote working, new platformised digital industries, gig economy
  • The enablers and barriers of a regional skills transformation for the green and digital transitions of industrial clusters and regional economies
  • Regional skills transformation and mismatch within shifting regional labour markets
  • Regional skills transformation and mismatch in regions as open economies: skills mobility, remote skills and migration
  • The opportunities and constraints of stranded and stressed regions: left-behindedness, regional low-skill traps, transitioning carbon-intensive regions
  • The links between vocational education, lifelong training and on-the-job upskilling and regional skills transition in the context of technological change
  • The opportunities and constraints of regional skills transition in emerging and developing economies
  • Policy debates and policy experiences to address the regional dimension of skill mismatch, skill formation and skill transition for just and inclusive growth

item.title: Smart systems and the governance of sociotechnical transformation
item.content:encoded:
Wanhao Zhang, Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU)

Younghoon Chang, University of Nottingham Ningbo China

Sameer Kumar, University of Malaya

Smart systems are now deeply embedded in various social contexts, functioning as sociotechnical arrangements that sense, classify, predict and intervene in everyday practices. This special issue seeks to understand how these digitally enabled systems reshape relations between humans, machines, organisations and institutions, and how they become consequential through design, institutional embedding and everyday use.

The issue addresses both how smart systems are governed and how they themselves participate in governing sociotechnical transformation. Key concerns include questions of behaviour, interaction, coordination, authority, accountability and power, particularly examining hybrid intelligence and human-AI collaboration. The special issue invites submissions examining smart systems not merely as technical innovations but as systems shaping governance, interaction and behaviour in organisational, institutional and everyday contexts.

Appel publié par Behaviour & Information Technology. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Smart systems in homes, workplaces, healthcare, education, mobility, public services and platform-mediated environments
  • Human-centred AI, hybrid intelligence and human-AI collaboration in organisational and everyday settings

  • Algorithmic decision-making, coordination, compliance and accountability
  • User adaptation, negotiation, resistance, appropriation and trust in relation to smart technologies
  • AI ethics, information privacy, surveillance, transparency and asymmetrical power in digital systems
  • Smart and digital health, care technologies and digitally mediated wellbeing
  • Digital work, algorithmic management, robotic management and the reconfiguration of organisational routines
  • Datafication, monitoring, prediction and automated feedback as modes of governance
  • Inclusion, exclusion, vulnerability and inequality in smart sociotechnical environments
  • Smart cities, digital government and platform-based public services
  • Comparative, cross-cultural or interdisciplinary studies of smart systems and sociotechnical transformation

item.title: Spatial inequalities and feelings of left-behindness: perceptions, imaginaries, and policy responses
item.content:encoded:
Max Roessler, University of Greifswald

Crhistian Joel González-Cuatianquis, Gran Sasso Science Institute

Stefania Fiorentino, University of Cambridge

Grete Gansauer, University of Wyoming

The special issue addresses how perceptions, imaginaries, and emotional dimensions of regional inequality intersect with policy responses to address feelings of left-behindness. Recent populist movements and political discontent in peripheralized regions have highlighted the need for scholarly understanding that goes beyond economic metrics to explore the subjective and narrative dimensions of spatial inequality and their influence on regional futures.

The collection seeks contributions examining spatial imaginaries, regional identities, and emotional associations tied to marginalized places, and how these shape both local perceptions and policy interventions. The special issue welcomes conceptual, theoretical, and empirical submissions from various methodological approaches and geographic contexts, with particular encouragement for early-career scholars and research from the Global South that explores how narratives and local agency intersect with regional development strategies.

Appel publié par Regional Studies. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Construction of narratives and imaginaries of and within 'left behind regions'
  • Significance of regional identities, histories, or social memories within peripheralized places for perceptions of the future
  • Material effects of spatial imaginaries, emotional associations of marginality, or feelings of discontent/left-behind-ness on regional development policy and planning
  • Epistemological assumptions and methodologies to examine imaginaries, narratives and visions within 'left behind' places and policy
  • Policy responses and best-practice examples to tackle feelings of perceived left-behindness, and/or empowering local agencies, contrasting feelings of neglect and institutional mistrust
  • The commonalities and differences of spatial imaginaries and perceptions of left-behindness across a variety of geographies (e.g., Global North versus Global South)

item.title: Sustainable Luxury Tourism: Opportunities, Tensions, and Impacts
item.content:encoded:
Kalliopi Chatzipanagiotou, University of Glasgow

Achilleas Boukis, University of Birmingham

George Christodoulides, American University of Sharjah

Raffaele Filieri, Audencia Business School

Luxury tourism is growing rapidly, yet research has largely focused on economic dimensions while neglecting broader sustainability, social, and ethical implications. A fundamental tension exists between luxury's exclusivity and the responsible resource use required for sustainability. While many luxury tourists express concern for sustainability, limited empirical evidence shows how these concerns translate into actual behavior or what trade-offs they accept.

The experiences of local communities and workers remain largely overlooked, revealing gaps regarding social inequality and regenerative development. Luxury tourism can amplify inequalities by concentrating wealth in exclusive areas while burdening local communities, ecosystems, and workers. Additionally, technological innovations like artificial intelligence and virtual reality are transforming luxury tourism production and consumption, raising questions about authenticity, cultural representation, and digital exclusion.

Appel publié par Journal of Sustainable Tourism. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

This special issue examines how shifting political contexts and policy decisions influence artificial intelligence innovation, governance, and investment globally. The call addresses the interplay between regulatory changes, technological development, and organizational strategy in response to evolving geopolitical uncertainties and governance frameworks around AI.

The issue seeks interdisciplinary research exploring how relaxed or tightened AI regulations affect innovation ecosystems, competitive dynamics, and cross-border collaboration. It welcomes submissions analyzing governance models, investment strategies, and the balance between rapid AI development and ethical considerations such as data protection and algorithmic fairness across different economic and institutional contexts.

item.title: The Agentic Supply Chain: Entering a new era in AI in Supply Chain Management
item.content:encoded:
Alexandra Brintrup, University of Cambridge

Thomas Choi, Arizona State University

George Huang, Hong Kong Polytechnic University

Dmitry Ivanov, Berlin School of Economics and Law

Recent advances in agentic Large Language Models have created new opportunities for autonomous decision-making in supply chains. This special issue seeks to advance rigorous research on how these AI agents can transform supply chain management by integrating perspectives from operations, AI, complexity science, and industrial engineering. While multi-agent systems have been studied for years, recent LLM breakthroughs now enable more flexible, scalable, and practical implementations that major corporations and technology providers are already exploring.

The special issue welcomes diverse research methodologies including technical solutions, modeling, empirical studies, and experimental work with practical implications. Topics span from using agentic systems for optimization and forecasting to managing risks, designing interorganizational coordination systems, and addressing technical and governance challenges such as trustworthiness, safety, and performance evaluation.

Appel publié par International Journal of Production Research. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Discourse on utilising agentic systems for complex scenarios in supply chain management: Risk and disruption management, logistics and supply chain optimisation, transportation routes, inventory management, quality control, demand forecasting, and warehouse planning and location, and cash flow predictions
  • Supply network design with agentic technology: Supplier relationship configurations, agentic digital twins to simulate inventory flows, sustainability implications across the supply chain, circular supply chains, supply chain visibility, and supply chain financing
  • Interorganisational agentic systems: Effective multi-agent negotiation and coordination, the design of mediative and persuasive agentic systems, preservation of organisational privacy during multi-agent communication
  • Hybrid systems: Integration of agentic systems with blockchain, IoT, Omniverse, and traditional multi-agent systems
  • Emergence and Complexity: Unintended consequences of agentic deployment at the system scale, governance, trustworthiness and safety, centralised versus decentralised control, human-in-the-loop agentic systems
  • Technical challenges: Performance evaluation, efficient task division, ablation analysis and back testing, sensitivity analysis, agentic architectures operating in high uncertainty environments, long-term horizon reasoning, overcoming hallucinations

item.title: The Disinformation Economy: Digital Markets of Influence, Conflict, and Polarization
item.content:encoded:
Carlos Diaz Ruiz, Hanken School of Economics

Sofia Ulver, Lund University

James Pamment, Lund University

This special issue examines the intersection of digital marketing, disinformation, and societal harm. The 'disinformation economy' refers to how platform architectures and advertising technologies enable actors to profit from spreading false information, incendiary content, and polarizing material. With billions of advertising dollars inadvertently funding fake news sites and influencers potentially profiting from radicalizing content, the business models underlying digital platforms create systematic incentives for disinformation production and circulation.

The issue invites multidisciplinary research exploring how marketing technologies, algorithmic systems, and monetization schemes contribute to disinformation spread and societal polarization. It also welcomes contributions examining influence operations that exploit advertising infrastructures, as well as solutions that can inform policy, business practice, and build societal resilience against online disinformation through interventions like media literacy, fact-checking, and platform governance reforms.

Appel publié par Journal of Marketing Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Whether and how programmatic advertising funds fake news
  • How do the recommender algorithms amplify incendiary content
  • How can AI-generated content be used to spread disinformation
  • Do the monetization schemes of the creator economy reward polarization
  • How do influence operations exploit marketing infrastructures
  • What initiatives and interventions can strengthen societal resilience to disinformation
  • What forms of platform governance can protect liberal deliberative democracies
  • What methodologies, including Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT), can be used to investigate disinformation on AdTech and social media

item.title: The Exotic States of Americana
item.content:encoded:
Alan Bradshaw, Royal Holloway, University of London

Joel Hietanen, University of Helsinki

Marketing and consumer research is extremely American on every level. Though consumer culture varies across the globe, what lies beneath is irreducibly North American. Consumer culture as a phenomenon is an American invention and export. Americana was in unprecedented ascendancy from the 1950s and 1960s, particularly with the neoliberal state apparatus that emerged in the early 1980s Reagan years.

Alternative historicizations exist, such as the Qing Dynasty, the Elizabethan court, and the Industrial Revolution. However, consumerism in its spirit, ideology, mode of subjectivation, seductiveness, excess, imperialism, and globalization is largely understood and experienced throughout the globe as fundamentally Yankee, as intrinsic to the US dollar itself.

Appel publié par Consumption Markets & Culture. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Histories of consumer culture as US soft power
  • Flattery and imitation: the keen attempts to reproduce Americana across the globe
  • American hegemony and the professionally polished field of consumer culture theory
  • Anthropologists, ironically or otherwise, explaining exotic Americana for the benefit of the rest of the world
  • Analyses of contemporary modes of Vassalisation
  • Resistances of all kinds: attempts to counter and break from American consumerism through experiments in commodification and hyper-consumerism
  • Submissions that are polemical, Gonzo, inspired by Baudrillard's America or Adorno's Minima Moralia or Why I Want to Fuck Ronald Reagan that are radical of heart and stylistically break with the norms and expectations branded into doctoral students

item.title: The future of creating and distributing value in digital health ecosystems
item.content:encoded:
Lauri Wessel, European University Viadrina Frankfurt (Oder)

Melanie Reuter-Oppermann, Maastricht University

Roxana Ologeanu-Taddei, University of Montpellier

Hannes Rothe, University of Duisburg-Essen

Sirkka L. Jarvenpaa, The University of Texas at Austin

Digital health ecosystems involve diverse stakeholders—providers, patients, and laypersons—interacting to shape care delivery. While information systems research has advanced in understanding the technological foundations, significant research gaps remain regarding how value is created and distributed in these settings. The special issue seeks papers addressing two core trajectories: understanding diverse forms of value that digital technologies create in healthcare ecosystems, and examining how value should be distributed among participants over time.

The journal welcomes both cumulative research advancing understanding of value creation and distribution, and contrarian studies challenging prevailing assumptions. Research often assumes large data volumes will generate substantial benefits, yet in practice clinicians frequently lack data in the required format, quality, or volume. Submissions should offer fresh perspectives on creating and distributing value in digital health ecosystems, informed by both information systems and adjacent disciplines.

Appel publié par European Journal of Information Systems. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • (Data-driven) change of professional roles, identities, and institutions in digital health ecosystems
  • The difference between creating value for intervention vs. for prevention
  • Design of inclusive and responsible digital technologies for healthcare and well-being
